translation_policy: Literal English renderings prepared directly from the pinned Sanskrit Śrīdhara Svāmī (Bhāvārtha-dīpikā) blocks. They do not replace the Sanskrit source and are not Vedabase translation or purport text.

entries.text:
Obeisance to Śrī Rāmacandra, whose lotus feet are tasted by the paramahaṃsas, who is the conscious nectar, and who dwells in the minds of devotees.

I worship that Nṛsiṃha in whose mouth Vāgīśā is present, on whose chest Lakṣmī is present, and in whose heart Consciousness is present.

I bow to that supreme abode called Śrī Kṛṣṇa, marked by the nine characteristics beginning with creation and secondary creation, the abode of the world.

I bow to Mādhava and Umādhava, the two Lords who bestow every attainment, whose selves are one another and who delight in praising one another.

In accordance with the tradition, and according to the order of what precedes and follows, this Bhāgavata Bhāvārtha-dīpikā is being expanded.

Where am I, dull-minded, and where is this churning of the ocean of milk? What atom am I there, where Mandara sinks?

I bow to that Mādhava, Supreme Bliss, by whose grace the mute is made eloquent and the lame crosses a mountain.

The divine tree called Bhāgavata has a seedling, is well-rooted, and rises with twelve trunks; from them it shines with devotion as its water-basin. Its shining branches number three hundred and thirty-two, its leaves are eighteen thousand, and it stands above all, exceedingly easy to obtain.

Now, not obtaining satisfaction of mind from the compositions of many Purāṇas, śāstras, and treatises, and being dissatisfied here and there, Vyāsa, after Nārada’s instruction, wishing to begin the Bhāgavata scripture, whose chief subject is the description of the qualities of Bhagavān, performs the auspicious act characterized by remembrance of the supreme deity taught by it, for the accomplishment beginning with the removal of obstacles to it: “Beginning with creation.” “The supreme” means the Supreme Lord. “We meditate” is a Vedic form in the optative of the verb dhyai; its meaning is “let us meditate.” The plural indicates the intention of the disciples.

He marks that very [Lord] by intrinsic and marginal characteristics. There the intrinsic characteristic is “truth.” The reason for truthfulness is this: in that Brahman the creation of the three qualities of māyā—darkness, passion, and goodness—having the form of beings, senses, and deities, is not false but true. Because, through its truth, even a false creation is perceived as though true, He is called the Supreme Truth.

The example here is “the exchange of fire, water, and earth.” Exchange is reversal, the appearance of one as another. It means that this appears as real through the existence of the substratum. In fire, the cognition of water is well known in mirage-water. In earth, such as glass, there is the cognition of water, and in water there is the cognition of glass and so forth, as appropriate. Or, in order to establish the ultimate truth of that [Supreme Truth] itself, the falsity of the other is stated: here this threefold creation is indeed false and is not truly existent. By the word “where,” connection with an apprehended limiting adjunct is excluded. By His own splendor alone the deception, characterized by māyā, is always removed in Him.

Note: the reading in an old manuscript is: “The cognition of water is well known in a desert mirage.”

He states the marginal characteristic with “beginning with creation.” “We meditate” on Him from whom the birth, maintenance, and dissolution of this universe arise. Here is the reason: in the effects such as space there is the Lord’s continuity as existence, and there is separation from non-effects such as a sky-flower.

Or, the word anvaya means continuity, and the word itarataḥ means exclusion. Because of continuity, Brahman in the form of existence is the cause, like clay and gold; because of exclusion, the universe is the effect, like a pot and an ornament.

Or, because [the universe] has parts, the connection is: its creation and the rest arise from Him through direct and indirect relation. Thus the śruti says: “From whom indeed these beings are born, by whom, after being born, they live, and into whom, when departing, they enter,” and so forth.

The smṛti too says: “From whom all beings arise at the beginning of the age, and in whom they enter dissolution again at the end of the age,” and so forth.

Then, since the intended object is to be meditated upon as the cause of the world because He is its cause, is primordial nature meant? No, he says: “the conscious one”—Him who is conscious. The śruti says: “He thought, ‘Let me create the worlds’; He created these worlds,” and reasoning also says that the effect of seeing is not something without sound.

Then is the individual soul to be meditated upon? No, he says: “self-ruling”—Him who shines by himself. This means that His knowledge is established by itself.

Then is Brahmā, Hiraṇyagarbha, to be meditated upon, because the śruti says: “Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning; he alone was born as the lord of what exists”? No, he says “by Him”: He made this Brahman manifest even to Brahmā, the first poet.

The śruti says: “He who first fashioned Brahmā, who indeed delivered the Veda to him—to that God who illumines the understanding of the self, I, desiring liberation, take refuge.”

It may be objected that Brahmā’s study of the Veda from another is not known. True; but He made it manifest to him through the mind, through the heart. By making the activity of the intellect’s modification begin, the meaning of Gāyatrī is shown. He will indeed say later: “By whom Sarasvatī, impelled before, spreading out the true remembrance of the unborn one in the heart, appeared from him bearing its own characteristic—may that foremost of seers be gracious to me.”

It may be objected that Brahmā himself could apprehend it by the rule of awakening after sleep. He says no: “in whom the sages are bewildered.” Therefore, because even Brahmā’s knowledge is dependent on another, the Supreme Lord alone, whose knowledge is established by Himself, is the cause of the world. For this very reason He is truth, because He gives existence to the non-real, and He is the ultimate truth; and, because He is omniscient, He is the one in whom deception is removed. By beginning with “we meditate,” the Purāṇa is shown to be in the form of the brahma-vidyā called Gāyatrī.

As stated in the Matsya Purāṇa: “Where, taking Gāyatrī as its subject, the expansion of dharma is described, and which includes the killing of Vṛtrāsura—that is accepted as the Bhāgavata. Whoever writes it and gives it, together with a golden lion, on the full moon of Proṣṭhapadā, goes to the supreme abode. The Purāṇa is proclaimed as eighteen thousand.”

In another Purāṇa: “The book of eighteen thousand [verses], equal to twelve skandhas, in which there is the Hayaśīrṣa brahma-vidyā and also the killing of Vṛtra, and which begins with Gāyatrī—that indeed they know as the Bhāgavata.”

In the Padma Purāṇa, Gautama says to Ambarīṣa: “O Ambarīṣa, hear daily the Bhāgavata spoken by Śuka. Read it even with your own mouth if you desire the destruction of worldly existence.” Therefore there is no reason to suspect that there is another scripture called the Bhāgavata.

Now, to turn the hearers toward it, he displays the superiority of the Bhāgavata over all scriptures dealing with the three kāṇḍas, saying “dharma.” Here, in this beautiful Bhāgavata, the highest dharma is explained. The reason for its being highest is that all deception marked by the intention of fruit has been completely abandoned in it. By the prefix pra, even the intention of liberation is rejected. Although dharma characterized only by worship of the Lord is being explained, the supremacy of dharma even with respect to the qualified subject is stated.

“For the non-envious”: envy is the inability to tolerate another’s excellence; [the phrase means] for those free from it. “Of the good”: of those compassionate toward beings. Thus its superiority over the scriptures concerned with the karma-kāṇḍa has been stated.

He states its superiority even over the scriptures concerned with the jñāna-kāṇḍa with “that which is to be known.” The object to be known is the real, ultimate object, not, as for the Vaiśeṣikas, an object in the form of substance, quality, and so forth. Or, by the word “real,” the individual soul, which is a portion of reality; māyā, which is the power of reality; and the universe, which is the effect of reality, are all meant. All of that is itself reality, not separate from it, and it can be known without effort.

What follows from that? He says: “bestowing auspiciousness,” bestowing supreme happiness, and also uprooting the three afflictions beginning with the affliction of the self. Thus its superiority over the scriptures concerned with the jñāna-kāṇḍa is shown.

He states superiority with respect to the author as well. It was first composed briefly by the great sage Śrī Nārāyaṇa.

He states superiority over the subject of the devatā-kāṇḍa with “what indeed.” By the other scriptures and the means taught by them, is Īśvara perhaps restrained and made firm in the heart immediately? The word vā is used concessively: rather, only somehow, after delay. But here, for those who desire to hear, He is restrained immediately at that very moment.

If this is so, why do all people not hear it? He says: “by the meritorious.” The desire to hear does not arise without merit. Therefore, because here the meaning of all three kāṇḍas is taught properly, this alone is superior to all scriptures; therefore the intention is that this alone should always be heard.

Now hearing it is prescribed not only because it is superior to all scriptures; this is also the fruit of all scriptures. Therefore he says that it should be served with supreme respect: “the fruit of the desire tree of the Vedas.”

The nigama is the Veda. It itself is the desire tree because it is the means of all the aims of human life; its fruit is the scripture called the Bhāgavata. That fruit was brought from Vaikuṇṭha by Nārada and given to me. I placed it in Śuka’s mouth. From his mouth it fell upon the earth in the form of the succession of sprouts—disciples, disciples’ disciples, and so on—descending gradually and without interruption. It did not fall from a height and shatter; that is the meaning. The future is indicated as though it were past, because of the scripture’s activity beginning in the future.

Therefore it is joined with a liquid in the form of nectar. In the world it is well known that a fruit touched by Śuka’s mouth becomes sweet like nectar. Here Śuka is the sage.

Nectar is supreme bliss; that alone is the liquid, the rasa. The śruti says: “He is rasa; having obtained rasa indeed, this person becomes blissful.” Therefore, O connoisseurs, O knowers of rasa, and among them O bhāvukas, O those skilled in the experience of a particular rasa—“fallen upon the earth” expresses the gaining of what is otherwise difficult to obtain—drink repeatedly this fruit called the Bhāgavata.

It may be objected: after leaving aside the skin, stone, and so forth, the juice is drunk from a fruit; how then is the fruit itself to be drunk? He says: “the form of rasa.” Since the fruit is itself the form of rasa, and since it has no rejectable portion such as skin and stone, drink the whole fruit itself. Here, because identity with rasa is intended, and possession of rasa is not intended, the word rasa is used without the possessive suffix, and the fruit is put in grammatical apposition to rasa. If “fruit” alone were stated, drinking would be impossible and the rejectable portion would be implied. To remove that, “rasa” is stated; and if “rasa” alone were stated, the fallen rasa could not be drunk, so “fruit” is to be understood.

Nor is the drinking of the nectar of devotion to be abandoned even in liberation. “Ālayam” means dissolution, liberation; the prefix ā has the sense of pervasion, “extending through liberation.” This is not neglected by the liberated, as heavenly happiness is; it is indeed served. He will say: “The sages who delight in the self, who are free even from bondage, perform causeless devotion to the Lord of mighty strides; such are the qualities of Hari.”

Thus, by these three verses, having turned the hearers toward the scripture that is about to be begun—through the excellence of its subject, purpose, and so forth, preceded by remembrance of the chosen deity, and through the ease with which it can be served—he begins the scripture with “at Naimiṣa.”

The rim of the mind-made wheel created and cast forth by Brahmā becomes worn away and blunted wherever it breaks; that is Naimiṣa, Naimiṣa itself being called Naimiṣa. Thus the Vāyu [Purāṇa] says: “This mind-made wheel created by me is cast forth. The place where its rim is worn away is the auspicious land of austerity.” Having said this, the Grandfather created a mind-made wheel shining like the sun; bowing to the Great Lord, he cast it forth. Those very delighted brāhmaṇas, bowing to the Lord of the worlds, went to the place where the rim of that wheel was worn away. That forest, famous through that event as Naimiṣa, is honored by sages.

For the reading “Naimiṣa,” the statement of the Varāha Purāṇa is to be seen. The Lord said to the sage Gauramukha: “Having done this, the Lord then said to the sage Gauramukha: ‘In a moment the army of the demon was destroyed by this. Therefore this forest will be known as Naimiṣāraṇya; truly it will be especially distinguished for brāhmaṇas.’”

“Animiṣa” is Śrī Viṣṇu, because His sight is not lost or closed; [Naimiṣa is] in His sacred field. Thus here itself Śaunaka and the others say: “In this Vaiṣṇava field.” “Svaḥ” is heaven; because Hari is sung in heaven, He is Svargāya. That alone is the world, the dwelling-place of devotees; “to Him” means for attaining it.

They sat down for a sattra, an undertaking whose period of observance was a thousand years. Or, “they sat” means “they performed it.” Because the verbal force of √ās is not intended, its suffix is uttered merely to express the suffixes in expressions such as “one should take,” “one should pour out,” and “one should approach.”

Those whose fires were offered at evening alone were those whose fires had been offered. Or, they were those whose fires had been offered with what is offered—curd and so forth. Or, they were those whose fires had been offered at morning alone. By this the completeness of the daily and occasional fire-offerings is shown. They asked what follows out of respect.

To ask the things they wished to know, they state Sūta’s extraordinary knowledge of all the scriptures in three verses. Itihāsa means the Mahābhārata and the rest, together with the traditions associated with them. They were not merely studied; they were also narrated and explained. The dharmaśāstras too were known.

What more? “Those which…” Vyāsa is the best among the learned; he knows the Vedas. He knows the two Brahmans, qualified and unqualified; hence he is called one who knows the higher and the lower. “You know”: you understand. “O gentle one”: O good man. [You know] through their grace. He states the cause of knowledge of the truth with “they would speak”: one who is affectionate would indeed speak even what is secret.
Directly means with the straightforwardness of the text. Exclusively means the unfailing means of the highest good.

He says that others should not determine it through a long period by hearing many scriptures and so forth: “generally.” O gentle Sābhya, in this age of Kali people are short-lived; among them they are dull, among the dull they are lazy, among the lazy they are very dull-minded, among those very dull-minded they are unfortunate, among the unfortunate they are crowded with obstacles, and among those obstructed they are afflicted by diseases and so forth.

Nor is the result accomplished merely by hearing many scriptures; this is what they say with “many.” “Many actions” means those in which there are many actions to be performed. “Having extracted” means having properly drawn out. By the statement thus extracted, the self—the intellect—becomes completely pacified.

Another question: “Sūta, you know,” in five verses. “May good be yours” is a blessing arising from eagerness. A blessing spoken at length would obstruct the account of Viṣṇu; therefore it is stated briefly. Thus it is said: “That is loss, that is a great breach, that is delusion, and that is confusion—when one does not think of Vāsudeva even for a moment or an instant.”

Bhagavān is one endowed with unsurpassed sovereignty and the other divine qualities. Those in whom Bhagavān, whose form is Being, is present as the object of worship are Sātvatas, devotees. The suffix aṇ is used in its own sense, as in rākṣasa and vāyasa. The form of the word is according to the ancient usage. Thus the word Sātvata is formed. He is their lord, their protector. He was born in Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva, for the special purpose that Vasudeva desired to accomplish.
O Sūta, O dear one, you ought to narrate this to us. In general, His descent is for the welfare of beings—for their protection—and for their prosperity.

While describing that power, they reveal their eagerness to hear His fame with the three verses beginning “having fallen.” “Having fallen into worldly existence” means having entered it. Even one who utters [the name] helplessly is freed from worldly existence; the reason here is that even fear itself flees from the name.

Moreover, those whose refuge is His foot, and for whom peace is the path or the resort—those sages, served merely by being near them, purify immediately. The Svar-dhunī is the Gaṅgā. Its waters have flowed forth from that foot and do not remain there. Therefore, though they purify through connection with that foot, they purify through repeated service, not immediately. By this the superiority of the sages is stated.

The fame of Him whose actions are worthy of praise by holy verses is to be praised. It removes the impurity of Kali and quiets the suffering of worldly existence.
Another question: “His.” The deeds are noble and great, beginning with the creation of the universe; [they are performed] by sages such as Nārada. “Forms” means forms such as Brahmā and Rudra.

Now, in another question. “Stories of incarnations” means the stories of the Matsya and other incarnations that appear at their respective times for the sake of maintenance. “Freely” means performing pastimes at will. It should be understood that, since the question about the purpose of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s incarnation has arisen, the question about His deeds has arisen as well.

With extreme eagerness, again desiring to hear only those deeds, they disclose the absence of satisfaction in themselves: “But we.” We are satisfied by yoga, sacrifice, and the rest. “The highest”: that from whom darkness departs. “Verse”: that whose verse is such. “In prowess” means that in the particular excellence of His prowess we are not satisfied; we do not consider it enough. The reason is “for those hearing the prowess.” Or, let others be satisfied, but we are not; this is the connection of the word “but.”

The sense is this: fullness is of three kinds—through filling the stomach and so forth, through ignorance of rasa, or through the absence of a special taste. Here, with “for those hearing,” filling is denied because the ear is space. With “knowers of rasa,” satisfaction like that of an animal through ignorance is denied. As in eating sugarcane, satisfaction through the absence of another taste is denied. “At every step” means at every moment; [His deeds are] sweeter than even what is sweet.

Therefore, with the intention “let him narrate the deeds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,” they say “has done.” “Beyond mortals” means deeds that surpass mortals, such as lifting Govardhana. The meaning is that they are impossible among human beings.

It may be objected: for those occupied with sacrifice, teaching, and the like, where could an opportunity to hear this arise? They say “Kali.” Knowing that Kali has arrived, and desiring to go to Viṣṇu’s abode out of fear of it, they are seated here in this Vaiṣṇava field on the occasion of the long sattra. They have obtained an opportunity in the story of Hari.

At this time, your being seen by us has itself been brought about by the Lord; they praise it with “you.” For those desiring to cross Kali, meaning worldly existence, and desiring to cross the difficult ocean as a ship’s captain [crosses it].

Another question: “Speak.” [You are] the protector of dharma, like armor; “your own position” means your own nature. The answer to this is the verse beginning “when Kṛṣṇa had gone to His own abode,” together with dharma, knowledge, and the rest.

Thus, in the first chapter, the sages asked six questions. In the second, Sūta gives the answers to four of them, beginning with “then.” Delighted by such good questions of the brāhmaṇas, Ugraśravas, the son of Romaharṣaṇa, having honored their words, respectfully began to speak.

The beginning of a discourse is salutation to the teacher and the deity. He states it with the three verses beginning “whom.” There, revealing the majesty of his own teacher Śuka through Śuka’s conduct itself, he says “whom.” “Who went forth” means who renounced and departed. “Not initiated” means one who came near for the purpose of initiation, [saying] “Initiate me.” Or, it means one who was not accompanied by anyone: alone. The reason is that he had abandoned duties, was devoid of duties, and did not enter the path of action because he was a lifelong celibate. Dvaipāyana Vyāsa, distressed and fearful from separation, called out “O son!” with the protracted accent. Although a protracted accent occurs in a distant call, the sandhi here is an archaic usage. At that time, because they were one with him in the form of Śuka, the trees resounded and gave the reply. The meaning is that he who answered in the form of trees did so to remove the continuation of the father’s affection. I bow to that sage. The adjective explains his being one with him. By the power of yoga he enters the hearts, the minds, of all beings; hence he is called the heart of all beings.

Note: in some manuscripts there is an additional reading: before this, because of his age, he was especially a child, not even qualified for the initiation ceremony.

Showing his compassion, he says “who.” For those wishing to cross the dense darkness called worldly existence. [It is] secret, hidden, among the Purāṇas. Four adjectives are given there as reasons [for taking refuge]: “having its own experience” means having its own, uncommon power; “the essence of all the śāstras and śrutis”; “one,” nondual, meaning incomparable; [and] “the lamp of the self,” the direct illuminator of the self-principle that operates with reference to the aggregate of cause and effect, called adhyātma. I approach it as refuge; I go to it.
That by which one conquers worldly existence is called victory, the book [called Jaya]. Let him recite it; by reciting it himself in this way, he instructs the other Purāṇikas.

He performs the honoring that was stated by “having honored their words.” O sages, I have been asked properly, as is fitting. This is for the welfare of people, because a well-considered question concerning Kṛṣṇa has been asked. Since even the question for extracting the essence of the meaning of all scriptures ends in Kṛṣṇa, it is stated in this way.

Here is the answer to what was first asked: “Speak of the one-pointed highest good, the essence of all scriptures.” Dharma is of two kinds: characterized by activity and characterized by withdrawal. Of these, the one characterized by activity, whose aim is heaven and the rest, is inferior. The higher dharma is that from which devotion arises, characterized by reverence for hearing dharma and the rest; it alone is the one-pointed highest good. What is it like? It is causeless, without the seeking of a result, and unobstructed, not overcome by obstacles.

It may be objected: “The brāhmaṇas desire to know Him through recitation of the Veda, sacrifice, giving, austerity without food, and so forth,” according to the śruti beginning “the brāhmaṇas desire to know Him through recitation of the Veda, sacrifice, giving, and austerity without food.” From such śrutis it is well known that dharma is an auxiliary of knowledge. How then is it said to be the cause of devotion? True, but it is through devotion, he says with “Vāsudeva.” “Causeless” means that it is inaccessible to dry logic and the rest, and is according to the Upaniṣads.

He states the contrast with “dharma.” If the dharma that is so called does not produce relish in the stories of Viśvaksena, then, although this labor has been properly performed, it should be understood to be merely labor. It may be objected that the dharma whose aim is liberation is also labor. Therefore he says “only”: it means fruitless labor. It may be suspected that even there there is the fruit of heaven and the rest; he rejects this with “only”: that fruit is perishable. It may be suspected that, according to the śruti beginning “the merit of the performer of the Cāturmāsya is indeed imperishable,” the fruit is not perishable. He establishes its perishability with the word “indeed”: the śruti, supported by reasoning, teaches its perishability—“Just as here the world accumulated by action is exhausted, so there the world accumulated by merit is exhausted.”

Thus the higher dharma, through devotion to Hari, extending as far as renunciation and knowledge of the self, has been stated. Others, however, think as follows: the purpose of dharma is wealth, the purpose of wealth is desire, the purpose of desire is pleasure of the senses, and from that pleasure there follows again the succession of dharma, wealth, and so forth. Thus they say: “From dharma come wealth and desire; for what purpose should it not be served?” He rejects this with the two verses beginning “of dharma.” The wealth, as fruit, of the dharma that, by the reasoning already given, extends up to liberation is not suitable as the purpose of dharma. Likewise, the desire, as the fruit, of wealth that does not deviate from such dharma is not remembered by the sages. Note: by the knowers of truth.

The fruit of desire, which is enjoyment of objects, is not the gain of sense pleasure. Rather, as long as one lives, that alone is the gain of desire. The meaning is that only desire sufficient for such living is to be served. And for the life of the living being, that wealth which is well known here as arising through actions by the performance of action is not the gain; rather, the gain is inquiry into truth.

Note: “to the end.” Note: “through the performance of dharma.”

It may be objected that “inquiry into truth” means inquiry into dharma itself, since some say that dharma alone is truth. He says in response: “The knowers of truth, however, call that itself truth.” What is that? It is called knowledge. “Nondual” excludes the view that consciousness is momentary. It may be objected that even the knowers of truth have mutually conflicting statements. Not so; the same truth is designated by different names. By the Upaniṣadic teachers it is called Brahman, by the followers of Hiraṇyagarbha it is called Paramātman, and by the Sātvatas it is called Bhagavān.

And that truth is attained only by devotion furnished with its accompanying means. The connection is: “that [truth].” Here, in “joined with knowledge and renunciation,” knowledge is indirect. They see that truth in the self, the knower of the field. What is that? The self, the Supreme Self. “Through what is heard” means through what is received by hearing Vedānta and the rest; by this the firmness of devotion is stated.

Having established the meaning that the fruit of dharma is devotion, not wealth, desire, and the rest, he concludes with “therefore.” O best of the twice-born, the satisfaction of Hari is the worship of Hari; perfection is the fruit.

Since dharma without devotion is merely labor, therefore dharma whose chief element is devotion alone should be performed; this is what he says with “therefore.” “With one [mind]” means with a one-pointed mind.

It has been elaborated that dharma without devotion is merely labor. Now he elaborates that devotion has liberation as its fruit, with “whose.” His repeated meditation is itself a sword; with it, the discerning cut the knot—the ego—that karma binds. Who would not develop relish in His story?

In the question concerning the stories of the incarnations, the answer is stated in the third [chapter]. Through the mention of the Puruṣa and other incarnations, and through descriptions of their respective deeds. Because it was said, “Now tell, O wise one, the auspicious stories of the incarnations of Hari,” he will enumerate the incarnations as the answer and first speaks of the Puruṣa with the five verses beginning “assumed.” “Produced from the great principle and the rest” means fully produced from the great principle, ego, and the five subtle elements. The sixteen parts are the eleven senses and the five great elements. Although the Lord’s form is not made of these, it is to be understood that it is stated in this way solely for worship of the Bhagavān who is the indwelling Self of the individual beings, in the form of the Virāṭ.

“Who is that Bhagavān?” In anticipation of this, he distinguishes Him: “whose water.” He who lies resting on the water, in the single ocean. There, yoga is absorption; as He expands sleep in the form of that absorption, His navel alone is a lake. From the lotus arising from it Brahmā came into being in the Padma kalpa. He assumed the Pauruṣa form.

“What kind of form?” He says this with “whose.” It may be asked: what sort of body did He have who lay upon the water? He says: that form of the Bhagavān is pure, not mixed with another quality beginning with rajas; therefore His sattva is powerful, unsurpassed.

This is said to be directly perceived by yogins with “they see.” “Abundant” means not small, and [it is] an eye whose nature is knowledge. He is endowed with immeasurable feet and the rest, and with a thousand heads and the rest; He shines with the thousands of crowns and the rest.

This is fixed, not subject to manifestation and disappearance like the other incarnations; this is what is said with “this.” “This” and the rest is the form of Nārāyaṇa. “Abode” means the place into which something is deposited, the place of entry at the end of the effect. “Seed” means the place of origin. Although it is a seed, it is not like other seeds, but is imperishable. He says that it is not only the seed of the incarnations but also of all living beings: Brahmā is His part, and Marīci and the others are a part of him; by Him [they arise].

He speaks of the incarnation of Sanatkumāra and the rest, and of its deed: “He alone.” Kaumāra, ārṣa, prājāpatya, mānava, and so forth are names of particular creations. The same God who assumed the Pauruṣa form, abiding in the creation called Kaumāra, became Brahmā, became a brāhmaṇa, and practiced celibacy. The words “first,” “second,” and so forth are only for indicating the numbering.

He speaks of the Varāha incarnation: “the second.” The deed is stated: “desiring to raise the earth for the coming into being of this universe.” Thus, everywhere, the incarnation and its deed are to be understood as having been stated.

He speaks of the incarnation of Nārada: “the third.” Having entered the creation of sages; that is, having become a divine sage there. He spoke the Sātvata, the Vaiṣṇava Tantra, the Pāñcarātra Āgama. From that Tantra the character of action as a cause of bondage departs; through it actions become non-actions, and their state is actionlessness. The meaning is that he taught that by which actions themselves become liberating.

Note: this text is not found in many old manuscripts.

He speaks of the incarnation of Nara and Nārāyaṇa: “the fourth.” “A portion of Dharma” means his wife; a half indeed of the self is a wife, according to the śruti. [He was born] in her creation. By saying “having become sages,” the fact that this is one incarnation is shown.

He speaks of the incarnation of Kapila: “the fifth.” [He taught] to the brāhmaṇa named Āsuri. That scripture in which there is a decisive analysis of the collection, the group, of the principles is Sāṅkhya.

He speaks of the incarnation of Dattātreya: “the sixth.” He was obtained as the son of Atri, having been chosen by him for that very purpose; it will be said later, “being pleased, [he said]…” How was he obtained? Anasūyā, under the pretext of desiring a child equal to Me, chose Me alone as her child; the meaning is that he did not find fault with her. “The science of inquiry” means the knowledge of the Self. “And from Prahlāda and the rest”: by “the rest” Yadu, Haihaya, and the others are included.

He speaks of the incarnation of Yajña: “then.” That Yajña protected the Svāyambhuva Manvantara together with Yāma and the other gods who were his own sons. At that time he himself became Indra; that is the meaning.
He speaks of the incarnation of Ṛṣabha: “the eighth.” Born from Nābhi, the son of Agnīdhra, he showed the path of the paramahaṃsas, the other āśrama honored by all the āśramas, to the steadfast.

He speaks of the incarnation of Pṛthu: “by the sages.” “The earthly body” means a royal body, the form of Pṛthu. In another reading, “pārthavam” means belonging to Pṛthu. “The herbs” is an indication of all objects. He milked this earth, all things. The absence of the augment aḍ is an archaic usage. O brāhmaṇas, through that milking of the earth this incarnation is the most desirable; it is from the root vaś, “to desire” or “to please.”

He speaks of the incarnation of Matsya: “the form.” At the flood, the joining of the oceans, in the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara. Although there is no dissolution at the end of a Manvantara, it should be understood that by some sport māyā was displayed to Satyavrata, just as it was unexpectedly displayed to Mārkaṇḍeya. “In the boat made of earth” means in the earth in the form of a boat. He protected [him]. “Vaivasvata” is a designation referring to the future.

In the fourth [chapter] the cause of the beginning of the Bhāgavata is described: Vyāsa’s lack of satisfaction despite austerity, recitation, and the rest. Saying, “I shall cause [it] to be heard with satisfaction,” [he speaks] to be spoken by one among many sages who is old, among many elders who is the head of the lineage, and among many such leaders who is rich in hymns, a knower of the Ṛg Veda. Therefore Śaunaka spoke, because he was such a one.
He speaks the story that he [Sūta] narrates.

“In what place?” and “for what reason?” Having composed the Mahābhārata and the dharmaśāstras and the rest, what was the reason for composing this collection again? “From where?” is a form with the case-ending tasil used in the general sense; the meaning is, “By what was he prompted?” [The answer is] Kṛṣṇa Vyāsa.

Since it was said, “He caused it to be heard,” how did Śuka’s exposition and the rest come about? To ask this, he states his indifference with two verses beginning “his.” “Equal-seeing” means seeing Brahman equally; therefore he is free from conceptual alternatives, with distinctions removed. Moreover, his mind has its end in one alone. He is awake because he has risen from the sleep of māyā; the smṛti says, “He is awake in that which is night for all beings.” Therefore he is hidden and appears as if bewildered.

He elaborates his freedom from conceptual distinctions with “having seen.” Seeing the sage Vyāsa following his son Śuka as he went forth, the naked apsarases, who were playing in the water, covered themselves out of shame even on seeing Vyāsa, who was not naked. By “even though not naked,” it is implied that his son was naked. They did not cover themselves with shame before the naked son who was going ahead. Seeing this wonder, [Vyāsa, you understand:] you have the distinction, “This is a woman and this is a man”; his sight is pure.

How was such a person recognized? The Kurus and the Jāṅgalas are particular countries. Having first reached them, he then wandered in Gajasāhvaya—in Hastināpura, whose name means “that which is called by the elephant,” because it was made by King Hasti.
Together with such a sage, in the dialogue in which this Sātvata, this Bhāgavata śruti, the collection [of the scripture], was heard.

This exposition requires remaining for a long time, but his remaining in one place is difficult; therefore he says “he.” He waits only for the time required to milk a cow, and not even for the sake of alms. Rather, making their hermitage, their house, a sacred place and purifying it—therefore it is wondrous that, being such a person, he speaks here.
The conduct of the listener is exceedingly wondrous; therefore he says, “Tell.” With the five verses beginning “the son of Abhimanyu,” “recite” means narrate.
“Emperor” means universal sovereign. “Or” expresses inquiry: for what reason, from what cause, did he disregard the wealth and prosperity of emperors?

“Whose foot-place” means whose footstool. “Indeed” makes it clear: bringing wealth, enemies bow down. O Sūta, this young man desired it while still young; the middle voice here is an archaic usage. [He desired it] together with his life-breaths.

If he was detached, what had he to do with wealth and the rest? He says “for welfare.” They live for the welfare, prosperity, and wealth of the world, not for their own sake. This being so, after becoming detached, why did this king abandon a body that was a support for others? The meaning is that one should not oneself abandon a life that depends on others.
Whatever you have been asked, tell all of it to us. Since I consider you to have crossed to the far shore of the subject of words, outside the Veda; here [the form] is non-metrical.

He answers the questions beginning “in which age,” preceded by the narration of Vyāsa’s birth: “when Dvāpara arrived.” When did this happen? He says, “at the third passage of the age,” at the third change. “In Vāsavī”: in Satyavatī, born from the power of Uparicara Vasu. The yogin, the knower, Vyāsa was born.

“Having touched water” means having bathed and so forth in the water; “seated” is supplied. “In a secluded place” and the rest are stated for the sake of one-pointedness of mind. By this the location of Badarikāśrama is indicated.

In the fifth [chapter] the greatness of Hari-kīrtana above all dharmas is taught by Nārada for the satisfaction of Vyāsa’s mind. He sat near Vyāsa, the brahmarṣi, who was greatly learned and greatly renowned. “Smiling, as if slightly laughing” indicates cheerfulness of the face. Or the word “as if” indicates an absence of qualification: he smiled because even though he was great, he was bewildered.
“Bodily” means the self identified with the body; is that self satisfied with the body? “Mental” means the self identified with the mind; is it satisfied with the mind or not?

Everything that you wished to know—the dharma and the rest—has been properly completed and correctly known. From the word “also,” it is meant that it has also been practiced. In the reading “ayi,” there is an address. The reason for its being complete is “great, wonderful,” and the rest: it is filled and made complete by all objects, dharma and the rest.
Moreover, the eternal, everlasting, supreme Brahman has also been inquired into, considered, and attained by you. “And yet you grieve”: the omitted sense is, “For what reason?”

The self is both bodily and mental; that is the root, the cause, of his lack of satisfaction. [Its nature is] unmanifest, unclear. O Nārada, we ask you. Brahmā is born from the Self; you arose from the body of that Self. Therefore we ask you, whose understanding is unfathomable, exceedingly deep.

He elaborates the unfathomableness of his understanding with the two verses beginning “that indeed.” The reason for knowledge of every secret is that the ancient Puruṣa was worshiped by you. What is He like? He is the Lord of the higher and lower, the controller of cause and effect. By the mind alone, merely by a resolve, He creates the universe with the qualities, and so forth.

Moreover, wandering through the three worlds like the sun, you are all-seeing. By the power of yoga, moving within all living beings like the vital wind, you are the witness of the self, the knower of the movements of the intellect. Therefore you are immersed in the higher Brahman through dharma, through yoga. Yājñavalkya has said: “Of sacrifice, conduct, restraint, nonviolence, giving, self-study, and action, this indeed is the highest dharma: seeing the Self through yoga.” And in the lower Brahman called the Veda, you are immersed in vows, self-study, and observances. Examine and discern whatever is deficient in me, meaning whatever would make it enough.

“Mostly unuttered” means mostly not spoken. Without the stainless fame of Bhagavān, even that knowledge of dharma and the rest by which Bhagavān is not pleased—I consider that knowledge itself deficient.

It may be objected that the fame of Bhagavān has indeed been described here and there. He replies with “as”: the word “and” includes the means of dharma and the rest. The meaning is that, just as dharma and the rest are stated as principal, the greatness of Vāsudeva has not been stated as principal.

He says that verbal cleverness concerning an object other than Vāsudeva is just as deficient as knowledge concerning an object other than Vāsudeva, with “not.” Even if a speech has colorful words, if it does not proclaim the fame of Hari, they consider it a crow’s bathing place, a pleasure-ground for those who are like crows. Why? The swans, the ascetics whose minds are dominated by goodness, do not delight there; they never greatly delight there. “Those whose abode is Uśik” means those whose residence is the lovely Brahman. There is also a pun: just as the famous swans moving in Lake Mānasa, dwelling in lovely clusters of lotuses, do not delight in a refuse-pit, a place of play for crows, even though it may contain varied food after the swans have left it, so the sages do not delight there.

Note: although the reading “iti śeṣaḥ” is seen in many places, it is unsuitable because that word is present in the original.

Even without verbal cleverness, speech whose chief subject is the fame of Bhagavān is pure; he says this with “that.” “That verbal emanation” means that use of speech; it destroys the sin of the people, the multitude of human beings. In that verbal emanation, even when it is poorly composed and contains incorrect words and the rest, in every verse there are names of Ananta marked by His fame. The reason is this: when there is a good speaker, great persons hear those names; when there is a good hearer, they recite them; at other times they themselves sing and glorify them.

He shows by the maxim of the lamp that action without devotion is empty: “actionlessness.” Brahman is free from action; because it has the same form as that, actionlessness is the state called naiṣkarmya. “Anointment” is a limiting adjunct, that by which something is applied; that which removes it is stainlessness. Even knowledge of this kind, if the feeling for Acyuta that is devotion is absent, does not shine at all sufficiently; it is not fit to become complete direct realization. Then, both at the time of the means and at the time of the result, action desired and of the nature of suffering—and even action that is causeless, not desired—if that action too is not offered to the Lord, how can it shine? Because, being outward-facing, it does not purify goodness.

Note: in some manuscripts the readings “bondage alone” and “mere deficiency” are found here.

Thus knowledge, verbal cleverness, and skill in action that are without devotion are altogether useless; therefore he says, “Describe only the deeds of Hari.” “Therefore” means for this reason. You are one whose vision is unfailing and true, whose hearing and fame are pure, devoted to truth, and by whom vows have been upheld; being thus endowed with great qualities, O treasure of great fortune, remember the various deeds, the pastimes, of Urukrama in samādhi, with one-pointedness of mind, for the release of all from bondage; and, having remembered, describe them. Since this is another sentence, the use of the second person is not improper.

He states another defect on the opposite side with “therefore.” For those who see differently from the deeds of Urukrama, and who, for that reason, intend some other meaning by another method, the mind produced by the sparkling forms and names presented for speaking is unstable and ill-founded; it never finds a place, a footing, in any object, like a boat struck and whirled about by the wind. Thus it is said: “In this matter, O joy of the Kurus, the resolute intellect is one-pointed; the intellects of the irresolute are many-branched and endless,” and so forth.

Thus it has been said that descriptions of dharma and the rest made in the Bhārata and elsewhere without the fame of Hari accomplish nothing. Rather, they have become contrary; he says this with “despised.” “Despised” means fruit-seeking action and the rest, which are blameworthy. For a person naturally attached, your instructing him toward dharma for the sake of wealth is a great transgression, an injustice. Why? He says: by whose words the ordinary person stands fixed in the belief, “This alone is the principal dharma”; the stopping of his fruit-seeking action is then done by another knower of truth, or by you yourself.

Or, by the śruti beginning “not by action, not by offspring, not by wealth, but some attained immortality through renunciation,” this is not considered an actual [injunction] being performed; rather, it is imagined to be intended for a person unqualified for the path of activity. Bhaṭṭas state this when presenting another view: “There it can be said in this way: this rule is for those people, such as the blind and the lame, who are able to undertake household life. Lifelong celibacy or the life of a wanderer must necessarily be adopted by them; therefore this is stated first,” and so forth.

In the sixth [chapter], to give Vyāsa confidence and to show the possibility of a previous birth, Nārada speaks of his own fortune, which arose from the narration of Kṛṣṇa.

Note: the reading “arose from Kṛṣṇa-saṅkīrtana” is also found.

Desiring to do the same himself, he asks about the conduct that would come after the teacher’s instruction: “by the mendicants.” After a departure to a distant country had taken place, [he asks about instruction] by those who teach knowledge.
“The further age” means the later part of life. You spent it. “This body,” the body that belonged to the son of a maidservant, you cast away.

This is the time characterized by the end of a kalpa; how did it not interrupt your memory? The absence of the augment aḍ is an archaic usage. The reason is that this is the complete negation, the denial, of everything.
“I did” means “I performed.” The separation of the r and ṣ sounds is according to the meter.

For some time I lived there, controlled by my mother’s affection; he says this with the three [verses beginning “one”]. She had me alone as her son. “Woman” and “foolish” are the causes of the continuation of affection.
He elaborates the meaning of “maidservant”: she was dependent, and therefore was not capable. A wooden woman is the example of extreme dependence.

Thus she cultivated affection, and I, ignorant of the directions and the rest, therefore lived there. In that brāhmaṇa’s household, because of the continuation of my mother’s affection, I waited for the time when it would cease; that is the meaning. “I lived” means I stayed. “Five years old” means five years of age.

“Coming out of the house” means coming out to milk her. The participial suffix is used in the sense of purpose: she came out to milk. “By the foot” means slightly touched or stepped upon; “bitten” means eaten.
Considering my mother’s death to be welfare for devotees, desiring the grace of the Lord and regarding it as such, I set out.

Having gone beyond prosperous countries, I saw a great forest; this is the connection with the fourth [verse]. The intended meaning is: I went with equal vision through countries endowed with various qualities and faults. “Prosperous” means flourishing; “countries” means regions. In that direction there were towns, villages, cow-settlements, and mines. Towns are royal capitals; villages are explained by Bhṛgu: “Where brāhmaṇas and the servants of brāhmaṇas dwell, that is called a village; it is also the dwelling of śūdras.” Cow-settlements are Vrajas; mines are places where jewels and the rest arise. Agricultural villages are kheṭas. Kharvaṭas are villages on the slopes of mountains, or, according to Bhṛgu: “Where a village stands on one side and a city on the other, the mixed settlement called kharvaṭa is supported by a river and a mountain.” Gardens are gardens of areca palms, flowers, and the rest. Forests are groups of naturally occurring trees; groves are groups of planted trees. All these [places I passed].
[I saw] mountains of varied minerals, such as gold and silver, and trees whose branches had been broken by elephants; those are the trees in which the waters are auspicious. [I saw] lakes.

[I saw birds] whose sounds were varied, the birds called leaf-chariots, awakened by their own cries; [I saw] lakes whose beauty was produced by wandering bees. Having gone beyond them, I saw a great forest. What was it like? It was dense and difficult with the stems of nala, bamboo, reed, kuśa grass, and kīcaka. The kīcakas are kinds of bamboo with large spaces within; they were terrible and hard to endure, of a fearful appearance, and a playground for serpents and the rest.

My senses and body were exhausted and I was overcome by thirst; I sipped water. “At the base of the pippala” means at the root of an aśvattha tree. “Taking shelter” means sitting down. “With the self” means with the intellect or the mind. “The self abiding in the self” means the Supreme Self abiding in the heart; “the self” means the Supreme Self.

Now, in order to speak of the birth of Parīkṣit, the hearer of the Bhāgavata, the punishment of Drauṇi for the killing of sleeping children is called the seventh [chapter]. [Having] heard Nārada’s intended meaning.

Note: In some copies the reading is “janma-karma-parīkṣitaḥ.”
On the Brahma-river—one dedicated to Brahman and resorted to by brāhmaṇas. [The place is called so] because it increases the sattra, the ritual action; thus [it is so named].

On a grove of badarī trees, adorned by a whole group of them. He concentrated the mind; he made it steady. He performed the meditation instructed by Nārada: “Remember his deeds in samādhi” [Bhāgavata 1.5.13]—that is the meaning.

“Fixed” means unmoving. Here the cause is “by bhakti-yoga,” “stainless.” First he saw the Puruṣa, the Lord. The reading may also be “pūrṇam.” And he saw māyā having the Lord as her support, dependent on Him.

And he saw the saṃsāra of the jīvas made by the Lord’s māyā—he says this with “by which.” Deluded by it, distracted by the covering of his own nature, although distinct from the three guṇas, he nevertheless obtains the anartha—such as doership—produced by identification with the three guṇas made by it.

He also saw that direct bhakti-yoga to Adhokṣaja which pacifies anartha. Having seen all this himself, he composed the Sātvata-saṃhitā, called Śrī-Bhāgavata, for the sake of the people who do not know thus. Therefore, by these three ślokas, the meaning of the Bhāgavata has been shown in summary. This is said: The Lord, controller of māyā through the power of knowledge, whose nature of supreme bliss is eternally manifest, omniscient and omnipotent; the jīva, deluded by His māyā, with his nature hidden and with qualities opposite to that; and liberation for him through knowledge obtained by devotion to the Lord. This was said by Viṣṇusvāmin:

Īśvara, embraced by Hlādinī and Saṃvit, is Being-Consciousness-Bliss; the jīva, covered by his own ignorance, is a mine of heaps of suffering.

And also: He is Īśa, under whose control māyā is; he is the jīva, afflicted by it; [one] whose supreme bliss is manifest; [one] whose very great suffering is manifest; distressed by distinctions arising from the reversal born of [dual] vision; remaining as one who enjoys through my māyā—this Nṛhari we praise; and so forth.
He displays the capacity of the Saṃhitā to pacify anartha with “in which.” “In which, merely while it is being heard”—what then when it has been heard [fully]? That is the meaning.
Having enumerated and purified.
For what reason? Vast, expanded.

“Nirgranthas” means those who have gone out from books. This is said in the Gītā:

“When your intellect has crossed beyond the delusion of bewilderment, then you will become indifferent to what is to be heard and what has been heard.” [Gītā 2.52]

Or, the knot itself is “grantha”—the knot in the form of anger and ego has ceased for them; that is, they are free from the knots of the heart. Now, to remove every objection beginning with “What need have liberated persons of devotion?” he says “such qualities.”

Note: The portion enclosed in the parenthetical marks is present in an old manuscript.

“Granted, let them perform devotion; but what is the reason for Śuka’s study of this scripture?” In answer he says “of Hari.” “He studied” means “he learned.” [He did so] because the devotees of Viṣṇu are dear to him. The meaning is that he desired their association in the context of exposition and so forth. By this, the answer has been given to the question, “How did Śuka begin the exposition, with [the statement] ‘his son, a great yogī,’ and the rest?”

To state the answer to the other question—“How did Parīkṣit listen by fasting unto death?”—with “his birth is greatly astonishing” and so forth, he says [the word] “Parīkṣit.” “Vilāpana” means liberation or death. “Saṃsthā” means the great departure. [The account is] in such a way that the rise of the stories of Śrī Kṛṣṇa comes about through it.

Here, intending to explain the birth of Parīkṣit, first of all he begins the account in order to state that the embryo was protected by Kṛṣṇa from Aśvatthāma’s brahmāstra, with “when.” When Drauṇi, Aśvatthāma, carried away the heads of Kṛṣṇā’s sons, the sons of Draupadī, then their mother cried; and Arjuna, the wearer of a crown and garland, consoling her, spoke [thus]—this is the syntactic connection with the third [quarter]. Why did he bring the heads of the children? In response to this expectation he says “in the battle.” Although the Pāṇḍavas are also Kauravas, nevertheless Dhṛṣṭadyumna, born in the Sṛñjaya lineage, was the commander of the Pāṇḍavas’ army; therefore “of the Sṛñjayas” is stated. “The destination of the hero” means heaven. “Atho” means afterwards. When the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Duryodhana, was in such a condition that his two thigh-bones were broken by the impact of the mace thrown by Vṛkodara.

“Of the husband”—of Duryodhana. “Sma” is used in the sense of deliberation. Thinking, “thus it would be pleasing,” [he did it]. The other sentence [says] that it was indeed displeasing to him. The reason for its being displeasing is given by “heinous.”

In the eighth [chapter], the protection of Parīkṣit from the weapon of the enraged Drauṇi, the praise of Śrī Kṛṣṇa by Kuntī, and the grief of the king are narrated.

The Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇā [Draupadī] and accompanied by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, went to the Ganges to give water to their dead relatives. Having placed the women in front, making the women go before. Because in that action the prescription is that women precede.

Having led [them] and given [the water]. In the water of that river, the Ganges, which is purified by the dust of Hari’s lotus feet. From the mention of bathing again, it is understood that they bathed at the beginning also.

“The lord of the Kurus”—Yudhiṣṭhira. “With his younger brothers”—accompanied by Bhīma and the others; “afflicted by grief for sons” is an adjective of the three [women].

Note: The reading “afflicted by grief for sons” is not found in many places.

“Accompanied by the munis.”

“By the cheaters”—the deceitful, Duryodhana and the rest. Those whose lifespan was damaged, destroyed, by acts beginning with the seizing of Draupadī’s hair.

“Having caused [him] to perform” and the rest is a summary of the future account. Like that of Śatamanyu, the performer of a hundred sacrifices [Indra].

“Śaineya”—Sātyaki, the grandson of Śini, together with Uddhava.

Seated on the chariot, he perceived, saw, Uttarā, the mother of Parīkṣit, running toward [him], agitated and bewildered with fear.

Uttarā prays to Śrī Kṛṣṇa with “protect, protect,” in two [places]. He says that there is no other fit to be prayed to. “From You” means than You; “fearlessness” means freedom from fear; “I do not see.” “Where” means in the world in which there is death among one another, mutually.
Here she reports the fear at hand. It rushes forward; it comes facing [her]. He whose missile is heated iron, made of metal. He says with extreme humility: “kāma”—as desired, as one wishes.
He understood the brahmāstra of Drauṇi, who was extremely enraged through defeat, as having been set in motion to make this world without the Pāṇḍavas, empty of Pāṇḍavas.
Therefore it came with many faces; he says this with “then indeed.” “Then indeed” means just at that time.
Seeing that danger, difficult to ward off because the brahmāstra cannot be turned back by other weapons. “Those whose self has no other object”—that is, those exclusively fixed [in Him].

Being within Vairāṭī Uttarā, he covered the embryo. The reason there is: because [he is] the Self, the inner controller. “Lord of yoga” is stated in order to establish entry even though He is externally situated. “For the continuation of the Kurus,” for their progeny. It is said thus because the Pāṇḍavas too are born from the Kuru lineage.
“Amogha” and “apratikriya.” It became completely pacified; it was fully quieted.

In the ninth [chapter], the exposition of all dharmas by Bhīṣma for Yudhiṣṭhira, and his praise of Kṛṣṇa and liberation, are described. He shows that the lack of discrimination for whose purpose it was increased by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, with “thus” [and so forth]. [It is] with the desire to know all dharmas. “Vinaśana” is Kurukṣetra. “Devavrata” is Bhīṣma.
“Good”—the horses in which are excellent; with those chariots.
“Sānugāḥ” means accompanied by the retinue, together with the family.
“There”—then. “They were there” means they had arrived at that very moment. “The bull among the Bharatas” means Bhīṣma.
“Son of Reṇukā” means Paraśurāma. “Brahma-rāta” means Śuka. “Āṅgirasa” means Bṛhaspati.
“Vasu-uttama” means Bhīṣma. “Knower of the division of place and time”: because he was unable to rise, he honored [them] with mind and speech while lying down; that is the intention.
He worshiped Him who was situated in the heart and seated before [him].

“Those seated nearby” means seated close by. “Praśraya” is humility; “prema” is affection; [he addressed those] joined by these two. In another reading, [those] bowed by the two. “He addressed” means he spoke. [He was] marked by sight made blind by tears of affection.

Note: Another reading is “prema-sannatān.”

He speaks the address with eleven [verses], beginning with “aho.” “O sons of Dharma!” “You ought not to live in a condition that is painful”—this “ah, what hardship!” is despised [as terrible]. “Ah, this is unjust too.” Because you are those for whom the brāhmaṇas, Dharma, and Acyuta are the shelter.

Moreover, “saṃsthite” means dead. “Bāla-prajā” means one whose sons are children. “And the daughter-in-law”—by this helplessness is displayed. “Toka” means offspring; “possessing them” means [she is] endowed with them. The meaning is that she obtained afflictions together with the offspring.
He wards off grief by attributing it to Time, with two [verses] beginning “all.” “Of you” also. “Under whose control” means subject to whose control.

Ah, Time is skilled in accomplishing what is difficult to accomplish, he says with “where.” “Kṛṣṇa” [and] Arjuna, armed and bow-bearing. Then, even there, calamity. The meaning is: even when there was the wealth of piety, bodily strength, strength and skill in weapons, arms, and divine [aid].

In the tenth [chapter], the arrival at Hastināpura of Hari, whose work is accomplished, and the arrival at Dvārakā of Him being praised by the women are described. “He made the kingdom”—thus the question is asked with “having killed.” Those who used to compete for their own inheritance, their wealth; or those for whom there was a battle over their own inheritance, who were aggressors because they sought to take wealth and so forth—having killed them. “Whose food was obstructed” means whose enjoyment was contracted by the grief of killing relatives, or whose enjoyment was obtained through gaining the kingdom. “How did he engage in the kingdom?” Or, “what did he do thereafter?”

Having caused the lineage of Kuru to sprout, by protecting Parīkṣit and making it germinate. What kind? “Burned by the forest fire of the lineage”: the lineage itself is a forest; the fire born from it, in the form of anger, burned it. And having installed [Yudhiṣṭhira] in his own kingdom.

Having stated the reason for his engagement, what did he do? He answers this. [His] knowledge arose: the world is dependent on the Supreme Lord and is not independent; by it his delusion, consisting of ego and the rest, was destroyed. Followed by his younger brothers, serving [him]. “The Unconquered”—Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone—is whose refuge. He ruled the earth up to the boundary, the ocean.

He describes his kingdom with three [verses] beginning with “everything desired.” The earth became a giver of all desires. “Vrajas” means cow-pastures. “With swollen udders”—[cows] with swollen udders; an udder is a receptacle of milk, meaning with large udders. “They sprinkled” means they moistened.
“Anu-ṛtu” means in each season.

“Ādhis” means mental anguish. “Vyādhis” means diseases. “Kleśas” means those caused by heat and cold and so forth. Those whose causes are the divine, beings, and the self—the afflictions beginning with the divine—did not arise in the creatures.
Now, to explain the journey to Dvārakā, he says “having stayed.” “Of the sister”—of Subhadrā.
“Him”—Yudhiṣṭhira.
“Yuyutsu”—born of Dhṛtarāṣṭra by a Vaiśya [woman]. “Gautama”—Kṛpa. “The twins”—Nakula and Sahadeva.
“Daughter of Matsya”—Uttarā. The mention of her again is due to increased delusion from separation from Kṛṣṇa, who protected the embryo. Or, “daughter of Matsya” [means] Satyavatī.

He states their inability to tolerate separation from Kṛṣṇa by the rule of inference from the stronger case, with two [verses] beginning “from the association of the good.” “Freed from bad association by the association of the good”—one from whom attachment to sons and so forth, the bad association, has been freed. Having once even heard the fame of Hari, which is pleasing when sung by the good, he cannot give up good association. Those whose intellects have been placed on Him, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, through seeing and the rest.
Therefore, with unwinking eyes, they used to move here and there for bringing offerings and so forth. Because they were fully bound by affection. Therefore, those whose minds had run after Him.

“Having come out of the palace” means when they came out. Because of eagerness, the excess of attachment, they checked the flowing tears, the tears streaming out, holding them in the eyes only. The reason is: “May there be no inauspiciousness for us”—for this purpose.
“Mṛdaṅga and the rest”—ten kinds of instruments.

Being praised by the Ānartas, having entered the city with relatives, the complete delight of the Lord of the Yadus is described in the eleventh [chapter]. With festivals, with the citizens rising, with flags and arches rising, with rows of shining jewel lamps, the Lord entered His own city. “Svṛddhān” means prosperous. “Dara-vara” means the Pāñcajanya conch. “He sounded” means he played [it].

“He” [means the conch]. The conch, being sounded and being filled by Bhagavān, shone, that is, became exceedingly beautiful—this is the syntactic connection. What kind of conch? One whose belly is white. Yet it has redness from the quality of the red lower lip of Kṛṣṇa, the Wide-Strider. Being present in the middle of the joined lotus-hand, that is, the lotus palms. How did it shine? Just as a royal swan in a mass of red lotuses [makes] a high sound, so.

“Of the world”: [the sound] which brings the fear of the world’s fear. “They went out to meet” means they went out to meet. “Those whose desire for seeing their lord” means those whose eagerness for seeing their protector [was present].

“There,” in that [place], [were] those by whom offerings, gifts, were presented to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. An example for the offering respectfully even to Him who is indifferent is “like a lamp to the sun.” “Like children [to] their father,” with the following [verse] connected: they spoke to Him, the friend of all and protector. “Protector” through friendship alone, not through desire. Here the reason is “self-delighting.” There too the reason is “fully satisfied” solely through attaining the own nature of supreme bliss.

What did they say? He says that with “we are bowed.” “Viriñca” is Brahmā. “Vairiñcyāḥ” are Sanaka and the others. In this saṃsāra, for those desiring the highest welfare, [Your lotus feet are] the supreme refuge. Why? Even Time, the lord of the superior ones such as Brahmā, is not powerful where [Your lotus feet] are.
Therefore, for our welfare, become [present] for us. O sustainer of the universe! We have become successful, fulfilled.

They state their fulfillment itself. “Oh, by You we are protected.” Because we may see Your form. That whose seeing is distant even for the residents of heaven; meaning, [Your form] difficult even for the gods to see. The face in which there is a glance made affectionate by a smile arising from love; that form in which such a face is present. That in which there is auspicious beauty in all the limbs.

They spoke compassionately, like children. “Whenever” means whenever. O lotus-eyed one! In the reading “no You,” “na” is a sixth-case [form] expressing disregard. “Having disregarded us,” having abandoned [us], He went away. “The Kurus” [means] Hastināpura; “the Madhus” [means] Mathurā, or [He went] to either. “There” means then. As, without the sun, because of blindness of the eyes, even one moment would be like millions of years, so too [it is] for us, Your people; that is the meaning.

“How” [means]: O Lord! The entire affliction of those who have surrendered, which is in the form of thirst, is dried up and destroyed by seeing You; because thirst arises in those who have surrendered [when they are without You].
“And thus”—hearing these and other words of this kind, granting favor with a glance of welcome, He entered the city of Dvārakā.
He praises that Dvārakā with five [verses]. [It is] protected by Madhu, Bhoja, and the rest, whose strength is equal to His own.

[He praises] that [city] whose beauty is [formed] by reservoirs surrounded by gardens and so forth, in which are sacred trees and creeper dwellings, creeper pavilions, possessing all opulences and flower wealth in every season. A garden is chiefly for fruits. A grove is chiefly for flowers. A pleasure-garden is a forest for play.

“Gopura” is the city gate. “Door” is the house door. [He praises] that [city] in which arches were made through festivity. Flags are marked with signs such as Garuḍa. Banners are marked with devices granting victory. [He praises] that [city] within which the sunshine was stopped by the ends of variegated flags and banners.

[He praises] that [city] in which the great roads and so forth were swept, their dust removed. Great roads are royal roads. “Rathyāḥ” are side roads. Marketplaces are streets of merchandise. “Catvarāṇi” are courtyards. [It was] strewn with fruits and so forth.

Having earlier stated in detail the punishment of Drauṇi and the rest for the purpose of the connection, in the twelfth [chapter] that very birth of Parīkṣit is described. Having made the promise, “Now I shall speak of the birth, deeds, departure of the royal sage Parīkṣit, and also the dissolution of the sons of Pāṇḍu; I shall speak the arising of Kṛṣṇa’s topics,” the standing of the Pāṇḍavas’ kingdom has been described, as a preface, beginning with Chapter Seven, along with the relevant context. Now he asks the introductory [question] after repeating what was stated: “by Aśvatthāmā.” “Released” means discharged. [The syntax is] connected with what follows: “tell [us] his birth and so forth.”
“He” is Parīkṣit. “After leaving” means after abandoning the body.
He says, “I request, not command,” with [the words] “if you think to narrate, then speak.” “To whom Śuka gave knowledge” is the reason for the desire to hear.

Although the king was without desire, such a grandson was born through Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s favor; to state this he speaks of the rise of his devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa with three [verses] beginning “he protected.” “Like his father,” he protected and ruled.

“Sacrifices” are those obtained by him; “worlds” are the future destinations. “Desirable to the gods” means wealth and the like desired by the gods; “objects of enjoyment”—did they produce any pleasure for the king? They did not produce [it], that is the meaning. Here the reason is that his mind is only in Mukunda. Just as garlands, sandalwood and so forth do not give pleasure to one who is hungry and whose mind is fixed only on food, so.
He states the subject at hand with “of the mother,” [the verse beginning] “situated in the mother’s womb.”

“Puraṭa” means gold. He who has a shining golden crown; [the suffix] -in is according to the rule beginning with rice and so forth. “Apīcya” means exceedingly beautiful to see; “darśana” is the form that is seen. By the words “dark” and “wearing lightning,” an analogy to a cloud accompanied by lightning is indicated. “Acyuta” means unchanging.

That which is heated and has passed beyond burning, namely gold, in earrings made of that is he whose [earrings]. “Eyes red with blood” means eyes exceedingly red from agitation. [The thought is] “Ah, the weapon-affliction even of my devotee in the womb!” Therefore [the redness] is from anger.

“Making the radiance of the weapon disappear” means destroying it. “The sun, lord of rays, [causes] snow to disappear.” The child situated in the womb saw such [a being] nearby. Having seen [him], he examined and thought, “Who is this?”

How did the immeasurable Self destroy it? Because His nature cannot be conceived. “Protector of dharma” means he who protects dharma. Or, “the protectors of dharma” are the kings; He is their Lord, because He is also their protector. There, where [the child] was seen by the one whose ten months could be counted, while he was looking, He disappeared then and there, not having gone elsewhere. Because the All-pervading One is everywhere.

“Udarka” means the later result. [This was] at an ascendant sign indicating the increasing excellence of all qualities, one greater than another. The reason is that in it was the rising of auspicious planets together with other favorable planets.
“Jātaka” means the birth-rite. “Maṅgala” means the auspicious day, puṇyāha.

“Varān” means excellent [gifts]. “Good food” means excellent food. “Knower of the tīrtha” means knower of the time for giving charity. [According to the statement:] “As long as the cord is not cut, the period of impurity does not arise; when the cord is cut, thereafter the period of impurity is prescribed.” Therefore he gave before that, or raw grain. “At the tīrtha of the people” means at the auspicious time of the birth of a son; “what is given at the birth of a son becomes imperishable,” according to the smṛti. [The text then says:] “The gods and fathers also come when a son is born to a twice-born,” and so forth.

O bull among the Pauravas! In this pure descending line of the Kurus, of the Kuru lineage. What kind of fate? Unopposed, hard to ward off. When [their] dissolution had occurred, [he] was given by Viṣṇu, who is capable of arising, for your benefit; because of this he will be named Viṣṇu-rāta in the world and will be a great devotee of Viṣṇu. He will also be great in qualities—there is no doubt. Thus the brāhmaṇas spoke to the king; this is the syntactic connection of the three [verses].

Vidura’s account concerning Dhṛtarāṣṭra by Vidura’s instruction is given in the thirteenth [chapter], with the consecration of the grandson, in order to speak of the king’s great path. Now, intending to narrate Parīkṣit’s deeds beginning with the subduing of Kali, it describes Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s departure through Vidura’s arrival; then, on hearing of Arjuna’s arrival and thereafter Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s disappearance, [it describes] the Pāṇḍavas’ departure, through three chapters. “Gati” is Hari. By that course of the self, he by whom everything desired to be known was attained.

That very [matter] he says. All the questions concerning karma-yoga, vows and so forth that he first asked, in the presence of Kauśārava, Maitreya. Afterwards, by mere knowledge of the meaning of three or four questions, having one-pointed devotion to Govinda, being fulfilled, he desisted from those questions. Thereafter he did not inquire further.

“Sūta” is Sañjaya. “Śāradvata” is Kṛpa. “Pṛthā” is Kuntī. “Kṛpī” is the wife of Droṇa. “Jāmayaḥ” are the wives of relatives. Other women also. “Like the returned life”—when life has failed because of a fault such as swoon, the limbs of the body—hands, feet and so forth—become motionless; when it manifests again they rise, so [did they].
[They were] helpless through the eagerness caused by separation.
“Him” means Vidura.

Birds indeed raise their young with great affection under the shade of their wings; similarly, do you remember us, raised under the shade of your partiality and protection? We were released from the multitude of calamities; he states the fact of our being raised thus.
“You” means by you. “By what livelihood was [it] maintained?” means [by what means] was the body maintained. And which holy places and so forth were served?

Your pilgrimage was not for your own benefit, but for the benefit of the holy places—thus he says with “those like you.” The holy places, which have become impure through contact with impure people, are again made holy places by the saints themselves. “Your inner self” is mind; “by Him situated there,” or by Him situated within your own heart.
“Is it well? Have you seen or heard [of them] anywhere?”
He gives the reason for not describing the destruction of the Yadu dynasty: “as a matter of fact.”
“Doing good” means instructing in the truth.

“Surely he is a śūdra—how could he instruct?” He is not a śūdra, but Yama was present in that form. What is the reason there? When Yama is present here, who is the bearer of punishment there? In response to this expectation he says “he administered.” It means he held [the office]. Because of the curse of Māṇḍavya. Indeed: the king’s men, once pursuing thieves, arrived near the sage Māṇḍavya who was practicing austerities; having bound and brought the thieves together with him, they reported to the king, and by his order they impaled all on stakes. Then the king, recognizing the sage, removed him from the stake and sought his forgiveness. Then the sage went to Yama and angrily said, “For what reason was I impaled?” He replied, “As a child you pierced a grasshopper with the tip of a blade of kuśa and played.” Having heard that, Māṇḍavya cursed him: “Because, when I was a child and did not know, you caused me a great punishment, therefore become a śūdra.”

In the fourteenth [chapter], the king, having seen the evil omens, became apprehensive; the disappearance of Kṛṣṇa, heard from Arjuna, is being narrated. “And of Kṛṣṇa”—by the word “and,” [he wished] also to know the intention. “A few”—seven. Even though time had passed, Arjuna did not come from Dvārakā. “Omens” means disturbances; “the foremost of the Kurus” means Yudhiṣṭhira.

“Fierce” means terrible. He says that very thing: of that in which the ordinances of the seasons are reversed. “Livelihood” means means of living. Those whose selves are joined with anger, greed and falsehood.

“Predominantly crooked” means abundant in deceit. “Conduct” means dealings. “Deceit” means cheating; that mixed with it, “friendship” means friendship. “Quarreling” of fathers and others with their respective counterparts means quarrel and so forth.
Having seen extremely inauspicious [omens], and having seen the nature of people—greed and so forth, irreligion—[he spoke] to his younger brother Bhīma.
“Or” is in the sense of conjecture. “For what reason has he not come?”—to this he says: “I do not know.”
“Api”—what? When he wishes to abandon the plaything of the self—the limb, the human drama, a means of play—that time has arrived.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the cause of our being [the object of] all human goals; therefore, with the intention that without separation from Him there would be no misfortune, he says [this]. “From whom”—from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for that reason. Arjuna will make this clear later. “And the worlds”—those attainable according to the performance of sacrifice—by whose favor.
“Not far” means near. “Of us.” “Indicating” means [the omens] announcing disturbances.
Regarding the bodily [omens], he says “the thighs.” The left thighs and so forth are throbbing. Trembling and quivering are present in the heart. These will give me an undesirable thing that is near.

Regarding the earthly [omens], he speaks in three and a half verses. “Śivā,” a female jackal, cries at the rising sun—she cries facing the rising sun. “Fire-faced” means vomiting fire through the mouth. “O limb”—O Bhīma. Looking at me, this dog barks with a leap, fearlessly.
“Useful [animals]”—cows and so forth—make me [pass] on the left themselves. Others, asses and so forth, make [a] circumambulation on the right. “Carriers”—horses.
“This pigeon” is a messenger of death, a sign of death. “Ulūka” is an owl. “Pratyūlūka,” its opponent, is “dhūka,” or a crow. By shrieks—disagreeable sounds—they desire to make the world empty.

“Smoky” [are] the directions; the encircling boundaries cover the world, fire alone. Regarding the heavenly [omens], he speaks in two and a half verses. “Nirghāta” is a thunderbolt falling from a cloudless [sky]. “Thundering ones” here are roars, together with them.

Having observed the entrance of Kali, and placing the burden on Parīkṣit, the king ascended to heaven—thus he says in the fifteenth [chapter]. “Kṛṣṇaḥ Arjunaḥ” is the division [of the expression]; having perceived a form that was the object of various doubts, “vikalpitaḥ” means [he was] perplexed. It is connected with the following “he was unable to speak” [1.15.2]. The reasons there are: “afflicted by separation from Kṛṣṇa”—made emaciated.
“By grief”—by that cause. “Mouth” and “heart”—those two are lotuses. He whose mouth and heart-lotuses dry up; he whose splendor is destroyed.

“Grief”—the tears of grief that arise. Having checked them in the eyes themselves and wiped away what had fallen with the hand, because Śrī Kṛṣṇa was out of sight, being distressed by the increased longing of love, he says to the king [as connected with verse 4].
