He states visarga. The Puruṣa, the Vairāja, and the creation of the moving and non-moving made by him—the creation by the Puruṣa—is visarga.

Note: “From Brahman, the Supreme Lord” means causal creation; but the creation through karma is Vairiñcī [Brahmā’s]—that is the meaning.

The victory of the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha is the excellence of the created [beings] through observance of their respective limits. “Sthiti” is station. His favor toward His devotees is nourishment. The dharma of the good, the lords of the Manvantaras favored by Him, is sad-dharma. “Ūtayaḥ” are the latent tendencies of actions; [the root] veñ is in the sense of extending a thread. They are spun, extended, by actions, hence “ūtayaḥ.” Or, this form is from the root vā in the sense of growth or combination. They are increased, joined, by actions, hence “ūtayaḥ”—that is the meaning.

Note: “Sad-dharma”—here the meaning is that “Manvantaras” has been stated.
The deeds of Hari’s avatāras and the good narratives of His followers are called īśānukathāḥ—this is the meaning.

He states nirodha. The lying down, the dissolution, of this self, the jīva, following Hari’s yogic sleep, together with the powers and adjuncts, is nirodha. Mukti is, abandoning the otherwise-imposed form—agency and the rest superimposed by ignorance—establishment in one’s own nature, as Brahman.

Ābhāsa is creation; nirodha is dissolution; from whom they arise, are ascertained and shine—He, known as Supreme Brahman and Paramātmā, is called the āśraya.

Note: “From whom” is an ablative in the sense of cause.

To show the nature of the āśraya clearly through direct experience, he speaks of the division beginning with adhyātma. This adhyātmika person is the jīva, the seer, identified with the instruments beginning with the eye; that same adhidaivika is the Sun and the rest, the presiding deity of the eye and the rest. There, because the division of both forms is in one alone, the adhibhautika is the visible body marked by the eyeball and the rest, the upādhi of the person, the jīva. This follows śruti beginning “This person is made of food and rasa” [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1].

Note: “Division” means distinction, division.

“One” [is understood] in the absence of one or the other; by their being established dependent on one another, he shows their non-self nature. Indeed, without the seen, the instrument, inferred from cognition of it, is not established, nor the seer; nor without that [instrument] is its presiding deity, the Sun and the rest, inferred from the activity of the instrument; nor does it operate without that [presiding deity], nor the seen without that [instrument]. Thus, in the absence of any one, we do not apprehend one [of them]. There, at that time, he who knows that triad through a cognition whose nature is consideration and sees it as witness—that is Paramātmā, the āśraya. Though they too are mutually supports, the adjective [self-supported] is intended to exclude that. He is his own support, not dependent on another, and he is the support of the others. Thus Bhagavān will say:

“The eye, form, the sun, the body and the aperture are mutually established; the self, which is other than these and the first, is established by its own experience, the accomplishment of all accomplished.”

Note: “Of these” means that, because the three beginning with adhyātmika are established through mutual dependence, he says they are not the āśraya.

Note: “The seen” is inferred from its cognition.

Note: “Without that” means without the instrument.

Note: “That triad” means the triad beginning with adhyātmika.

By this very variability, their being made of māyā is also stated. Therefore the contradiction stated by “The worlds with governors were formerly imagined by the limbs of the Puruṣa; His limbs by the worlds with governors” is also resolved.

While elaborating the division beginning with adhyātma, he states the mode of origin. The promise “Whatever I was asked by you about this from the Vairāja Puruṣa, as it was, that I will narrate” [ŚB 2.9.45] is fulfilled. He states it beginning with “the Puruṣa.” The Vairāja Puruṣa, breaking the egg and separating it, emerged; that is, He stood separately. Seeking, considering, a place to lie. Since He Himself was pure, therefore He created pure waters called Garbhodaka.

He explains dwelling in the waters through the derivation of the name Nārāyaṇa.

“By that” means by that dwelling in the waters. Because the Puruṣa is Nara, and because the waters arise from Him, they are called Nārāḥ; they are His abode, hence Nārāyaṇa—that is the meaning. It is said:

“The waters are called Nārāḥ; the waters are indeed the sons of Nara. The waters were formerly His abode; therefore He is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.”

Note: “By derivation” means by exposition, that is, by etymology.

He states His power. “Substance” is the material cause. “Action” and the rest are instrumental causes. The jīva is the enjoyer. By whose grace they exist and become capable of producing effects—that is the meaning.

Yoga itself is the couch, the bed; therefore [He lies] on it. “Vīrya” is the body in the form of an embryo. [It is] golden, abundant in radiance, as it were.

Note: “Embryo-form” means the aggregate body consisting of the fourteen worlds: “In the waters, at the proper limit, he cast the seed; that egg became golden, equal in splendor to a thousand suns”—according to Manu’s statement.
The elaboration of that very [body is stated] with “now” and the rest.

The ether that is inside the body; from it, [and] from the power of action, while being one who moves variously there. “Ojas” is the power of the senses. “Sahas” is the power of the mind. “Bala” is the power of the body. From that subtle form whose nature is power, the prāṇa called Sūtra [arises]. “Great” means chief. “Asu” is the prāṇa of everyone.

Obeisance to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Obeisance to Śrī Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.

In the Third [Canto], the description of creation is [made] through thirty-three chapters.

Creation from Brahmā is impossible because of the disturbance of the qualities through the glance of the Lord.

There, in the first chapter, the conversation of Vidura, who, having abandoned his relatives, had gone forth, with Uddhava is spoken first.

Having formerly described in brief the Bhāgavata spoken by Bhagavān Brahmā, he again speaks the Bhāgavata spoken by Śeṣa in detail.

Indeed, the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata tradition proceeds in two ways: on one side, in brief, through Śrī Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Nārada and the rest; but on the other, in detail, through Śeṣa, Sanat-kumāra, Sāṅkhyāyana and the rest. There, in the second [way], through the dialogue of Śrī Nārāyaṇa and Brahmā, the Śrī-Bhāgavata was explained briefly by the four verses beginning “I alone existed” and so on. The same was stated somewhat elaborately through the dialogue of Brahmā and Nārada as the ten characteristics. The beginning of the Third [Canto] is to speak that same [Bhāgavata] uttered by Śeṣa in great detail.

There in the Third [Canto], first the meeting of Vidura with Maitreya [is described] in four chapters; then the detailed creation together with secondary creation in eight; then, by the introduction of secondary creation, the Varāha incarnation in seven; then a summary of secondary creation in one; then, in that context, the Kapila incarnation in four; then the account of Kapila in nine. Thus the Third Skandha proceeds through thirty-three chapters. At the end of the Second Canto it was promised:

“[I shall explain] the measure of time and the form bearing the characteristics of the kalpa. As previously, I shall explain the Pādma-kalpa; now hear.”

In order to set out in detail the meaning that was thus promised, Bhagavān Śuka introduces the history with “thus” and two [verses]. “Rich” means complete with all prosperity.

Moreover, he says [what is] highly praiseworthy and not fit to be abandoned: the house well known as belonging to you Pāṇḍavas, [in which] this Śrī Kṛṣṇa was engaged as minister and messenger. “This” is a designation because of the presence of intelligence. The Paurava king Duryodhana, having abandoned that house, entered it uninvited. The reason is: “made one’s own,” accepted as belonging to oneself.
Where did the meeting take place?

“Varīyasi” means superior, excellent. [The question is one] from which the rise of a small matter does not become such. [It is] enlarged by the approval of the good through the expression “good.” Or, it is praised by the reply, the speech, of the good Maitreya—that is the meaning.

He states the offenses of the Kauravas as the reason for abandoning even a house not fit to be abandoned—beginning with “when,” in eleven [verses]. The action in “then the kṣattā went” is connected with the eleventh [verse]. “Yaviṣṭha” means the youngest, Pāṇḍu. “Vibandhūn” means fatherless.

[Draupadī,] the queen of the Kuru-lord Yudhiṣṭhira, was removing with her own tears the breast-kumkuma of his own daughter-in-law; or she was removing the breast-kumkuma of the enemy women by the killing of their husbands.

Of the one relying on truth, taking truth as his refuge, who had returned from the forest, requesting his share, his portion, at the proper time, he did not give it when asked, being devoted to darkness, delusion [serving his son, or ignorance].

Note: “Serving his son, or ignorance” is a variant reading in some copies.

The words of the persons, Bhīṣma and the rest, which were paths of nectar, pouring forth nectar, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra or Duryodhana did not consider very important. “Kṣata” means destroyed, [one] whose fragment of merit is [destroyed]. The fragment of merit was not a cause of happiness, fame, dharma and the rest, but was only a cause of attainment of the kingdom; because even that had been destroyed, he disregarded it—that is the meaning.

Now he shows the defeat caused to Vidura himself—“when” and the rest, in six [verses]. When he was called by the elder Dhṛtarāṣṭra into the inner house for counsel, entered [it], and, having been asked for counsel, [Vidura] then spoke that. What is it that ministers even today call “Vaidurika,” the word of Vidura, renowned?

He says the same—“of the one without an enemy,” in three [verses]. Give the share to the one enduring your offense, which is unbearable. Where Bhīma, in the form of a snake, living together with his younger brothers, breathes, breathing with anger. For that reason you greatly fear [him].

“Do not be proud, thinking, ‘I have many sons like that,’” he says: Mukunda has accepted the Pārthas as his own. And He is Deva, there too Bhagavān, not mundane. Moreover, He is present together with the kṣiti-devas, the brāhmaṇas, and the devas beginning with Indra. Since He is there itself, the brāhmaṇas and devas [are there]—that is the meaning. He dwells happily in His own city alone, and has not gone elsewhere. Moreover, He is the deity, the worshipful one, of the Yadu-devas, since all kings are there itself. Therefore give the share of the Pārthas.

If Duryodhana does not consider that, then he says: this very one is offense embodied; he has entered the houses and remains. The reason for his being offense is that he is a hater of the Person, a hater of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Who is he? The one whom you nourish with the thought “son”; but he is not an apatyam. “Apatya” is indeed said to be [one] from whom one does not fall. “Your prosperity has gone,” he reproaches. Therefore abandon this inauspicious one quickly. How can a son be abandoned? He says: for the welfare of the family; for there is the maxim:

“One should abandon one for the sake of the family; for the sake of the village one should abandon the family; for the sake of the people one should abandon the village; for one’s own sake one should abandon the earth.”
Having said thus, this kṣattā Vidura, whose conduct was desirable to the good, was dishonored, insulted, by Duryodhana together with Karṇa, Duḥśāsana and Śakuni.

He states the insult—“who,” and so on. Being a son of a maidservant, he is unworthy of invitation here. And he is crooked. He explains crookedness: nourished by the strong food of the one whose [food] it was, toward that very one he is adverse, acting in the work of others. Therefore let him be banished from the city. “Breathing” means breathing, with only life remaining—that is the meaning. In an alternative reading, [he is] inauspicious like a cremation ground.

In the Second [chapter], lamenting from separation from Kṛṣṇa, Uddhava described to the kṣattā the childhood deeds of Kṛṣṇa, breathing heavily.

Thus, since Uddhava was asked about dear news, he explains through six [verses] his inability to answer, being overwhelmed by longing from separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, beginning with “thus.” He whose Lord was remembered [is meant].

He elaborates this by the reasoning from the more evident, in two [verses]. Even one who is five years old, imagining some [child] as Kṛṣṇa for child’s play, performing service with only imagined means, although requested by his mother for the morning meal, did not desire that food.
He reached old age.
He was completely satisfied by the nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet, and deeply immersed in that very bhakti-yoga, intense and making [him] helpless.

All whose limbs were bristling and expanding with horripilation, shedding tears of grief with closing eyes. By that Vidura he was recognized as one whose purpose was complete, whose aim was fulfilled. Since the love that he had for Bhagavān, its expansion, its flood, he was immersed in that.
Bhagavān alone is the loka; therefore. “Human world” means attachment to the body. Smiling, he attained wonder through remembering Bhagavān’s cleverness, such as the destruction of the Yadu dynasty.

Being afflicted by separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he replies: Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone is the sun. When He has set, and when the relatives asked about by you have been swallowed by the great serpent of Time, ever wakeful, what welfare shall I say?

Lamenting, he says: unfortunate, without fortune. Those who, although living together with Him, did not know, “This is Śrī Hari.” As, when the moon, born in the ocean of milk, was there, the fish there knew it only as some beautiful aquatic creature, and not as made of nectar, so it is. Or, as [one knows] the moon reflected in water.

They did not know solely because of lack of fortune, and not because of lack of the means of knowledge, he says: “They know His sign settled in the mind,” [that is the meaning]. Thus, exceedingly mature, expert. Thus, they delight in one place alone. Although they were such, they considered Him, the abode of beings, the existing Lord, the best of the Sātvatas, the foremost of the Sātvatas.

Those Yādavas touched and pervaded by the Lord’s māyā, who say, “This Yādava is our relative,” and those such as Śiśupāla, having taken refuge in hostility toward another, and censuring [Him] as entirely non-existent—the intellect of one like me, whose self is sown in Hari, whose mind is deposited in the Lord, does not wander through their words and does not reach delusion. The others alone are fools—that is the meaning.

When there is the question, “Who is that Hari?” he replies, “having shown” and so on. Having shown His own reflection, His Śrī, His form, for this long a time to those whose eyes were unsatisfied because they had not performed austerity, He disappeared, taking away, cutting off, the eyes of the world, because there was no other such object to be seen.

He describes that same form in three [verses]. It is suitable for mortal pastimes. It causes wonder even to Himself. Since it is the highest place, the highest limit, of the abundance of beauty, the utmost excellence of fortune. In Him the limbs are ornaments of ornaments.

The auspicious path of the eyes, causing supreme bliss. The people situated in the three worlds, every living being, now, at this time, here, in this form. Whatever skill, expertise, there is in the later creation, the creation of the later world or the creation of man, he considered that to have completely gone, exhausted; beyond this its skill does not exist. Even though the form of the creator is not subject to creation, this is the view of the people that has been stated.

Pervaded by affection, the laughter, dance, amusement and playful glance; by these, after His own laughter and the rest, honor was obtained by those [women]. Their eyes followed along with Him, and their minds followed only Him as He went. Their tasks had remaining; they remained with their tasks unfinished.

He states the reason for seeing such a form: His own forms alone are peaceful and unpeaceful. There, when the peaceful forms were being afflicted by others, He was compassionate, whose self had become compassionate. Though unborn, He was born, manifested. As fire, although eternally existent, manifests in pieces of wood in the form of the great element, so. The reason for the birth of the unborn is this: “Great” means the mahat-tattva; He is connected with that great portion of the unmanifest whose portion is a small part of the effect.

In the Third [Canto], having come to Mathurā from Vraja, he described what was done by Kṛṣṇa, beginning with the killing of Kaṃsa, and what was done in Dvārakā.

“Śam” is an indeclinable; the meaning is, desiring to make happiness for His parents. [He dragged him] from the high royal platform. Kaṃsa, the lord of the hosts of enemies. Even the drawing out of life from him was for the sake of the parents’ happiness.
“Brahman” means the Veda, together with its details and the six limbs and the rest. The meaning is: bringing the son through the tearing open of the belly of Pañcajana.

The kings invited by Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka. The shortening is a Vedic usage. In the reading “samāhṛtā,” the meaning is “drawn.” By what means? By a form equal in color to Śrī, Lakṣmī. Although she alone invited Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and not all [the kings], nevertheless her beauty was the cause of their coming; therefore it is said that they were invited by her. In the sight of these [kings], placing His foot upon their heads, He carried her away, desiring the Gandharva custom, the form of mutual agreement, to become [her husband]. What kind of her? Having taken His share of Śrī, Lakṣmī, and because she had offered herself to Him. “Suparṇa” means one who flies well. Or, as Garuḍa, [He took] His share, nectar—that is the meaning. Or, “the one whose name has the same two syllables as Śrī Rukmiṇī” is Rukmī; Śiśupāla and the others were invited by him. For what purpose? With the desire that their prosperity might come about with the daughter of Bhīṣmaka. There, Śiśupāla’s invitation was with the desire to become her husband, and that of Jarāsandha and the others with the desire for that wedding festival. The remainder is as before.

“Kakudmat” means bulls with unpierced noses. Or, [it means] having made them with pierced noses. Although the pride of those whose pride had been broken by the taming of those bulls was broken, they still desired [the princess]; therefore He slew those ignorant armed kings, untouched by their weapons.

When He went to heaven to give the earrings to Aditi, then the Lord, although independent, like an ordinary man dependent upon a woman, desiring to please His beloved Satyabhāmā, brought the celestial tree Pārijāta. For whose sake, on whose account, Indra, impelled by a woman, followed that Kṛṣṇa to fight. His undertaking a battle with Him, who accomplishes His own purpose, was indeed inappropriate; therefore he says, “This is a play-animal.” This is Indra.
Having seen His son Bhauma slain by the Sudarśana discus, being summoned and requested by his mother, Dharitrī, the Earth, He gave the remaining kingdom to her son Bhagadatta.
There, in the inner apartments, those [women] who had been carried away by Bhauma accepted [Him] through the glances sent forth and impelled by joy, bashfulness and affection.
He took the hands of these women, being suitable to each one, with proper rites, together with the manner appropriate for marriage.
Equal to Himself in all respects, with all qualities. The expansion of the various abode of Prakṛti, māyā, was by His will. Or, [it was] by the desire of the benefactor of Prakṛti to become various.

“Time” means Kālayavana. “Rundhataḥ” means obstructing, covering. By Mucukunda, Bhīma and the rest, as mere instruments, He Himself killed, caused [them] to be killed. By that He gave His own men splendor, power or fame.
He caused Śambara, Dvivida, Bāṇa, Mura, Balvala and some others to be killed by Pradyumna, Rāma and the rest. Or, “causing to kill” is the reading. Dantavaktra and the rest He Himself slew.
The connection is, “causing the kings to be killed.” What kind? Those whose armies, coming to Kurukṣetra, made the whole earth tremble.
That [one is] Kṛṣṇa. Seeing [Duryodhana], whose fortune and life were destroyed, whose thighs were broken, lying on the earth, He did not rejoice; He did not obtain satisfaction.

He explains the manner of not rejoicing—“how much?” and so on. “With Droṇa and the rest” means with the roots, the causes. “Which” means [the one] furnished with eighteen akṣauhiṇīs. The shortening is a Vedic usage. “How much is this great burden of the earth that has been removed?” Very little—that is the meaning. Since there remains the unbearable army of the Yadus, caused by My portions such as Pradyumna, [the burden is not removed].

No other means is effective here. But when a quarrel arises among these copper-eyed ones through the intoxication produced by drinking madhu, then this alone is their means of being killed; there is no other. Although they are of one self, when I arise, they will themselves disappear through quarrel—that is the meaning.

In the Fourth [chapter], having heard of the death of his relatives, for the attainment of self-knowledge, by the instruction of Uddhava the kṣattā approached Maitreya.

“Permitted by those brāhmaṇas”: they ate and drank Vāruṇī and Paiṣṭī liquor.
“Maireya” means Vāruṇī itself. When the sun sets, by its fault [there is destruction]. “Mardana” means destruction.
Having approached the Sarasvatī, having sipped water.
And I was told earlier, in Dvārakā.
That which was intended is the destruction of the dynasty and the rest.
“Kṛta-keta” means one who has made a residence, made a shelter. “Aketana” means without a residence, without a shelter.
“Viraja” means free from rajas, made of pure goodness. “Vidita” means known, marked. “Kauśa” means silk.

Having placed [the foot] upon the upper part, the left thigh. “Apāśrita” means supported from behind; a young, tender aśvattha tree is that by which [He was supported]. “Tyakta-pippala” means one who has abandoned worldly enjoyment. Yet “akṛśa” means not emaciated, full of bliss.
“Dvaipāyana” is the well-wisher and friend of him, because he is the son of his own guru and the disciple of Parāśara—that is the meaning.

His neck was bent by the feeling of joy. In another reading, by the weight of joy. With the glance in which there was a smile together with affection, allowing [me] to rest, making [me] free from fatigue.

O Uddhava, I know the desire in your mind. I give you that which is very difficult for others to obtain. In the sacrifice of the assembled world-creators and Vasus. O Vasu, in a former birth you were a Vasu; then, desiring to attain Me, you worshipped Me. Therefore I give, I shall give, that means to you. [It is] difficult to obtain by others who have turned away from Me.

He praises his fortune. This birth of yours is the last among births. If in this [birth] My favor has been obtained, because you saw Me in solitude, as I was abandoning the worlds of human beings, through pure devotion, fortunately this good has happened—that is the meaning. “The worlds of human beings”: by the word “human” living entities are meant; abandoning their worlds, going to Vaikuṇṭha—that is the meaning.
He points out exactly what was said by “I give.” Formerly, in the Pādma-kalpa. In the first creation, at the beginning of creation. That by which My glory, My līlā, is manifested.

Thus favored and addressed, I was addressed by Him. I became a recipient, a vessel, of the favor that is the compassionate glance at every moment. In another reading, “at every moment, the recipient of favor.” Shedding tears of grief, he spoke, he said.

I am not desiring only the cessation of my own ignorance; rather, I am eager for service to You, and, seeing conduct that does not fit You, confusion arises in me. Therefore, to pray, “Give me knowledge of truth,” he says, “Who indeed?” Among the four, beginning with dharma, nevertheless, O Bhūman, I am eager for service to Your lotus feet; I do not choose them.

Vidura’s meeting with Maitreya was stated in four chapters. But their dialogue is now described through two cantos. “At the source of the celestial river” means at Haridwar on the Ganges; he was seated, not busy with action. The reason is that his knowledge was unfathomable, unlimited. Maitreya’s gentleness is straightforwardness and the like, and his qualities are compassion and the like; he was fully satisfied by them. In another reading, Maitreya was satisfied, contented, with Vidura’s gentleness and the like.

He explains the questions with “for happiness” and the next fifteen [verses]. “By them” means by those actions. “Happiness” means happiness or the cessation of another suffering, that is the meaning. Or he would not attain anything else. What is that? When this is expected, he indicates that very [thing] with “satiation” and so on. Then, by those actions, he would again and again attain suffering alone. In this kind of saṃsāra, let the all-knowing Bhagavān state whatever is proper and fit for us to do.

Because of daiva, which is the cause of former karma, [for] the person averse to Kṛṣṇa, and therefore practicing adharma, and therefore greatly afflicted, auspicious beings wander for his benefit. You have the nature of doing good to others—that is the meaning.

Therefore, O best of the sādhus, instruct us in the path that is auspicious, of the nature of happiness. By that path, when He is perfectly worshiped, being situated in the heart, He gives knowledge together with attainment of the truth—direct perception of the self together with it. “Purāṇam” means supported by the beginningless Veda as authority.

The verbal connection of “does activities” and so on is with “describe” in the fifth verse. “How”—by what method—as the Puruṣa-form, having accepted an incarnation, being the controller of the three-guṇa māyā; therefore wholly independent, [describe] the activities that He performs. He asks especially about the activities, beginning with “how.” “Desireless” means inactive or free from desire. “Having established” means having made well-situated. “Vṛtti” means livelihood.

“In His own” means in His own heart-space, having entered and placed [this]. “He whose activities are withdrawn.” “In the cave” means in Yoga-māyā. “In many ways” means in forms beginning with Brahmā.

By the distinctions of incarnations beginning with Matsya, sporting, He performs whatever activities, in whatever manner. Again he reveals eagerness to ask specifically with “the mind” and so on. “Suśloka” means holy fame; “the crown of them,” through excellence shining above them—that is the meaning of Him.

“Adhilokanātha” means the lord of the lords of the worlds. “Alokas” means the regions outside Mount Lokāloka. He arranged, created [them]. “Where”—in which [there are] all the beings, their groups; “their distinctions are presided over” means that the authority for each respective action is appointed. Or [it means] that the authority for each respective action is dependent.

Moreover, by the manner in which the nature of living beings, the action made by that, the form made by that, and the designation made by that [arise], He made their distinctions. The creator of the universe, self-born, self-established.

An objection is raised: “In the Mahābhārata everything has indeed been heard by you; what is the use of further questions?” To that he says: “The higher” are the three classes [varṇas]; “the lower” are Śūdras and others; their observances are dharmas. “Me” means by me. “Repeatedly” means again and again. “We became satisfied” means we were satisfied by hearing them, because they bring insignificant happiness. But the stream of nectar of Kṛṣṇa-kathā that is indicated there—apart from that [stream]. There is no sufficient understanding there, that is the meaning.
Here is the reason: “Who?” [he asks]. “Whose feet are holy places”—of Kṛṣṇa. “From the name”—from the stream of nectar of His topics. “In assemblies”—in gatherings. “By sages”—by Nārada and others.

He says that the Mahābhārata’s purpose too is precisely this: “The sage”—Kṛṣṇa, Veda-Vyāsa, desiring to speak of the qualities of Bhagavān in the Nārāyaṇīya section at the end of Mokṣa-dharma. The descriptions of artha, kāma and so on, however, are only for leading the mind into Hari’s topics; he says this with “in which.” The minds of people were surely led into Hari’s topics by descriptions of mundane happiness serving as a gateway. It is said in the Itihāsa-samuccaya:\n\n“Describing desires to the lustful, describing greed to the greedy, what fruit does a man obtain, as if dropping a blind [man] into a well? Having described those two here for the purpose of entering the minds of people, by histories bearing purifying meanings they are censured here again. Otherwise, how would a wise, greatly compassionate sage describe those two, which are causes of terrible bondage in saṃsāra, for people?” Thus [it is said].
He states the result of entering the mind into Śrī Hari’s topics: “That” means the topic, or the mind. “Elsewhere” means in mundane happiness. What then? He says “of Hari” and so on.

Those who do not delight in a topic of this kind, he laments. “Pitiable” are those, and he laments those even more pitiable among them. There, the ignorant who do not know the purport of the Mahābhārata are pitiable. But those who, even knowing it, are averse to Hari’s topics—of them too [it is to be] understood: “more pitiable.” Unblinking time casts away the lifespan of those. Here is the very reason: their verbal, bodily and mental activities are merely vain argument, path and recollection.

Therefore, O Kaupārava, for the welfare of this universe, having extracted Hari’s topic, which is the essence among all topics, proclaim it to us. Having extracted it just as a bee extracts honey from flowers.

In the Sixth [chapter], he describes the creation of the Virāṭ body by those entered by the Lord, and also the distinctions beginning with adhidaiva made by Bhagavān there itself. Of the own powers beginning with mahat, existing without coming together, their world-process is asleep, whose world-creation [is meant]. Or, having seen the state of the instruments of the sleeping living beings, He entered—this is the connection with the latter [part of the verse].

The power called Prakṛti, whose awakening is by Time, or which agitates its own effects, is called “designated by Time.” Because of entry together with Prakṛti, the entry of the twenty-three principles has been stated. He entered as the inner controller.
In the form of exertion, by the power of activity. “Karma” means their activity, or the unseen [karma] of the living beings.
“Awakened” means [the] karma whose power of activity is awakened. The group of twenty-three [principles], impelled by the divine Lord. “By portions” means by parts. The Virāṭ body is the Adhipuruṣa.
He explains “birth” with “by the Supreme Lord.” The group of beings who create the universe. “By mātrā”—it was agitated, transformed, not in its entirety. In which the worlds are situated.
He is called the Adhipuruṣa. “In the egg-shell” means in the middle of the universe. Together with all beings, the living beings lying [within].

“Garbha” is Virāṭ, in the form of the effect. The divine power is the power of knowledge; by that, in one form, as consciousness delimited by the heart. The power of action is the power of activity; by that, in ten forms, as prāṇa: prāṇa and the other five—Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkala, Devadatta and Dhanañjaya—these are the five. Thus, by difference of function, prāṇa is tenfold. The power of the self is the power of the enjoyer; by that, according to distinctions of adhyātma and the adhi-divisions, He divided the self into three.

To establish his capacity for such division, he states his excellence with “this indeed.” The self of all beings, of living creatures, without remainder. Because individual beings are his portions. The jīva is a portion. The statement of incarnation is with the intention of the manifestation of Nārāyaṇa in him.
He explains the meaning of the previous verse. “With adhyātma” means the senses that are adhyātma, together with that. “Virāṭ” [is understood] everywhere.

To elaborate the distinctions beginning with adhyātma and so on, he says “remembering” and so on. “We shall bring you the offering that has been announced, O unborn one” and so on [Bhāg. 3.5.48]. “By his own splendor” means by his power of consciousness. “He performed austerity” means he considered, “I shall do thus.” From the śruti, “whose austerity is made of knowledge.” “For expansion” means for obtaining various functions.
“Me” means from me. Hear.

He explains the abodes with the next fourteen [verses], beginning with “of that fire” and so on. “Mouth” is split open, born separately. “Foot” means its own place. He entered with his own portion, his own power, together with speech. This [is] the jīva. “It undertakes what is to be spoken”—that is, it pronounces sound. Everywhere, that which is split open is the foundation. The [terms] beginning with fire and ending in the nominative are adhidaiva. The sense organ beginning with speech, in the third case, is adhyātma. What is to be understood is adhibhūta.
“Of Hari”—of the Virāṭ [form].
“Tvaṣṭā” is Āditya.

In the Seventh [chapter], having welcomed the sage’s speech that cuts doubt, Vidura again properly uttered various questions. With “Now your divine pastimes strengthened by Yoga-māyā” and so on, [Maitreya] having said that Bhagavān performs creation and so on playfully through the qualities of māyā, Vidura seems to please Maitreya with speech in the form of a request, by way of an objection arising from not knowing the purport.

How can there be activity for one without modification, and qualities for one without qualities? The statement “as sport” removes absence of purpose, not contradiction to the nature [of the object], that is the meaning.

Even sport like that of a child is not appropriate because of partiality, he says. “Udyama” means he sets in motion, engages. In a child’s play there is desire as the cause of engagement. Or, from another [cause], through another object or through another child’s engagement, he gets a desire to play. But for the Lord, who is satisfied in Himself, how can there be desire? And for one always withdrawn from anything else, unattached and nondual, how can there be desire to play with another? That is the meaning.

Also, what was said—“remembering, the Lord of the universe-creators, the [offering] announced to Adhokṣaja” and so on—namely that the Lord performs creation and so on for the enjoyment of the jīva under the upādhi of avidyā. He repeats that too in order to object: “He created” and so on. He created with that guṇa-mayī māyā which produces delusion such as doership and enjoyership in the self, the jīva. It is said in the First [Canto]: “By which the jīva, although transcendental, bewildered, considers himself constituted of the three guṇas and accepts the calamity made by it” and so on. Here too, “therefore the Lord’s māyā, the bewilderer even of the māyāvādins” and so on. “He establishes” means He protects, maintains. “He will cover over” means He will make it hidden in reverse order. In another reading, “by reverse order He will hold it completely in Himself.”

This would be possible if the jīva were the support of avidyā, but it is not possible, he says with “from place” and so on. The self, the jīva, whose awareness is not destroyed by place and so on, because its nature is Brahman—how could it be joined with Aja? There is no disappearance from place, like the light of a lamp, because of its omnipresence. Not from time, because of its eternality like lightning. Not from state, because of its immutability like memory. Not from itself, because of its reality like a dream. Not from another, because of its nonduality like a pot and the like. Thus, for one whose awareness is not lost by these [causes], how could it be joined with Aja? Here Aja is avidyā itself, not Māyā, because there is no opposition between Māyā and awareness.

Moreover, he objects that, precisely because the jīva is of Brahman’s nature, even saṃsāra does not exist for it. The enjoyer abiding in all fields is in reality Bhagavān alone, because as consciousness-form there is no difference from Him. And this being so, whence this jīva’s misfortune, loss of bliss and so on, or suffering caused by karma? Because there is no relation with karma. Otherwise the same consequence would apply to Īśvara too, that is the meaning.
In him, ignorance itself is the danger, the fortress. Remove that mental impurity, delusion.
Having been prompted, challenged, as if smiling, as if revealing maturity. But in reality, free from pride.
That this māyā of Bhagavān, the Lord of inconceivable power, is opposed by reason—that is the objection. He repeats the contradiction only: bondage by avidyā and wretchedness of a liberated person.

Here he gives an example: just as, without an actual thing such as cutting the head, the reversal of the self—“my head has been cut”—for the observer, the witness of a dream, appears merely false, so.

Then why would it not appear for Īśvara too? To that he says: just as the quality of trembling and so on, produced by water as a limiting adjunct, is seen only in the moon reflected in water, not in the moon situated in the sky, likewise the quality of the non-self, the body and so on, although unreal, belongs only to the jīva, the self who is the seer identified with it, and not to Īśvara—that is the meaning.

He states the means for the cessation of that: “that indeed” is the quality of the non-self; through the disposition of withdrawal, the compassion of Vāsudeva, and through that bhakti-yoga toward Him, by it [the non-self] is covered, becomes unseen. With “gradually” he indicates according to the practice.

Then, when is the cessation of all unwanted things? In response to this expectation he says: when there is withdrawal of the senses, steadiness. Where? In the self of the seer, in the form of the inner controller. Then immediately. The example “like one asleep” applies only to the complete dissolution of suffering, not to rising again.

With bhakti-yoga he shows the cessation of suffering, with “without remainder.” Repetition of the qualities and hearing too. When this is obtained in the self, the mind, what further need is there to state it by reasoning in loving meditation, which is superior to hearing and chanting?

Welcoming the answer, he reveals his own fulfillment with the six [verses] beginning with “cut off.” Although there is no distinction in being consciousness-form, the doubt I had—“How can Īśvara have creation of the universe and so on, and how can the jīva have saṃsāra?”—has been cut by your well-spoken, reasoned statement, which was a sword. Therefore now my mind enters correctly into both: Īśvara’s independence and the jīva’s dependence. Thus the doubt, “How can there be bondage by avidyā for the self whose nature is awareness not destroyed, or whence its cessation?” “In both” means in bondage and liberation.

In the Eighth [chapter], Brahmā arose from the navel of the one lying in the water. Not knowing Him, and being afraid in the water, he nourished the powerful one by austerity. He praises the listener: “Fit to be served by the good.” “Bata” means “ahā.” Because you were born here in this lineage as the protector of the world, Dharmarāja, you became. Of what kind? One for whom Bhagavān Himself is foremost. Here is the reason: “Ajita”—you make it new at every moment.
For those who have obtained great suffering for little happiness, I begin to act for the cessation of that suffering.

Since there is the expectation, “Who is this Bhagavān? To which sages did He speak? And how was it obtained by you?” he answers with “seated” and the next seven [verses]. “On the earth” means at the surface of Pātāla. “Of unobstructed being” means of unobstructed knowledge. Therefore, [He is] beyond Saṅkarṣaṇa, Śrī Vāsudeva.

He further characterizes Him: experiencing on the path of meditation His own seat, His own shelter, named Vāsudeva, of the form of supreme bliss; honoring and worshiping Him greatly with the highest excellence. Having held the lotus-bud of His eyes inward, turning them within, slightly opening them, for the advancement of Sanat-kumāra and others by a glance of mercy.

This is an adjective of the sages in half a [verse]. “Moistened with the water of the celestial river” and so on. The idea is that, descending from Satyaloka to Pātāla for hearing Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, they descended continuously through the middle of the Ganges alone. “The two feet are placed”—on which lotus? On that lotus, touching it and bowing. What kind? He says: they worship that lotus with many offerings so that it is accompanied by love. “Desiring a boon” means desiring [Him as] husband.

Reciting the deeds performed. By what? With speech in which, through love, the words stumble. “Those who know those [deeds]” are tat-jñāḥ. “Sahasra” means a thousand; in the thousand crowns are the best jewels, by which the thousand raised hoods of Him are illuminated—they asked Him; this is connected with what came before.
It was spoken by that Saṅkarṣaṇa to Sanat-kumāra.

Principal in the dharma of the paramahaṃsas. “Desiring to speak” is the ātmanepada form, because the substitute for √brū, “to speak,” is both-pada. “To the endowed one” means to the one who followed, who was associated.

“Spoken by Pulastya”—here is the narrative: hearing that his father had been eaten by a rākṣasa, Parāśara began a rākṣasa sacrifice; at Vasiṣṭha’s words he withdrew. Thereafter Pulastya, pleased because his own lineage was protected, gave the boon, “You will become a speaker of Purāṇas.”

Thus, having shown the continuation of the disciplic succession from Saṅkarṣaṇa, for describing the vibhūti he speaks of the lotus-born [Brahmā]: when [the universe] was inundated, submerged in the water of the one ocean, then Śrī Nārāyaṇa, whose eyes were open and whose consciousness-power was not concealed, closed His eyes. Abandoning play with Māyā, He rejoiced in the bliss of His own nature alone. Therefore He was desireless, inactive.
The impelling of the power of Time, again for awakening at the time of creation. “In His own position” means in His own station. For the absence of external activity, the example is “like fire.”

While existing together with His own consciousness-power, sleeping by Yoga-nidrā, with His own power of Time appointed beforehand for awakening, He whose system of action, the course of activity, was brought about, saw the absorbed, merged [beings].

Whose glance is intent on the subtle cause for the creation of the world. Pierced and agitated by the rajo-guṇa that follows Time, the very subtle object, becoming about to arise, arose from the navel region—this is the meaning.
That very subtle object, becoming the lotus-bud, rose up. By Time, which awakens the actions unseen of the living beings. Its self is Śrī Viṣṇu, whose source it is.

That lotus, made of the worlds, manifests all the qualities and objects to be enjoyed by the living beings, and thus [it is called]. The one from whom it was born is that very Viṣṇu. “O” is a form of address. He entered with power not at all diminished, entering as the inner controller. In that lotus presided over by Viṣṇu, the creator Brahmā became. What kind? He is Veda-made by himself, not one who obtained the Veda through study. Who is he? He is the one whom they call Svayambhū, because his fatherhood is unseen. At the end of the previous kalpa he had become one with Nārāyaṇa in sleep; when He awoke, in that Padma-kalpa he attained manifestation through the lotus—that is the meaning.

In the Ninth [chapter], having seen Nārāyaṇa pleased by austerity, the unborn Brahmā praised Him, suffering in the one ocean, desiring creation of the worlds. Revealing fulfillment through knowledge of Bhagavān and lamenting the ignorant, he says “You are known to me.” By worship over a long time, now You are known by me. Alas, for embodied beings this is indeed a defect: that the truth of You, Bhagavān, is not known. You alone are fit to be known because You are real; nothing else, because it is unreal. Besides You there is nothing. Even what appears to exist is not purely real. How can the unreal appear? He says: because of the agitation of the guṇas of Māyā, You alone shine as vast and many-formed.

An objection: You too do not properly know that this form seen by you is constituted of guṇas, while only nirguṇa Brahman is real. To this he replies with the two [verses] beginning “form.” By the emergence of the taste of awareness, by the manifestation of the cit-śakti, from whom darkness is always withdrawn, this form of Yours has been taken and revealed by You alone independently for the favor of the worshipers. Of the hundred incarnations consisting of pure goodness, it is the one seed, the root. To show that, he shows its being the seed of the guṇa-avatāra with “whose navel” and so on.

O Supreme! “Unpierced splendor” means uncovered luminosity; therefore without alternatives, without distinction; therefore bliss alone. I do not see Your nature, which is of this kind, as different from this form; rather, this alone is That. For this reason I have taken refuge in this form of Yours. He says “also” because of its fitness. “One” means foremost among objects of worship, which is the creator of the universe. Therefore “not the universe” means other than the universe. Moreover, “made of elements and senses” means the cause, the self, of the elements and the senses.

Thinking that even so this is only qualified and recent, he says “that indeed”: exactly this, O auspicious one of the worlds, which You have shown to us worshipers in meditation for our welfare. It is not fitting to grant us, whose minds are fixed on the path of the unmanifest, a vision of You with limiting adjuncts, that is the meaning. Therefore, to You we offer obeisance in accordance with [that], with continued following. Then why do some not honor Me? To that he says: “the one who disregards”—those fixed in bad association and atheistic sophistry.

Those who worship You with respect are fulfilled, he says with “but those.” “Śruti” is the Veda; it itself is “wind,” by which [He] is carried, brought near. “You do not depart.” Those who hear Your topics with great respect, You shine eternally in their hearts—that is the meaning.

Then what? He says “so long as.” When wealth and so on are present, there is fear; when they are gone, sorrow; then again longing; thereafter disgrace; nevertheless abundant greed, thirst; and when they are somehow obtained again, the false insistence “mine.” The root of affliction is the cause of fear, sorrow and so on. “Would not choose” means would not take refuge. By merely taking shelter of Your feet, fear and so on cease; how much more when You manifest, that is the meaning.

It was said that those who, although desireless, do not honor You partake of hell. But those who, being averse to hearing Your topics and so on, are devoted to desired actions are extremely dull, he says. “Struck by daiva” means their intelligence is destroyed, their minds ruined. Whose senses are turned away from the association in the form of hearing and chanting and so on, which removes all suffering. “A-kuśala” means not conducive to welfare.

He shows the lack of welfare itself. Hunger and thirst, and the three dhātus—vāta, pitta and śleṣman—by these. Seeing these creatures afflicted by the very difficult-to-bear, intolerable fire of desire and by unceasing anger, my mind sinks.

An objection: since this saṃsāra of this kind is not ultimately real, why is lamentation made? To this he says “so long as.” “This separateness of the self” means the state of the body and so on. “Whose strength is great” means Your Māyā, in the form of the objects of the senses, whose strength is great. “Would not cease” means would not stop, bringing about a collection of suffering, in which the fruits of actions exist. In the reading “this separateness,” so long as he sees this body and so on as separate from You, even though useless, it would not cease.

Let it be so for the non-discriminating, but the discriminating are liberated, so what need have they of bhakti? To this he says: whose senses are engaged and afflicted during the day, and at night there is not even a little sense pleasure, because at night, when they lie without sleep, by seeing dreams their sleep is broken in an instant, and their plans and efforts for objects are struck and thwarted on every side by daiva.

Having spoken of the saṃsāra, the non-cessation, of nondevotees, he states its cessation for devotees with “You.” You sit in the heart-lotus purified by bhakti-yoga. He whose path has been seen through śruti, through hearing. Moreover, even without hearing, whatever form of Yours Your devotees meditate upon in the mind by their own desire, that You make manifest, reveal, for the favor of the good, the devotees.

To devotees who are desireless You are very easily accessible, not to others, he says with “not” and so on. With abundant, powerful worship-services such as flower offerings and so on. With the compassion for all beings that is inaccessible to the non-good, the nondevotees. “The cause of favor” is “one” and so on.

Since You are not greatly pleased with those who have desires, obtaining desires is therefore not the highest fruit of actions, but pleasing You alone. The connection with desire is for inducement by an intermediate fruit, he says with “for men.” Worship of You, Bhagavān, alone is both the action and its purpose, and is the superior fruit of action. The reason for its superiority is that the dharma offered to You is never destroyed, never perishes, whereas dharma for the sake of desire perishes after giving desire.

Therefore we bow to You alone, he says: eternally, always, to the one whose delusion of difference is removed by consciousness of His own nature alone. Moreover, knowledge alone is the intelligence, the vidyā-śakti, of whom. Or “dhīṣaṇa” means support. Therefore, to the Supreme. The reason is that the sport, the play, of that Māyā which is the cause of the origin of the universe and so on belongs to Him. We have made this obeisance to You.

Showing His lordship by granting kaivalya merely through utterance of the name, he offers obeisance with “whose.” Those in which there is imitation of incarnations and so on: the imitations of incarnation are “Devakī-nandana,” the son of Devakī, and so on; the imitations of qualities are “all-knowing,” “lover of devotees” and so on; the imitations of activities are “lifting Govardhana,” “enemy of Kaṃsa” and so on. Even at the departure of life, even helpless, they merely recite and utter [these names]. “Śamala” means sin. “Uncovered” means with the covering removed. They attain ṛta Brahman.
In the Tenth [chapter], to speak of the answer to the question about Time, its emergence [is described]. Creation, however, is said to be tenfold according to divisions beginning with prākṛta.
“Me” means by me. “Speak” means speak. Or [it means] “make [it] manifest.”
“Prompted” means requested. He says “situated in the heart,” not that those questions had been forgotten by him, that is the meaning.
“In the self” means in Śrī Nārāyaṇa, having fixed the mind in the Self.

“The lotus-born Brahmā by which he stood after presiding”—the kta [suffix] is in the agent. He saw that lotus and the water. What kind were the lotus and water? They were shaken by that wind whose force was made by the time of dissolution; “fell down” is connected with the latter [part of verse 5]. He whose knowledge and strength had greatly increased drank up everything—this is [the meaning of] “fell down” in verse 6.
“Puṣkara” means lotus. “The three worlds previously merged, I shall create them as conceived.”

Having been impelled and appointed by Bhagavān for the action to be performed, he then entered the lotus-bud and divided that one into three in the form of the worlds. To remove the doubt, “How can the creation of three worlds come from one lotus-bud?” he states its vastness: in the form of fourteen worlds, two-sevens; in many ways, even more than that. “To be conceived” means fit to be conceived. Therefore making the three worlds from it is not astonishing, that is the meaning.

To state the reason for division in the form of three worlds, he says “so much”: this three-world form is said to be a particular arrangement, a distinction of structure, of the world of living beings, the place of enjoyment for living beings, created each day. An objection: since the Supreme Brahmā too does not differ in being a jīva, why is there not daily creation of Brahmaloka too? To that he says “indeed”: because it is the ripening, in the form of fruit, of desireless dharma, which is the cause. This is also indicative of Satyaloka, of the worlds beginning with Mahas and of their inhabitants. Because the three worlds are the fruit of desired action, they have origin and destruction in each kalpa. Because the worlds beginning with Mahas are the fruit of desireless dharma appropriate to worship, there is no destruction until two parārdhas. And the liberation of those situated there generally occurs thereafter, that is the meaning.

Having heard of differences in the creation of worlds according to differences of Time, desiring to know that very Time, he asks. “What characteristic, what nature called Time, have you spoken? Describe it properly.” How is Time constituted? What are its subtle and gross forms? That is the meaning.

Here the nature of Time is stated generally; in the next chapter specifically. “The interaction of the guṇas”—the transformation beginning with mahat that is performed by it alone—that is Time, this is understood. It will also be said in the Eleventh [Canto]: “The interaction of the guṇas is Time, nature and the sūtra.” In itself it is without distinction, unsupported anywhere, not delimited, without beginning or end, that is the meaning. To show this precisely he says “Puruṣa”: Īśvara performs creation and so on with that as the instrumental cause. “Upādāna” is that which is accepted as an instrumental cause. He created that very self in universal form, in which that Time is both material and instrumental cause, because there is no created thing separate from Himself. This is merely a statement of the thing; only this is intended: He created with Time as the instrumental cause.

Showing the absence of a created thing separate from Himself, he shows Time’s being the cause of creation with “the universe.” The universe, absorbed and withdrawn by Viṣṇu’s Māyā, being only the subtle elements of Brahman, was delimited and separately manifested by Īśvara as agent, with Time as the instrumental cause. “Whose form is unmanifest” shows its being without distinction in itself.
To show its being unsupported, he states the unsupportedness of the flow of the universe, its effect: as it exists now, so it existed before, and it will exist afterward.

Having thus defined Time generally, intending to define it specifically, he restates the previously mentioned distinctions of the creation that is its cause with “creation.” That which is prākṛta and vaikṛta is the tenth [creation]. For its cause he states a threefold dissolution: by Time alone, nitya dissolution; by substance, such as the fire of Saṅkarṣaṇa and so on, naimittika dissolution; by the guṇas devouring their own effects, prākṛtika dissolution.

He elaborates those same creations, from “the first” and so on through the end of the chapter. The characteristic of mahat is the inequality of the guṇas from the self, Hari. “Of ahaṃ” means of ahaṅkāra. Its characteristic is “where” and so on. The three creations beginning with dravya and so on are to be described; “bhūta-sarga” means the creation of the tanmātras and “bhūta-sūkṣma-sarga,” that is the meaning. It is endowed with the power of matter, the producer of the great elements.

Thus in the Eleventh [chapter], Time is described by characteristics beginning with the atom; from yuga, manvantara and so on, the beginningless kalpa is described. Having thus defined the tenfold interaction of the guṇas, which is the indication of Time in general, now, to define its special nature, he defines in two [verses] the object to be measured by it. Of an existing effect, among its parts, that which is the final part and has no part [remaining]. “Many” means not having reached the state of an effect. “Uncombined” means not having reached the state of an aggregate. Therefore it always exists, even when the effect and aggregate states have disappeared; that is the atom to be known. What is the proof there? He says: from the things assembled, the humans who transact have the illusion of unity, the cognition of a composite. Thus in the Fifth [Canto], while rejecting the composite, he will say “a distinction made by whose collection.” It is imagined because otherwise the effect cannot be accounted for, that is the meaning.

Having stated the subtle, he states the gross with “of the existing itself.” The unity of the whole existing, of the mere effect established in its own nature, whose final portion is the atom and which has not attained another transformation, is the Paramamahān. Its masculine form is because it is opposed to the atom. An objection: every substance has many distinctions and is mutually different; how can there be unity in it? To this he says: “without distinction” means without a desire for distinctions and continuous, without a desire for difference; all the manifestation is Paramamahān, that is the meaning.

Just as this substance is subtle and gross, so Time too is inferred. By the word “and,” the middle state is included. The configuration of the state beginning with the atom is “consumption,” meaning pervasion; by that, the power of Hari, called Bhagavān, unmanifest in itself, consumes, pervades and delimits—thus [it is meant]. “All-pervading” means capable in origin and so on.

He elaborates this with “he” and so on. The Time which consumes the atomic state of the existing universe is the atom; the Time which consumes its entirety, without distinction, is the Paramamahān. This is the meaning: in the movement of the sun that will be described with “situated in the planets, stars and constellations” and so on, the time in which the sun crosses atomic space is the atomic Time. The time in which it crosses the whole planetary shell consisting of twelve zodiac signs is the Paramamahān, Time in the form of a year. Through its recurrence, in the order of yuga, manvantara and so on, it extends to the end of two parārdhas. Thus in the Fifth [Canto] the divisions of Time and so on will be described through the movement of the sun alone.

Now he describes the middle state of Time, beginning with the characteristics of the dvy-aṇuka and so on. Two atoms make an aṇu; three aṇus make a trasareṇu. He says that it is directly perceived with “in the sun-rays through a lattice.” It is known in the sun-rays entering through a window. What is it? That which, because of extreme smallness, followed only itself and went. In another reading, “followed only itself and is known,” not [following] the earth.
In which there are one hundred parts in the form of truṭis—that is a vedha.
Those are three nimeṣas; [the group] is taught as a kṣaṇa. Fifteen kāṣṭhās make one laghu.

Six or seven nāḍikās make a prahara. It itself is a yāma, the fourth part of day and night. Six when decreasing, seven when increasing. It should be understood that this excludes two muhūrtas of the sandhyā portion. There too the word “or” is for non-fixedness, because it is impossible to count those differences each day.

Now he states the measure of a nāḍikā. “Measure” is a vessel made of six palas of copper. A māṣa is five guñjās; with four of those [māṣas] a rod four aṅgulas long is made, with a hole made at its root. The time in which water measured by one prastha enters through that hole and the vessel becomes full and submerged is one nāḍikā. Here, if the pala and the hole are greater it sinks quickly; if smaller, slowly—this is the rule regarding the pala and the rod.
“Ahani” means ahorātra, day and night.
Six months make an ayana. “In the day” connects with this subsequently.
“In the day”—they call the day and night of the gods [a day and night]. Twelve months [make a year].

By this order, he says that this sun constantly diminishes life: the planets, beginning with the moon; the constellations, beginning with Aśvinī; the stars, the other nakṣatras; and the Time-wheel indicated by them. Standing there, the unblinking Lord, the all-pervading one whose nature is Time, the sun, traverses the universe, the planetary shell consisting of twelve zodiac signs.

The differences beginning with the year should be seen according to the differences of solar, Jovian, civil, lunar and stellar months. Some, however, say this: when saṅkrānti occurs on the first day of the bright fortnight, the simultaneous beginning of the solar and lunar months occurs; that is a year. Then, by the solar measure, six days increase in a year, and by the lunar measure six days decrease in a year; because of the twelve-day interval, the two have an earlier and later occurrence. Thus, through the gradation of the interval, five years pass. Within them there are two intercalary months. Again there is the sixth year.

Such Time in the form of the sun is to be worshiped by the ever-vigilant, he says with “who.” He runs in divine space, causing the power of seeds and so on, concerning the created effect beginning with the sprout, to expand in many ways by his own power in the form of Time, directing it toward the effect. Who is he? A distinction of elements, a particular great element, the sun in the form of a mass of light. For what does he run? For the cessation of the person’s delusion—delusion is bewilderment, for the cessation of that. The meaning is that, by the expenditure of lifespan and so on, he turns away attachment to sense objects. But for those with desires, expanding the fruit of heaven and so on, made of the guṇas, through sacrifices, worship him, the activator of the five-year cycle.

“This” refers to the measure of lifespan calculated as one hundred years according to each one’s own measure. A kalpa is so called because the three worlds are fashioned—created—each day. “Beyond it” means outside the three worlds; “those who know” means the knowers.
“By perfected yoga” means by yoga that has attained perfection.

“By twelve” is to be understood as “by twelve thousand years,” from the force of the following verse. “Sāvadhānam” means “bounded” or “defined”; it includes the sandhyā and the portion at the end, the sandhyāṃśa.

In the Kṛta-yuga [there are] “four thousand” [years], and in its sandhyā and sandhyāṃśa [there are] four hundred [years] in each, thus eight hundred. The same is to be applied to Tretā and the other yugas.

At the beginning of a yuga is the sandhyā; at its end, the portion is the sandhyāṃśa. The yuga is the interval between those two whose numbers of hundreds have been stated. He states its distinguishing feature with “where”: the specific dharma beginning with gavālambha is prescribed there—that is the meaning. General dharma exists even in the sandhyā and sandhyāṃśa.

“Four-footed” means complete. In Tretā and the subsequent yugas it diminishes by one foot at a time. It diminishes because irreligion increases by one foot at a time. This is merely a statement of its nature for the purpose of producing detachment, not for the purpose of restricting dharma.

Beyond the three worlds, extending from Maharloka and the like through Brahmaloka, one thousand four-yuga cycles constitute one day. In that [day] the creator of the universe, Brahmā, closes his eyes—he sleeps.
Here he states the duration of the day in four and a half verses beginning with “at the end of the night.” “Enjoying” means protecting the fourteen Manus; the meaning is “pervading [the period].”
That [creation] is so called because it causes the three worlds to function.
With his own forms—the Manvantara incarnations—with Manu and the others serving as instruments, and with the agency of the Puruṣa manifested, he protects the universe.

He now describes the state that has come with night, in five [verses]. “A portion of darkness” means merely a trace of darkness. “Whose activity is withdrawn” means whose power has been retracted. “In which everything has entered” means in which the entirety has entered.

He makes that [state] clear with “that alone.” “Are dissolved after [it]” is a construction in which the object is expressed as the agent; the meaning is “they become invisible.” How? They are as when the moon and sun are absent.
Being afflicted by the heat of the fire at Saṅkarṣaṇa’s mouth, which is a form of the Lord’s power, they go to Janaloka.
The oceans, swollen by the end of the kalpa, are [meant]. “Violent agitation” is what they possess, and [the waves] are driven by fierce winds.
“Those whose abode is Janaloka” are the inhabitants of Maharloka who have gone there, together with others [who dwell there].
“At the beginning of the former half” means at the beginning of the former half [of Brahmā’s life]. Through these three verses there is merely a statement of the fact.
“That” [yad] is the reason for [the kalpa’s] being called Pādma.
But this [Pādma-kalpa] is mentioned at the beginning of the second [half].

“Thus, after stating the measure of the lifespan of the created beings as determined by Time, he now states the reality free from limitation by Time—‘This Time’ in five verses. It is only spoken of conventionally; its lifespan is not calculated by this sequence. It is the unmanifest, free from the limiting adjunct of the effect, and therefore unlimited, beginningless, and the Self of the universe, the cause of the universe.”

“Because Time is incapable of delimiting that, he says this: although this Time is a lord and capable [of ruling], he is not capable of limiting the complete fullness. For he is lord only of those who identify with their abode, body and home.”

“He explains ‘fullness’: [the cosmic egg] is produced together with the sixteen transformations and the eight prakṛtis. ‘This shell of the universe, into which [he] has entered, is perceived like an atom’—this connects with what follows. What is it like? Inside it extends fifty crore yojanas; outside it is covered by seven [layers], beginning with viśeṣa and earth.”
“With what kind [of coverings]? With those [layers] each successively ten times greater than the measure of the cosmic shell. Not only is this one [cosmic egg] seen; other [eggs] are also seen.”
“The cause of all causes. ‘Dhāma’ means ‘essential nature.’”

“In the Twelfth [chapter], because the creation beginning with the Kumāras and the mind-born [sons] did not prosper, the creation through sexual generation by division of the body—that is, Manu’s creation—is described.”

“‘At first’ means [at the beginning]. In his own creation, Brahmā first created the modifications of ignorance. There, tamas is non-manifestation of one’s true nature; moha is the notion ‘I am [this] body and so on’; mahā-moha is desire for enjoyment; tāmisra is anger when that [enjoyment] is obstructed; and andha-tāmisra is the notion ‘I alone am dead’ at its destruction. The same is stated in the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa]: tamas is non-discrimination; moha is confusion of the inner organ; mahā-moha is the desire for ordinary enjoyment; andha-tāmisra is death; tāmisra is called anger; this fivefold ignorance has arisen for the great soul. Patañjali also states these same [five] as avidyā, asmitā, rāga, dveṣa and abhiniveśa [ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion and clinging to life], saying that there are five afflictions. Or they are those taught by Viṣṇusvāmin: ignorance, error, difference, fear and grief. This is stated in ‘the error arising from one’s own perception,’ and so forth.”
“He did not think it abundant” means “he did not approve of it; he did not rejoice in it.”

Although the creation of Sanaka and the others does not occur in every kalpa, it is spoken of here because it is a Brahmā-creation. In truth, the principal creations and so on alone occur in every kalpa; Sanaka and the others, created in the Brahma-kalpa, merely continue [in subsequent kalpas].
“Svabhūḥ” means Brahmā.
“Avadhyātaḥ” means disregarded. “The instruction was rejected” means [the instruction] was not accepted by those [sons].
“That [child] was his anger”: the child himself was that anger of his.
“Like a boy.”
“Previously” means earlier; indeed, they were made by me.
“Sa-yoṣaṇaḥ” means accompanied by a woman or wife. Create progeny endowed with these places and names.
“Sattva” means strength. “Ākṛti” means the blue-red color. “Svabhāva” means fierceness, by that [strength].
“Seeing the groups of Rudras.”
“Sraṣṭā” means “will create.”
“From adhara-dacchada” means from the lower lip.
To speak of the creation made through another body, he states the reason for abandoning that body, beginning with “Vāk” and so on.
“From you” means from you—those earlier than you, Brahmās and others; by them this was not done. “Others” means those later than you; they too will not do it. “Born of the body” means desire.
“Of the powerful” means of the exceedingly powerful. Even for them this is not “suślokya,” something that produces good fame, when it is the conduct of such powerful persons [that is followed].
“Tanvam” means body.

[The Vedas] arose from the four mouths of the creator Brahmā, who was contemplating “How shall I create [the worlds]?” They were fourfold, assembled and well-connected, as before, in the previous kalpa.

“Cāturhotra” means the work of the four [priests], beginning with Hotṛ and the others. “Karma-tantra” means the expansion of the sacrifice, together with the Upavedas and logic. The āśramas and their occupations also came into being.
“Mukhataḥ” means from the mouths.

He states the order of the creation of the four priests’ functions: “Śastra” is a hymn of mantras not sung, the Hotṛ’s work. “Ijyā” is the Adhvaryu’s work. “Stuti” is praise; “stoma” is the collection of ṛks arranged for that purpose, prescribed in passages such as “the Trivṛt stoma becomes …,” and performed by the Udgātṛ. “Prāyaścitta” is the Brāhma’s [work].
He states the order of the Upavedas: “Āyurveda” and so on. “From his own mouths.” Sthāpatya is the science of Viśvakarma.
He states the order of the sacrificial activities: “Ṣoḍaśī and Uktha” and so on. Purīṣī is the construction [of the altar]; Agniṣṭut is Agniṣṭoma.

“Vidyā” means cleanliness. The highest purity is held, according to Smṛti, to be the knowledge of the Lord by the knower of the field. “Dāna” means mercy, because of the statement that giving fearlessness to living beings is not even equal to a sixteenth part [of something]. Thus there is no contradiction with the First Canto statement: “Penance, cleanliness, mercy and truth are the four legs in Kṛta.”

He states the fourfold divisions of each āśrama beginning with brahmacarya: Sāvitra brahmacarya is the three nights of one studying the Gāyatrī beginning with initiation. Prājāpatya is one year for one observing vows. Brāhma is [brahmacarya] until the completion of Vedic study. Bṛhat is lifelong celibacy. Vārtā is a livelihood such as farming that is not prohibited. Sañcaya is a livelihood beginning with officiating at sacrifices. Śālīna is a livelihood without asking. Śiloñcha is a livelihood based on fallen grains. “One word” is an ancient usage. Thus these are the occupations in household life. Alternatively, “śiloñcha” is a locative singular in a dual compound; the meaning is that, with these distinctions of livelihood, they remain situated in household life.

Four are situated in the forest. Vaikhānasa means a livelihood from food that grows and cooks without cultivation. Vālakhilya means abandoning previously stored food when new food is obtained. Audumbara means living on fruits and so on gathered from the direction first seen after rising in the morning. Phenapa means living on fruits that have fallen by themselves. Kuṭīcaka is primarily devoted to the duties of one’s own āśrama. Bahvoda makes action secondary and knowledge primary. Haṃsa is devoted to the practice of knowledge. Niṣkriya has attained the truth and is inactive. All these are successively superior.

He states the origination of logic and the rest in order, beginning with the first: Ānvīkṣikī and the others are the sciences of liberation, dharma, desire and artha. “Bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ” separately are three [vyāhṛtis]; together they are the fourth. As Āśvalāyana says, “Thus the vyāhṛtis are taught separately and together.” Alternatively, “mahaḥ” is the fourth. The Śruti also says so. “From the small ether of the heart.”
“Snutaḥ” means from the sinews. Anuṣṭubh is “snāvān,” according to the Śruti.

Having stated that in the Mahā-kalpa Brahmā became the form of Śabda-brahman, he now shows that and states the origination of the letters with “sparśa” and a half [verse]. Sparśa is the five groups beginning with ka. Svara is [the vowels] beginning with a. Ūṣman is the set of four—śa, ṣa, sa and ha. Antaḥ-stha are ya, ra, la and va. The seven notes begin with Ṣaḍja and so on. “Vihāra” means play.

Therefore, because Brahmā has sound as his body, he says that the Supreme Lord always shines: Vaikharī is manifest; Praṇava is unmanifest; the Supreme Lord, higher than that Brahmā who has these as his self, shines. What is He like? Brahman is complete; there, in the unmanifest aspect, He shines pervading in the form of Brahman, and in the manifest aspect He shines in the forms of Indra and others, enriched by various powers.

The body previously created, becoming fog, was darkness. Then [he accepted] another body associated with permitted desire. The body of Śabda-brahman, however, always exists. He states the reason for accepting another body with “of the ṛṣis” and so on.
He states the thought itself with “Alas.” “Being occupied” means doing work or engaging in activity.
“While doing” means doing what is appropriate.
Therefore, because Brahmā’s form became twofold, out of astonishment they still call it “kāyam.”
“The woman” means she was his queen.
“They became [growth]” means they attained increase. He explains this with “and he too.”
“Because of whose progeny [the world was filled].”
“In the Thirteenth [chapter], when Manu desired to create, [the account is given of] the earth suddenly submerged, the Lord’s rising as a boar to lift it, and the destruction of the demon.”
“The son of Svāyambhuva,” because he is a portion of his body.
“He whose shelter is Viṣvaksena, Hari himself.”

Therefore he says that his character should be heard. “Of those for whom there is long effort”: this, as the principal meaning, is the meaning of what is heard by those persons whose effort is long. “Īḍita” means praised. “The hearing of qualities” means the hearing of the qualities of those Bhāgavatas in whose hearts Mukunda’s lotus feet are present.

“Sahasra-śīrṣā” [means] Śrī Kṛṣṇa of a thousand heads; “in whom His feet are placed as a pillow” means Śrī Kṛṣṇa affectionately stretches His feet on whose lap. “He addressed him” means he spoke to him—the sage Maitreya. “Being inspired” means being impelled by him.
“Veda-garbha” means Brahmā.

“You alone are the father of everyone,” because you alone are the giver of birth, livelihood and nourishment. Therefore, although you have no need of anything else, still [tell us] by what action our service to you should be; prescribe that—this is connected with the following [line].

O worshipful one, among the actions within our capacity, say which action should be performed; tell us, “This is to be done.” Having performed it, in which [case], [there will be] fame everywhere in this world and progress in the next world.
“To you two” means to you both; “may there be well-being, may there be auspiciousness.” “Please instruct me” means [you have] yourself offered and disclosed [everything]; therefore I am pleased.

“Apaciti” means worship. “Let the command be accepted” is understood. “Free from envy” means those from whom envy has gone—the thought, “Sanaka and the others do not do it; what shall we do?” [has gone].
“Rule the earth” means rule or protect the earth. “The Puruṣa” means Hari.
He will be pleased with you, the protector of the subjects.

“What fault is there for me in the Lord’s not being satisfied, since He is indifferent?” To this he replies with “of whom.” “Whose form is sacrifice” means whose form is sacrifice. “From whom the purpose has departed” means that it is only labor. “Because the self itself is not honored”: because He Himself, the Self, is not honored; when He is not satisfied, one’s own purpose is not accomplished, since He is the Self of all.
“I shall live” means “I will live.” “O destroyer of disease” means destroyer of sin. “Give permission [for the place]” means give permission, [saying] where I should stay.
If [the question is] “which earth?”, he says “whose abode”: that [earth] is the place. “O Lord, of this goddess.”

“Although previously the drinking [of the waters] was done, [the earth] had again suddenly fallen into the waters that had arisen; [she was] submerged. “I shall lift [her]” means “I shall rescue [her].”

He states the thought itself: “While creating” means while [he] exists as creator. “By the waters” means by the waters. “Gone to Rasā” means gone to Rasātala. “Appointed by the Lord for creation”: may He Himself perform or bring about what I am to do.
“Varāha-toka” means a small boar. “Situated in the sky” means being situated in space.
“Citradhā” means “in various ways.”
“Previously [He] was seen to be the measure of the tip of a thumb. A gaṇḍa-śilā is a large stone; [He became] equal to it. “Yajña” means Viṣṇu. “Perturbing my mind by concealing His own form.”
“While [Brahmā] was deliberating thus.” “Jagarja” means “He roared.” “[He was] equal to the king of mountains.”
“By His uncommon roar.”

“Ghargharita” means a sound imitating that species. [It was] the destroyer of the distress that had arisen through uncertainty. The repetition of “they” is intended to indicate their renown. “By the three purifying mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur and Sāma [Vedas],” they praised [Him].
“He whose form is expanded and praised by the Vedas. Therefore he recited the qualities of himself in response. Then, having understood the Brahman—the Veda uttered by them.”
