“Tirodhānena” means by the power of disappearance, even though [they] are perceptible [as present].

“Pratyātmyena” means by a reflection corresponding to the self. A reflection is an appearance of the self. “Ātmanā ātmanaḥ mānaḥ” means admiring oneself by oneself; [it is] the movement, such as shaking the head, of a beautiful person who sees a reflection. Therefore those created by that [reflection] constantly become paired through mutual honoring.
That [form] was in the nature of a reflection. [They praised] him through actions, that is, through descriptions of his valor.

“Bhoga” means expansion, extension, the spreading of the feet and so on, by a body possessing that. “Anupacita” means not grown, not having attained increase. That [body] was endowed with enjoyment, anger, and so on.

From that body, those hairs which fell away became ahis. “Sarpas” means those which crawl by contractions of the feet and so on, moving away from that [body]. Therefore they are Nāgas because they are not [possessed of] “agā”; the meaning is that they are very swift. Because they were born from [a body possessing] bhoga, their necks are greatly expanded by the bhoga, the hood. All these are cruel through association with its anger. Their secondary divisions of species are well known in the Sarpasiddhānta.
When he became one who thought [himself thus], then he created the Manus.
“Pura” means a body, a person-shaped city. He created and gave his own human-form body to them, to those Manus.

“That which has been done by you is well done.” They call this well-done-ness. In that creation of the Manus are rites beginning with Agnihotra. Therefore in this [creation] all of us together eat the food, the share of the oblation, and so on. O Brahman.

Having spoken of the creation of bodies, he speaks of the creation of sages with “by austerity” and so on. “Vidyā” means worship. Here “yoga” means āsana and so on. “Su-samādhi” means samādhi endowed with dispassion, sovereignty, and so on, and he was endowed with that. “Hṛṣīkeśa” means one whose senses are under his own control. Being Hṛṣīkeśa, Brahmā, the sage, created the sages as progeny.
What is that body of which he gave a part? To this he says “yat” and so on. In that are samādhi, yoga, ṛddhi—that is, sovereignty—tapas, vidyā, and virakti.

In the Twenty-first [chapter], the arranging of Kardama’s marriage with Manu’s daughter is described by Viṣṇu, who was pleased by [Kardama’s] austerity and knowledge. “Edhire” means “they increased” or “they made [it] grow.”
The syntactical connection is with the third [verse]: “Tell me how they protected dharma and the earth.”
“Of that Manu.”
“Yuktāyām” [means] endowed with the characteristics of yoga, beginning with yama and so on. “How manyfold did he create offspring?” means, how many sons did he produce?
“Mānavīm” means the daughter of Manu. Having obtained Ākūti and Prasūti as wives, how he created beings—that too should be told; that is the meaning of the conjunction “ca.”
“Daśa-sahasrāṇi saṃvatsarān” is the meaning: ten thousand years.
“Tataḥ” means in that penance. “Kriyā-yogena” means by the method of worship. “Samprapede” means served. [He served] the bestower of boons to the surrendered, the devotees.
“Śabdaika-vedyam” means Brahman known only through sound. Assuming a body consisting of that, he showed that self [to Kardama].

That Kardama, seeing Him situated there, fell upon the earth with his head and praised Him with words; this is the syntactical connection of the four [verses]. “Padma-utpale” means lotus and water-lily, opening in day and night. [He saw] Him whose garland consisted of white lotuses and water lilies, and whose lotus face had a mass of smooth dark locks.
He whose plaything was a white water lily. He whose smile and glance touched the mind, producing joy.
He on whose chest was Śrī, and on whose neck was the Kaustubha.
Whose nature is affection alone, whose dharma is self-established, and whose mind is of that kind.

“Without You, the highest bliss—fie on one who desires other boons. Nevertheless, have mercy on me, the miserable one, by granting the boon.” “Bata” expresses joy. O worshipful one! O reservoir of all being! By us, through seeing you today, the complete fulfillment of the eyes has been enjoyed. He establishes that seeing you alone is the great fruit. Those whose yoga, increasingly brought to excellence by the virtuous over births, has become mature—such yogīs also aspire to that sight of you.

While censuring devotees with desires, he says “those.” O Lord! Those who, for a mere fraction of desires available even in hell, have their intelligence destroyed by Your māyā—only they worship [You]. But You indeed grant them those desires.

Since I, who censure those with desires, am myself such, he says “similarly.” A “gṛhamedha” is a householder. In that [stage], desiring to marry a wife who is a cow yielding the three aims of life, I, wishing to marry, have approached the root, the foot, of You, the desire-yielding tree. “Should something else be worshiped for the sake of desire and so on?” No, because this alone is the root of all the human aims.

“Then why do you not worship only for the sake of liberation?” [The answer is] because of lack of eligibility. He says: O Lord above rulers! Since You are Prajāpati, by Your command this world, struck by desire, is bound like an animal by a rope. O Śukla, embodiment of pure dharma! I too, indeed following the world, bear an offering to You; I follow Your command consisting of action. [I offer it] to the unwinking one, whose nature is time. The meaning of the conjunction “ca” is: “I desire a wife for that purpose.” I do not merely bear an offering as one following the world, but also for the purpose of paying off the three debts—this is indicated by the word “kila.”

By “to the unwinking one” it is said: “I perform action, being afraid of You whose nature is time.” But this fear does not exist for Your devotees; he says this in two [verses]. Having abandoned worldly affairs, those who follow worldly affairs, and beasts, and having disregarded people like me, again inert through action even though discrimination is present, they have taken shelter of the umbrella that is Your feet. He speaks of them: the discussion of Your qualities is wine, because it causes forgetfulness of saṁsāra; it is nectar because it brings delight. By that, the bodily conditions—hunger, thirst, and so on—have been removed by them; this is the syntactical connection with the next [verse].

Your three-naved time-wheel, rotating on the axle that is imperishable Brahman, although running with tremendous speed and cutting short the world, does not run cutting short the lifespan of these devotees. How is it constituted? “Bhrami” means rotation on the axle in the form of ageless Brahman. Although “bhramad” should be said, because of its tendency to move excessively, “bhrami” is used figuratively as a designation of non-difference. It has thirteen spokes, including the intercalary month. It has three hundred and sixty day-and-nights as joints. With the word “śata,” the non-elision of the case ending is an archaic usage. It has six seasons as rims. Innumerable moments and so on are its leaves, streams shaped like leaves. Its three Cāturmāsya periods are the supporting rings, the naves. “Karāla-srotas” means tremendous speed. It should be understood that by these descriptions alone a year-shaped wheel has been described.

“Why do You ask me, who am without adjuncts and indifferent?” Nevertheless, because You are the agent of the creation of the universe and so on through māyā, You alone are to be asked. He says: Although being one alone Yourself, by those powers such as sattva, accepted within the self through Yoga-māyā under Your control and serving as causes, You create that universe. “That universe.” An example for not requiring a means other than Yourself is “as [a spider does].”

Although, because it is produced by māyā, You do not wish to give sense-object happiness to devotees, nevertheless produce it according to our intention; he says “not this.” O Lord above rulers! You expand by Your māyā, for us who worship You, the material world, the state in the form of the subtle elements, and the happiness of sense objects beginning with sound. Although this material world is not desired by You, let it be for our favor and, after the three debts have been paid, for liberation—that is the meaning. When, through Your causeless mercy, You are perceived in an eternal form, splendidly marked by a wreath of Tulasī leaves, the sight of such a You bestows enjoyment and liberation.

I bow to You who grant enjoyment and liberation. The reason for granting liberation is that, through realization, the purpose of action—the enjoyment of the fruits of karma—has ceased in You. The reason for granting enjoyment is that by You the mechanism of the world, the instrument of the universe, has been made to turn through Your own māyā. Therefore I bow to Him whose lotus feet are worshipable by those with desires and without desires. In a person who is insignificant and possessed of desire, or in [his] worship, He showers desires; therefore [He is called] that.
“Amṛtena” means that which produces happiness. He whose eyebrow moves through a glance accompanied by a loving smile.
“Caityam” means the feeling in the heart. “Me” means by Me; that was arranged beforehand. “For the sake of which alone I was worshiped—that [has been arranged].”
Those whose mind has been gathered, concentrated, on Me—whatever worship of Me they perform, in persons like you it certainly should not be utterly false or fruitless.
“Vikhyāta-maṅgalaḥ” means one whose prosperity is well known, characterized by good conduct and so on.
O brāhmaṇa, with your wife or queen.
“Prabho” [means], “O one endowed with the disposition of worshiping Me!”
“Yatra” means in that wife. “Samāhitam” means fixed through resolve or intention. “Nṛpa-vadhū” means a princess, a king’s daughter.

“Te vīryam ātmani bhṛtam” means your seed held within her, retained. She who will give birth will partake [of it]. “Vīrye” means in the daughters produced from the seed. The sages will easily establish sons for themselves [in them].
“Nideśam” means command. “Uśattamaḥ” means pure sattva. “Tīrtham” means a worthy recipient; by that, a gift is indicated. “In Me” means [with] the fruits of all actions offered [to Me].
By household life, having shown compassion, and by renunciation, having given fearlessness, you will see yourself and the universe united as one in Me.
The remainder is understood as: “I will descend into Devahūti together with your seed.”
“Pratyag-akṣajaḥ” means one who is born or manifests in the inward senses. “Pariśritāt” means surrounded by the river Sarasvatī.

Whose path is the path of the Siddhas, the path to Vaikuṇṭha, praised by all the Siddheśvaras perfected through austerity, mantra, and so on. Or, he went along the path of the Siddhas, which is praised by all Siddheśvaras and is sought by Siddhas. Listening to the Sāman made manifest by the wings of Garuḍa, the lord of winged vehicles—for scripture says that the two wings are Bṛhat and Rathāntara—and hearing the uttered Stoma, the collection of ṛks that form the basis of the Sāman—for scripture says “Stoma is the self”—is intended. In the compound reading, “uttered Stoma” means a group of stotriya verses, and the Sāman has that [as its self].

“Śātakaumbhāḥ” means golden; [they are] the ornaments or coverings in which [the chariot is furnished]. Having mounted that chariot, placing his daughter on it, he traveled around for the purpose of searching for a husband. “O Sudhanvan” means Vidura. “Yad ahaḥ” means that day.

To show that by mere entry [into it] he obtained supreme bliss, he describes the hermitage with seven verses beginning with “yasmin.” “Prapanne” means when Kardama had arrived. In which [there was] auspicious, healthy, sweet-as-nectar water.
In which auspicious deer and birds were calling, and which was endowed with clusters, groups, of auspicious trees and creepers.

“Ghuṣṭam” means resounded. In which there was the play or roaming of intoxicated bees. In which there was the display, the dance-excitement, of intoxicated peacocks, who were like dancers. In which intoxicated cuckoos called one another.
Decorated with trees beginning with kadamba.
Chirped sweetly by birds beginning with kāraṇḍava.
Surrounded by deer and so on. There, “kroḍa” means boar; “śvāvic” means porcupine; “marka” means monkey; its variety is “gopuccha.” “Hari” means a monkey or a lion. “Nābhi” means a musk deer.
“Huta” means fire, the fire suitable for a brahmacārin, by which [the offering is made].

“Ugra-yuk” means one whose yoga is intense; [the hermitage was] shining with that body. The speech uttered by that Bhagavān is itself a digit of nectar, a digit of the moon made of nectar. By hearing that nectar, he was not excessively emaciated, although he had become thin through austerity.

“Prāṃśum” means tall. “Upasaṃśritya” means having gone near; the verb “he saw” from the preceding [verse] applies: [he saw him] dirty. “Arhaṇam” means a great jewel, by which [one is honored]; “asaṃskṛtam” means unpolished, so that it appears dirty.
“Uṭajam” means the leaf hut [which he] reached. “Puraḥ” means before him, at his feet. Having greeted the one who bowed with blessings, he received him respectfully with worship.
“Caṅkramaṇam” means touring. “Hi” means because.
He bows to Viṣṇu situated in Manu: [the verse begins] “ya…” “Sthāne” means at the time of each respective function. “Śuklāya” means to Viṣṇu.

The meaning of the five [verses] beginning with “na yadā” is this: Although your coming can occur even as a result of touring everywhere for the protection of dharma, nevertheless, if there is a special task, let that be stated. Having mounted the victorious chariot in which clusters of jewels are set, when you do not tour the globe of the earth, then the religious laws would be broken—this is the syntactical connection of the three [verses]. [It is] one whose Kodanda bow makes a fierce sound. [The laws] by which the varṇāśramas are bound. “Bata” means ah or alas.
“Niraṅkuśair” means by unrestrained men who are the causal instruments. “Śayāne” means while [the king] lies or rests without concern.
“Nirvyalīkena” means with joy, without deceit. “Pratipadyāmahe” means we accept.

In the Twenty-second [chapter], Manu’s giving Devahūti, his daughter, to Kardama, as instructed by Viṣṇu, is described. “Evam āviṣkṛtaḥ” [means] one whose excellence in all qualities and activities has thus been revealed and praised—[he is] Emperor Manu. As if bashful from hearing his own praise, or from apprehension of refusal, he spoke to that sage. “Upāratam” means withdrawn, intent on cessation.

Intending to inform [Kardama], “My daughter is to be married by you,” [Manu says] that the connection between you and us was already arranged by the Lord; he says this in the two and a half verses beginning with “Brahmā.” “Ātmanah parīpsayā” means with the desire to make the self complete or protected. The completion or protection of the self consisting of the Vedas is propagation of the Vedas, by his desire. “Yuṣmān” means you, the brāhmaṇas. “For their protection” means for the protection of the brāhmaṇas. “Brahma” means the brāhmaṇa class; “kṣatra” means the kṣatriya class.
Thus that very Lord protected. Who is he? He who has the nature of cause and effect, who is all-encompassing. Yet he is immutable and changeless.
To inform him, he praises the sight of him and so on in three verses beginning with “tava.”
“Akṛtātmanām” means those whose minds are not brought under control.
Favor is only in the form of instruction and so on. “Uśatīḥ” means beautiful, bright, or pure.
He petitions [him] with seven verses beginning “sa bhavān.” His mind is afflicted by affection for his daughter. The petition has been made heard or communicated.
“Sister of Priyavrata and Uttānapāda” removes the doubt about making her a putrikā. By [the words] “my daughter,” it is shown that she is a kṣatriya girl suitable for you.
“This is Devahūti.”

Objection: attachment to the narration of Hari indeed uproots karma, yet taste for it does not arise. What is to be done? He answers with “for one desirous of hearing”: through service to holy places, there should be service to the great for one who is free of sin; from that comes faith in this dharma, then desire to hear, and then taste—that is the meaning.

Then, in “of those who hear”: [the Lord is] He whose hearing and chanting are holy, the friend and benefactor of the saintly. Being present within the heart, He [removes] the inauspicious things there—the latent desires beginning with lust.

Then, in “when they are almost destroyed”: the word “almost” is used because complete destruction of all inauspiciousness occurs only after realization. Through service to the devotees or to the Bhāgavata scripture, devotion becomes firm and unwavering because there is no cause for distraction.
Rajas and tamas, together with the states arising from them, such as lust—by these the mind is not pierced or overpowered. It becomes clear and quiet.
Through the yoga of devotion to Bhagavān, for one whose mind is serene and therefore whose attachments are released [the realization of Bhagavān’s truth arises].

He states the fruit of realization with “is broken.” The heart itself is the knot—the ego, which has the form of tying consciousness to inert matter. Thus “all doubts” means doubts such as uncertainty. “Actions” means those whose fruits have begun. When Īśvara, who is the Self in His essential nature, is seen and directly realized, [these are destroyed]. The word “indeed” shows that this occurs immediately after realization.

While showing proper conduct, he concludes with “therefore.” Devotion to Vāsudeva is shown as the special object of worship: it brings serenity to the self and purifies the mind. [The reading] “prasādinīm”—“bringing serenity”—is also found.

To establish this very point, he states Vāsudeva’s superiority even though the three beginning with Brahmā are one in essence. Here, although the one Supreme Person alone bears the different names Hari, Viriñci, and Hara for the maintenance, creation, and dissolution of this universe, among them auspicious results arise only from Vāsudeva, whose body is sattva. The sandhi in “Hari-Viriñci-Hara” follows an archaic usage.

With an example, he explains how a distinction in the limiting adjunct produces a distinction in the result. From the earthly [element] comes wood, which by itself lacks movement and illumination; from wood comes smoke, whose nature is movement and which is rich in the action taught by the three Vedas, though only slightly because of its connection with action; from that too comes fire, which is made of the three Vedas because it serves as an instrument of ritual action. Similarly, from tamas comes rajas, and from it a [partial] vision of Brahman that illuminates Brahman. The word “but” indicates that tamas, which has the nature of dissolution, and rajas, through knowledge conditioned by an adjunct, give only a slight approach to Brahman-realization, not realization in full, because rajas is distracting. Brahman-vision comes from sattva. Thus even Brahmā and the others, whose adjuncts are these qualities, possess progressively distinct excellence.

He gives the conduct of earlier authorities as evidence for devotion to Vāsudeva, with “they worshiped.” “Then,” that is, for this reason; “formerly,” the Lord Adhokṣaja, the pure sattva, the embodiment of sattva. Those who follow them likewise here in saṁsāra become fit for welfare.

One may object: some people are also seen worshiping others. True. But seekers of liberation do not worship others; only those with desires do so—this is stated in the next two verses. “Lords of beings” includes, by implication, fathers, lords of progeny, and the like. “Free from envy” means not reviling other deities.

Those whose nature is rajas and tamas; therefore, those whose character is like that of the fathers, elemental beings, and the rest. They desire wealth together with sovereignty and progeny, and so they are of this kind.

Because Vāsudeva was said to be worshipable as the giver of liberation, he now says in two verses that He is also the object toward which all scripture’s intended meaning points. “Those for whom Vāsudeva alone is supreme” means those for whom He alone is the goal of all scriptural purport. One might object that the Vedas are visibly centered on sacrifice. He anticipates this by saying that they too are centered on Vāsudeva, since they are intended for His worship. “Yoga” means the yoga scriptures. One might object that these too are concerned with practices such as posture and breath control; they are said to be centered on Him because those practices are means of attaining Him.

“Knowledge” means the scriptures of knowledge. One might object that they are concerned only with knowledge; knowledge too is said to be directed toward Him. Here “austerity” means knowledge. “Dharma” means the dharma scriptures dealing with gifts, vows, and the like. One might object that these are aimed at heaven; “destination,” meaning the fruits such as heaven, is said to be directed toward Him because it is an aspect of His bliss. Alternatively, by “the Vedas” it is stated that all [scriptures] are directed toward Vāsudeva because the Vedas are their root. In that case, one should understand the passage as answering the objection that the scriptures aim at diverse matters—sacrifices, yoga, ritual practice, and so forth—by saying that even those matters are ultimately directed toward Him.

One may object: the harmony of all scriptures is seen in the Reality endowed with the play of creating the world, entering it, regulating it, and so forth; how then can everything be directed toward Vāsudeva? He answers with four verses beginning “He alone.” These four verses answer the question, “Please describe His glorious deeds.” “With the form of the existent and nonexistent” means in the form of effect and cause. “And without qualities” is construed as “although He is intrinsically without qualities.”

His being the cause of the universe has been stated. He now speaks of the play characterized by entering and regulating it, with “by that.” When the qualities, beginning with space, have unfolded, He enters within them, as though endowed with qualities, as though thinking, “These qualities are under My control,” although in reality He is not so conditioned. For through knowledge—His conscious power—He is expanded and made exceedingly powerful.

He speaks of the play of assuming many forms with “as.” In their own sources—the things that manifest them—He is placed within them, without being confined by them. He is the Universal Self, the Supreme Person. Although He is the inner controller in living beings, He is described as though manifold because each source appears to make Him manifold. Or, [this may be understood] in the form of the knower of the field. The source also records the variant reading “in the form of the field.”

He speaks of the play in the form of enjoyment with “this one.” This Hari is the subtle elements of beings, the senses beginning with hearing, and the mind as the self; through these He is the enjoyer in the four kinds of beings that He Himself has fashioned. This indicates His independence. By His will He enjoys their qualities—the objects corresponding to each—or the causative meaning may be understood: He causes [them] to enjoy. Alternatively, [the verb] may mean “He protects”; in that case the middle voice is an archaic usage, in accordance with the remembered rule “bhuj in the sense of protecting.”

He now answers the question, “Sūta, you know.” “He nourishes” means “He protects.” This is the purpose common to all incarnations. The specific purpose of Kṛṣṇa’s incarnation will be stated in Kuntī’s prayer. “World-nourisher” means the maker of the world. He is attached to the līlā-incarnations among the gods and others.
He speaks of the Tortoise incarnation. The mighty Lord assumed the tortoise—the kūrma form—in the eleventh incarnation and supported [it].

He speaks of the Dhanvantari incarnation. “Dhanvantara” means the form of Dhanvantari; the use of the ordinal “twelfth” first is an archaic usage. He presents the thirteenth [incarnation] itself as the form together with its deeds. After “he made [them] drink,” one must supply “nectar.” “As the woman Mohinī” means in that form, deluding the other demons. Having brought nectar in the form of Dhanvantari, he made [them] drink it in the form of Mohinī—this is the meaning.
He speaks of the Narasiṁha incarnation: [He bore] the Narasiṁha form. “Erakā” means a knotless blade of grass.

He speaks of the Vāmana incarnation with “the fifteenth.” The form is called Vāmana because it diminishes the pride of the wicked, or because it is short. [He is] one wishing to take [the earth] back from him, having cut it away and wishing to seize it.
He speaks of the Paraśurāma incarnation with “incarnation.” “Three times” means threefold; accordingly, “seven times over” means seven occurrences, [making] twenty-one times—that is the meaning.
He speaks of the Vyāsa incarnation with “then.” Seeing people of little intelligence—people of limited understanding—He divided the [Vedic] branches for their benefit.
He speaks of the Rāma incarnation with “in a human.” Having attained human divinity in the form of Rāghava, [He acted thus]; thereafter comes the eighteenth [incarnation].
He speaks of the Rāma-Kṛṣṇa incarnation. In the expression for the twentieth, the letter t is elided in accordance with the meter. Having obtained two births bearing the names Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
He speaks of the Buddha incarnation with “then.” [He is] the son of Ajana. In the reading “son of Jina,” Jina too is that same person. In the midst of the Kīkaṭas, in the region of Gayā.
He speaks of the Kalki incarnation with “thereafter.” At the junction of the ages; at the end of Kali, He will be born from the brāhmaṇa Viṣṇuyaśas.

He states the unmentioned incarnations collectively: “Incarnations are...” As an example of their being innumerable, [he says] “as.” “Undiminishing” means free from decline, from the root √das in the sense of decline. “Rivulets” are small streams flowing from a lake; [they flow] by the thousands.
He speaks of the Lord’s manifestations of power: “the sages,” [and the rest].

He now states the special distinction. Some are portions of the Supreme Person, and some are manifestations of a portion or of a particular power. Although the incarnations beginning with Matsya possess omniscience and omnipotence by virtue of being incarnations, they manifest their powers of knowledge and action only as needed. In empowered authorities such as the Kumāras and Nārada, a portion or a specific power enters them as appropriate: knowledge enters the Kumāras and the others, while power enters Pṛthu and the others. Kṛṣṇa, however, is Bhagavān Himself, Nārāyaṇa directly, because all powers are manifested in Him. He states the purpose common to all of them: the enemies of Indra—the demons—relieve the world when it is afflicted and troubled, making it happy.

He states the fruit of reciting this [account] with “birth.” The birth is secret, exceedingly mysterious. “With purified intent” means being pure. [The devotee] is freed from the mass of suffering, from saṁsāra.

A question may arise: if liberation has been stated, how can there be liberation while the soul remains connected with two bodies? The intended answer is that the connection with the two bodies is only the play of ignorance arising from the Lord’s māyā; therefore its cessation through the knowledge produced by hearing this and the like is reasonable. The gross body of the formless, consciousness-only self—the jīva—is fashioned from the qualities of the Lord’s māyā, in forms beginning with the mahat. It is made in the place of the Self; that is, the body is made to stand in the Self’s place.

When asked how this occurs, he explains with an example that the body is superimposed by covering the true nature. Just as a mass of clouds supported by the wind is superimposed upon the sky by unintelligent people, or just as the dust belonging to the earth is superimposed upon the wind through its grayness and the like, so the body—with the properties of something seen—is superimposed upon the Self, the seer. That is the meaning.

Moreover, the implication is that another form, beyond this gross form, is also superimposed. What is it? It is the unmanifest, the subtle. Its cause is “formed by the unexpanded qualities.” An arrangement means a transformation such as hands and feet; it is formed from qualities that are themselves untransformed. It is called unmanifest because it has no distinctive shape. Why is it accepted? Because it is not seen or heard as an object. Whatever has a distinctive form is seen, as we are, or heard, as Indra is; this is not so. What then is the evidence for its existence? “He is the jīva” means the jīva’s adjunct, since the word jīva is used for the subtle body—the adjunct of the jīva—in passages such as “the jīva, freed from the jīva...” The meaning is that it is imagined as the jīva’s adjunct. One might object that the gross body alone should be the jīva’s adjunct because it is the jīva’s seat of enjoyment; why posit another? He answers: because from the subtle body comes renewed birth. Departure, travel, and return are impossible without it.

Having thus stated the two adjuncts, he declares the jīva’s Brahman-nature by negating them, with “where.” When these gross and subtle forms are negated by right knowledge of one’s true nature, through devotion consisting of hearing, reflection, and the like, they are fit to be rejected. He gives the reason for their being negated by knowledge: they were fashioned in the Self by ignorance. “That is Brahman” means that then the jīva itself becomes Brahman. What is Brahman like? “Vision”: its nature is knowledge alone.

Even so, since the Lord’s māyā—the cause of transmigration—continues to exist, how can there be Brahmanhood? He answers with “if.” “If” is a statement of doubt used in a certainty, as in “if the Vedas were authoritative.” “Vaiśāradī” means belonging to the all-knowing Lord; “this divine [māyā]” plays through the wheel of saṁsāra. When this māyā ceases, what ceases? The intellect, that is, knowledge. The meaning is this: as long as she produces the covering and projection of the Self as ignorance, she does not cease. When that very [māyā] transforms into the form of knowledge, it burns the jīva’s adjunct, which has the form of existent and nonexistent, and then ceases by itself, like a fire without fuel. Then the knowers of truth say, “He is fulfilled,” having attained the nature of Brahman. What follows? He is honored and shines in his own glory, whose nature is supreme bliss.

Just as birth and the rest for the jīva are māyā, so also birth and the rest for Īśvara are māyā—this is stated with “thus.” “The actions of the non-agent” means the deeds of one who is not an agent. “The births of the unborn” means the births of the Lord, the master of the heart and the inner controller.

What, then, is the difference between the jīva and Īśvara? He answers that the difference is independence alone. “The sixfold [field]” means the objects of the six senses. He perceives them from afar, receiving them like a scent, but he does not become attached to them. Why? Because He is the lord of the six qualities, the controller of the six senses.

One may object: what need has Īśvara for the activities of creation and the like, or for enjoyment of sense objects? He answers, “not.” A person of poor understanding cannot know the playful acts of the Ordainer of the world through skill in reasoning and the like. Those who praise [Him] expand the forms with their minds and the names with their speech. The plural “with speech” follows the intention of the Veda; alternatively, it means “together with the minds.”

He says that a devotee somehow knows [Him]. “Without māyā” means with an uncoiled, noncrooked disposition; “continuous” means uninterrupted; “with conformity” means through favorable service. Such a person should worship the fragrance of His lotus feet. “The path” means His essential nature. An old manuscript adds the objection: if no one knows Him, liberation would be impossible. It then explains the same words as saying that one who continually and favorably serves the fragrance of His lotus feet knows His essential nature.

He honors the sages who have entered the path of devotion, because a devotee alone knows the truth of Bhagavān. Therefore, O revered ones, you are omniscient, blessed, and fulfilled. Why? Because through questions such as these you make the movement of your minds take Vāsudeva as its identity—directed to Him alone, who is the Self of all. When this state is present, the terrible cycle of existence, consisting of the sufferings of the womb and the whirl of birth and death, does not occur again.

“Sūta, what is this unprecedented scripture that you are describing?” He answers: it is equal to Brahman and equal to all the Vedas; it contains the deeds of the Most Glorified Lord. Its sage is Vyāsa.
He states the beginning of its transmission through that lineage: “this very [teaching].” “The son” means Śuka.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not explain this verse here.
He was seated with the supreme renunciation of one who has resolved to fast until death. “O brāhmaṇas” means [the words were spoken] from the brāhmaṇa-seer [Śuka].

“I have understood” means “I have known.” Because the word “there” can be construed in different ways, its repetition is not a fault. [I shall narrate] as I learned it, not as a display of my own invention; even there, according to my ability and in accordance with my understanding. I have stated it briefly, and I shall make you hear it in detail.

Here, seeing the mixture of the duties of the ages and the like, that sage reflected on what was beneficial for all classes and stages of life. “Knower of the higher and lower” means one who knows the past and the future. Seeing the mixture of the duties of the ages brought about by time—whose speed is unmanifest—and seeing that condition age after age on earth. “The conditions of material beings” means bodies and the like; their decline is caused by time. “Without sattva” means lacking courage; “of poor understanding” means slow-minded.

The four priests characterized by the Hotṛ, the four reciters, are the four officiants; the ritual to be performed by them is the cāturhotra. “Pure” means purifying, and “for the continuity of sacrifice” means for the uninterrupted succession of sacrifices.
He explains the fourfold division itself with “Ṛg,” and so forth. “Separated” means made distinct.
“Dāruṇa” means cruel, because of the undertaking of practices such as the black-magic rites taught in the Atharva Veda.
“Dividing” means having separated them.
He states the purpose of dividing the Vedas with “those very.” Those very [Vedic branches] that had formerly been retained by people of exceptionally great intelligence.

“Women and śūdras” means the relatives of the twice-born, the lowest among the three higher classes. For them, let welfare—the means to good in the form of religious action—be attained in this very manner. Therefore, out of compassion for them, the sage composed the account of the Mahābhārata.

In this manner, for the welfare and good of living beings, even through action directed toward the Self of all. His heart was not greatly satisfied. Considering the reason for this lack of satisfaction, he spoke these words to himself.
“Without deceit” means with an honest, guileless mind: they honored and worshiped [him].

“Embodied” means the self who has become identified with the body; in truth that self is all-pervading and complete. Through his own essential nature he only appears as though incomplete, as though he had not attained identity with it. “Brahma-radiance” means the splendor produced by excellence in hearing and teaching the Veda. Among those who possess that radiance, he is the very best. Or, he not only appears as though incomplete, but even though possessing Vedic radiance he appears as though he were not the best. A variant reading says “even though most charming.”
He himself considers the reason for his incompleteness with “why.” “Mostly” means to a great extent, because those very dharmas are dear to Acyuta.

One may object: if the path of activity is censured, then on the path of renunciation, with all actions abandoned, what need is there even to speak of Hari’s glory, since one directly experiences the Lord’s blissful nature? He answers with “discerning.” Only someone discerning, who has withdrawn from all activity, is capable of knowing the Lord’s blissful, nondual nature; a person lacking discernment, whose nature is activity, is not. He is infinite because His deeds have no end in time and no boundary in space. Therefore, O Infinite One, show Him to a person identified with the body and therefore acting through qualities such as sattva. Another reading has the vocative “O becoming one.”

So far he has said that desired dharma is a cause of harm and that Hari’s līlā alone should be described. Now, with the intention that even steadfastness in one’s obligatory and occasional duties should be disregarded in favor of instruction solely in Hari-bhakti, he says “having abandoned.” One may object: if a person worships after abandoning his own duty and becomes fulfilled through the ripening of devotion, there is no concern. But if he dies or falls while still immature, there would be harm caused by abandoning his own duty. He answers: if he falls from worship, dies, or otherwise slips, there is no fear of harm for one who relishes devotion, since he has no qualification for karma. Even if such a person were born in a low womb, where could his misfortune be? None at all, because the latent tendency toward devotion remains. But for those who do not worship, what benefit has anyone gained merely from his own duty? The genitive in “of those who do not worship” is intended only to express relation.

One may object: even from the action of one’s own duty there is indeed the fruit of reaching the world of the ancestors, as the revelation says. He answers with “for that alone”: one should strive for that purpose—the bliss of Bhagavān’s devotion—which wandering beings, from the highest Brahmā down to immovable life, do not obtain. The genitive has the same force as before. Sense pleasure, however, is obtained by other means, through previous action, everywhere, even in hell, just as suffering is obtained without effort. A manuscript adds: “He should strive only for the bliss of devotion to Bhagavān, because it is difficult to obtain.”

He establishes the statement “where could his misfortune be?” A servant of Mukunda, even if somehow born in a bad species, will never enter transmigration like one devoted only to action. Why? Because, remembering the embrace of Mukunda’s feet, he would not wish to abandon it again. This person is seized and controlled by the taste of devotion; alternatively, he is one whose attachment to the delightful rasa is firm. As Bhagavān said: “Then he strives again for perfection, O joy of the Kurus; carried by that former practice, he is drawn onward even against his will.”

Having said that Hari’s līlā should be described as the chief subject, he asks: who is Bhagavān, and what are His līlās? “This universe is Bhagavān Himself.” Yet He is other than this universe: the world is not separate from Īśvara, whereas Īśvara is separate from the world. The reason is that the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world arise from Bhagavān; these very acts display His līlā. Alternatively, “this universe is Bhagavān” means that the jīva, who appears to be other, is also Bhagavān. The conscious and unconscious world has no existence apart from Him; He alone is the one Reality. The word “indeed” indicates the authority of statements such as “all this is Brahman.” You yourself know this. “A measure of space” is displayed to fulfill the meaning of the revelation “a person who has a teacher knows.”

He says that you have no need of a teacher because you are an incarnation of Īśvara. O you of unfailing vision, know yourself—although unborn—as born for the welfare of the world. Why? Because you are a portion of the Supreme Person. Let the greatness and exploits of mighty Hari be described and made prominent.

He says that all your austerity and the rest will thereby bear fruit. “Hearing” and the other words denote steadfastness in these practices. This alone is the unfailing, eternal meaning and fruit of austerity, hearing, and the like: the description of the qualities of the Most Glorified Lord.

He elaborates the fruit of hearing Hari’s account in the company of the good through his own history. In a former kalpa, in a previous birth, I became the son of a servant woman of reciters of the Veda. I was appointed to serve the yogins. This occurred during the rainy season, the four-month period, when they wished to remain together in one place.
All fickleness had departed from him; he was self-controlled, with his senses restrained. He had abandoned the means of play and was compliant, following their wishes.

With the permission of the twice-born, he used to eat the remnants clinging to their vessels. Through that food I became free from sin. The continuation is that his mind developed a taste for their dharma: worship of the Supreme Lord alone.

“I heard” means “I learned.” “With my faith” means with a faith naturally perfected in me, not one forcibly produced by someone else; therefore the word “my” is not redundant. “Step by step” means every word. [I heard it] in Him whose fame is dear to hearing.

Having developed a taste for the Lord whose fame is dear to hearing, my mind became steady, unfailing, and unobstructed. Through that mind I see only the defining mark of the gross and subtle body projected by my own māyā, my own ignorance, in me, the Brahman beyond the world—not that such a body truly exists.

Thus, when the meaning of “you” had been purified and known, and the distraction produced by the body and the like had ceased, firm devotion arose—the devotion that removes its causes, rajas and tamas. “The glory of Hari continually” means at the three times of day.

[This is spoken] of me, whose meaning of “you” had been purified by knowledge and whose devotion had become firm, and who was humble. “Most secret” is knowledge of the truth of dharma that serves as the means; the knowledge of the distinct Self that is attained through it is more secret; and knowledge of Īśvara, attained through that, is the most secret. They taught the Bhāgavata scripture, the scripture spoken by Bhagavān.
He shows that very knowledge by discriminating it from the previously described knowledge of the meaning of “you,” with “by which alone.” “I knew” means “I came to know.”

He indicates the secret of the dharma that serves as the means. It is the medicine that removes the threefold affliction and purifies sattva. What is it? Action offered to Bhagavān. What is Bhagavān like? He is Īśvara, the controller of all, and yet He is also Brahman, whose complete nature never falls away.

One may object: how can action, which is the cause of transmigration, remove the threefold affliction? He answers with two verses that it is possible because the materials differ, giving an example. The very substance—such as ghee—from which a disease arises, being itself merely the cause of that disease, does not purify or remove it. But when it is combined with other substances as a medicine, it does purify it, as in the example.

Thus actions become capable of bringing about the destruction of the self—that is, the cessation of action—when they are offered to the Supreme Lord. The sequence is shown: first service to the great, then His grace, then faith in His dharma, then hearing the Lord’s story, then love for Bhagavān, through that knowledge distinguishing the two bodies, then firm devotion, then knowledge of Bhagavān’s truth, and finally, through His grace, the manifestation of divine qualities such as omniscience.
One may object: ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, and that knowledge arises from bhakti-yoga; how, then, can action destroy action? He answers with “what is here.”

He shows through proper conduct that action performed as an offering to Bhagavān produces bhakti-yoga. When they perform actions according to Bhagavān’s instruction, they recite and remember the qualities and names of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. That instruction is: “Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī, do that as an offering to Me.”
The role of devotion in the form of recitation and remembrance has been stated; he now states its role as the cause of knowledge in two verses. “We meditate with homage” means “we bow mentally.”
“Formless” means without a form other than the form expressed in the mantra. The person who worships Him becomes one of correct vision.

Thus, when I had acted in this way, Hari gave me knowledge and the rest, making me like Himself. He says this with “knowing.” Knowing His own instruction as practiced by me, and also my loving feeling [toward Him].

Therefore you too should act in this way. O one of boundless learning, proclaim the renowned glory of the Infinite. By hearing and understanding it, the desire of the learned to know is brought to completion; those afflicted by suffering do not regard another method as a means of calming their afflictions.
His mind was conquered and brought under control by devotional feeling, and his eyes were filled with drops of tears born from eagerness.
His limbs were covered with horripilation from the overwhelming weight of love, in a great flood of bliss, the vast ocean of supreme joy. He saw both—himself and the Supreme [Lord].
“The beloved of the mind” means the desired object. “That which removes sorrow” means that which takes away grief. “I arose” means “I became upright.”
Having placed the mind in the heart and made it steady, I became unsatisfied and distressed, as though unable to bear the separation; this is supplied by the context.
“Beyond the range of speech” means Īśvara, who is the object of perception. A variant reading says “beyond the range of the Vedic words.”

“Alas” is a compassionate form of address. “Do not [show Yourself to] me” means “I am not fit to see You.” Why? Because the impurities, such as lust, of unsuccessful yogins—those whose yoga has not reached completion—have not been matured and burned.

“Where, then, were You seen?” He answers: “I showed it only once,” and did so in order to create attraction toward Me. What use is desire directed toward You? He answers: “the man whose desire is for Me”—the desires that lie in the heart.
Even through a short period of service to the good, and after abandoning what is blameworthy, he will leave this body and attain My people, the status of My attendants.
“In the creation of beings” means in their creation, and “in their restraint” means in their dissolution. Alternatively, it means the restraint of the creation of beings.

That well-known great wonder is the breath of the Great Being, as in the revelation “this is the Ṛg Veda,” and so forth. What is He like? Īśvara, the controller of all. “Whose sign is the sky” means whose form is the sky. Though present, He is not marked by anything; He is the signless one. To that unseen Bhagavān I offered my reverence, bowing down. Through this I became the recipient of His compassion.

While continually reciting the names of the Infinite, I became free of shame and free of envy; this is supplied by the context. An old manuscript does not contain the words from “of the Infinite” through “reciting.”

At the appointed time, death appeared suddenly, like lightning. “Like lightning” gives the example of sudden appearance. The adjective “sau­dāminī” makes the comparison vivid. It may refer to a garland named Sudāmā, meaning lightning born at its edge; alternatively, Sudāmā may be a crystal mountain, and lightning born near a mountain of crystal is especially clear. Or “lightning” may mean something near at hand, according to the etymological tradition. An old manuscript preserves the explanation beginning with “Sudāmā” through the etymological citation.

When the Lord applied that [form] to me—namely, the pure, sattva-made body of a Bhagavān’s attendant that had been promised when He said, “Having abandoned this blameworthy world, you will attain My people”—the karma that had begun to bear fruit came to an end, or the end of the begun karma was itself its result. My five-element body fell. This indicates that the bodies of the Lord’s attendants are not produced by karma, and are pure, eternal, and so forth.

After taking in and withdrawing the three worlds, I entered, together with the breath, into the middle of the all-pervading Brahmā, who wished to sleep upon the waters of the single ocean. A passage of the Kūrma Purāṇa says: “Then, descending, the Universal Self entered the body of the discus-holder and attained Vaiṣṇavī sleep, becoming one with Viṣṇu.” In the reading “in his own resting place, in the waters,” understand that “Brahmā” is spoken with the intention of expressing non-difference from Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
From the vital airs and senses, I and the sages headed by Marīci were born.

Those devoted to action do not go beyond; those who have reached Brahma-loka through austerity and the like do not go within. But, by the grace of Mahā-Viṣṇu, while maintaining an unbroken vow of celibacy, I wander both within and without. My movement is unobstructed everywhere. A variant reading says “those who have gone to the outer world.”

Why do you wander? He answers: by the command of the Lord, for the welfare of the world. “Given by the Lord” means given by Īśvara. The seven notes—niṣāda, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, ṣaḍja, madhyama, dhaivata, and pañcama—are Brahman because they reveal Brahman; he is adorned with them. This means that he possesses the naturally established seven notes. “Having formed a melody” means having made it rich with melodic elaboration.
He states his own purpose: “he sings forth.”

He states the purpose for others. “Measures” are the sense objects, and “contacts” are their enjoyments; their minds are distressed by desire for them. The recitation of Hari’s deeds alone is a boat in the ocean of becoming. This is not established merely by the authority of revelation; it is directly seen through agreement and difference—when it is present, and when it is absent.

He strengthens the certainty “this alone” through experience. What does not pacify the mind through restraints and the other disciplines pacifies it directly through service to Mukunda. If it is pacified somehow by service to Mukunda alone, how much more by describing His qualities? That is the meaning.
What pleases your mind has also been explained.
“Having addressed” means having requested and given permission. “Spontaneous” means free from any resolve directed toward his own personal purpose.

“I wipe away” means “I remove the tears of sorrow.” The phrase “O brāhmaṇa’s lowest” identifies Droṇa’s son as an aggressor: tradition remembers six kinds of aggressor—one who sets fire, poisons, attacks with a weapon, steals wealth, seizes land, or takes another’s wife. Here “aggressor” indicates one armed with a weapon and, by implication, the killing of a son. “I shall bring [him] before You” means “I shall bring him near with arrows released from the bow Gāṇḍīva.” “Having placed his head upon the ground” means having made it a seat; though a son, he was still unshaven.

“Graceful” means beautiful and varied speech. “He” means Arjuna. Acyuta alone was his friend and charioteer. He was armored, carried a formidable bow, and had the monkey, Hanumān, on his banner. He pursued the Guru’s son in his chariot.

“Rushing upon” means running toward them; he is Droṇa’s son, the killer of a child. His mind was agitated and his heart trembled. He desired to preserve his life, not his fame, and fled across the earth as far as he could go. The comparison is to Brahmā fleeing in fear of Rudra after becoming an animal and attempting to obtain his daughter. A reading “like the sun” alludes to a story in the Vāmana Purāṇa: a demon named Vidyunmālī received a golden aerial vehicle from Rudra, flew behind the sun and darkened the night with its radiance; the sun drove it away and brought it down, and Rudra, angered on hearing this, fled in fear of the sun. The demon’s vehicle fell at Vārāṇasī and became known as Lolārka.

“Without refuge” means without protection. One might think that flight itself is his protection; no, for that too was brought to a halt. “With weary horses” means the chariot whose horses were exhausted. “The weapon of Brahma’s head” means the brahmāstra. “Son of a twice-born” indicates his lack of foresight.
That was the brahmāstra. “Collected” means having concentrated his awareness. Though he did not know how to withdraw the weapon, the reason he could launch it was that he was in mortal danger.
Seeing the radiance released from the weapon blazing in every direction, and then seeing the danger to his life.
Before presenting his request, he first praises Kṛṣṇa in four verses. For those being burned by saṁsāra, He is the liberation—the one who frees them from it. This is the meaning.

You are directly Īśvara. Why? Because You are the Person beyond prakṛti. Why is that so? Because You are the primal cause. Although He is the cause, he states His changelessness: having overcome māyā, He remains established in the Self whose nature is liberation.

You alone also give the three human aims, he says with “He.” You who remain having overcome māyā arrange the fruits of dharma and the rest for the person overcome by māyā. This is done through Your power.

By this incarnation too, Your favor toward the side of the good is revealed. Could the burden of the earth not be removed by Your mere will? He answers: [You appeared] for the contemplation and protection of Your own relatives, and also for Your one-pointed devotees.
Having praised Him, he presents his request: “What is this, what is its nature, and from where does it arise?” The word “perhaps” expresses uncertainty.

This is the weapon of Brahmā belonging to Droṇa’s son. When his life was threatened, it was merely displayed; he was not skilled in using it, because he did not know how to withdraw it. “You know this” means “You understand this matter.”

“Withdrawal” means making it thin and bringing it to an end. Therefore destroy the blazing, formidable power of that weapon with the power of the brahmāstra itself. Your weapon, once launched, will subside on its own after you withdraw it, since you are skilled in weapons.

“The enemies” are those very foes, and “the hero who kills them” is Phālguna, Arjuna. Having touched water and performed ācamana, he circumambulated Śrī Kṛṣṇa. He did this in order to withdraw the brahmāstra.

The powers of the two brahmāstras, enclosed by their arrows, met one another and grew. They covered heaven, earth, and the sky, just as at dissolution the fire from Saṅkarṣaṇa’s mouth and the sun, joining together, increase in force.
“The two” are Droṇa’s son and Phālguna. Those being burned by them thought the radiance to be the fire of universal dissolution.
“The disturbance of the worlds” means their overturning and destruction. Perceiving Vāsudeva’s intention, he withdrew both brahmāstras.

He was the son of Kṛpī, born in the line of Gautama. His eyes were copper-red from anger. The comparison for his lack of compassion is to an animal. The comparison for binding him as a matter of dharma is to a sacrificial animal; the rope is the cord with which he was bound.

To establish that Arjuna remained devoted to dharma even while overcome by grief and anger, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s words are given in six verses. He desired to take [Droṇa’s son] to the camp, the royal residence, and appeared to be angry.

Just as the jīva’s birth and the rest are māyā, so also the birth and the rest of Īśvara are māyā—this is stated with “thus.” “The actions of the non-agent” means the deeds of one who is not an agent. “The births of the unborn” means the births of the Lord, the master of the heart and the inner controller.

Even the killing of an enemy who is asleep, and of a child, is not righteous. He demonstrates this through alternatives: one intoxicated by drink; one heedless; one insane through possession or madness; one dull and unable to act; one who has taken refuge; and one whose chariot has been broken.

His killing in the form of punishment is itself his welfare, the attainment of his human purpose. For without the fault being removed by punishment and atonement, that person would descend to a lower state. The tradition says: “People who have committed sins, when kings inflict the proper punishment, go to heaven purified of their stain, like the righteous.”
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.
Although he had been instructed to do so, he did not wish to kill even the killer of a son, because he himself was a great and noble person.
“The beloved charioteer of Govinda” means the one whose charioteer was dear Govinda. He acted for the sake of the mother who was grieving for her sons.

He was brought in this way, with contempt, and made to face downward by the blameworthy act he had committed. Seeing the offender with compassion, she—whose disposition was gentle and beautiful—[spoke].
The two actions “he bowed” and “he spoke” indicate his agitation and bewilderment. He could not bear bringing him in bound.

“Together with the secret” means together with the concealed mantra. “Release” and “withdrawal” mean the use and retraction of the weapon; the group of weapons is included with both. Moreover, Kṛpī is the body, the very self, of Droṇa, and is his half. The revelation says that the wife is half of a man’s self, and the ritual texts show that husband and wife have one form through the fire rite. One may object: if her husband was dead, how did she live? He answers: she did not follow her husband, because she was the mother of heroes and had sons.
Therefore, O rulers acting in this matter, the venerable family of your teacher must not be made to undergo suffering. Rather, it must be honored and revered.
“One whose child has died” means one whose son is dead.

He states the opposite fault with “by whom.” The action of that royal family, together with its descendants, is afflicted and pervaded by grief; it burns the family of the brāhmaṇas, whose members are the agents [of the punishment].

The six qualities of the queen’s speech are to be seen in the six preceding verses: “righteous” means not contrary to dharma; “just” means not contrary to justice; “with the secret” and the rest are explained accordingly; “with compassion” is “he is half of her self”; “without deceit” is “O knower of dharma”; and “equally” is “do not let both [mothers] cry,” because their suffering is equal. “The great one who was angered” is a stern statement offered as beneficial instruction. O brāhmaṇas, the king approved and welcomed the queen’s words.
Nakula and the others also approved. Yuyudhāna is Sātyaki.
For Droṇa’s son, in that condition, killing alone was best; otherwise there would be the prospect of his falling into hell. “He killed” means “he slew.”

The meaning of the statement about four arms is this: when Bhīma began to kill him and Draupadī suddenly began to stop it, Kṛṣṇa manifested four arms in order to restrain both. Arjuna, His friend, was uncertain about what to do.

“Worthy of killing” means one who deserves death. “A brāhmaṇa must not be killed” is the rule established by the scripture I have made. Yet tradition also says: “Even an aggressor who is learned in Vedānta may be killed; by that one does not become a killer of a brāhmaṇa.” Uphold both instructions.

He says, “Fulfill your promise.” While consoling the beloved Draupadī, you promised his killing; make that promise true, and make it pleasing. In killing him, Bhīma’s wish is fulfilled; in not killing him, Draupadī’s wish is fulfilled; both wishes are Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s concern.
Do not regard this subduing of the brahmāstra as an ordinary matter; do not think the Lord is merely human. “This universe” is [also included in the wonder being revealed].
[She offers this obeisance] together with Kṛṣṇā, Draupadī.

“I bow to You.” One might object: how can You bow to me, who am younger? He answers: You are the Primal Person. Why? You are beyond prakṛti. Why is that? You are Īśvara, the controller even of prakṛti. Therefore You are established as the fullness within and without all beings. Yet You remain unperceived.

Māyā itself is a curtain, a concealing power; by it You are covered. Therefore I, being ignorant and unacquainted with bhakti-yoga, merely bow to You. You are called Adhokṣaja because knowledge born from the senses does not reach You. You are imperishable and unlimited, and so You are not perceived by a deluded person identified with the body.
This is for the supreme swans—the paramahaṁsas—in their discrimination between the Self and the non-Self. Indeed, [even] women [may approach You in this way].
Having stated that You can be reached through the yoga of knowledge and devotion, she again simply offers obeisance, in the two verses beginning “to Kṛṣṇa.”
“Whose navel is a lotus”; “whose garland is made of lotuses”; “whose eyes are clear like lotuses”; and “to Him whose feet are marked with lotuses.”

She remembers the favors He has bestowed, saying this in two verses. The meaning is: Your affection for me is even greater than a mother’s. “O Hṛṣīkeśa, just as Devakī, imprisoned by Kaṁsa, was freed by You, have I likewise been freed?” The rhetorical question expresses a great difference. She was imprisoned for a long time and freed only once, and she was afflicted by grief; her sons were not protected, and she has another protector. I, however, together with my sons, was repeatedly and quickly protected from a multitude of dangers, and You alone were our protector.

He now enumerates the multitude of dangers: Bhīma’s poisoning through the giving of poisoned food; the great fire, the burning of the house of lac; the man-eating demons, such as Hiḍimba, through encountering them; and the wicked assembly, the place of gambling. We were protected from all sides.
In those very calamities, what kind of vision was there? A vision from which there is no return to worldly existence and no repeated seeing of You [as the indwelling Lord].

Prosperities, however, stand in the way of the highest good, she says. “Birth in a noble family”; “one whose pride grows through birth and the like”; and even the ability to utter “Śrī Kṛṣṇa Govinda”—You are an object within the reach only of those who possess nothing.

She bows again to fulfill her present wish. You are the entire wealth of devotees who possess nothing. From You the movements of the qualities concerned with dharma, artha, and kāma have withdrawn; therefore You are the Self-delighting One. Why? You are peaceful, free from attachment and the like. Moreover, You are the Lord of liberation, capable of granting it.

One might object: “Why do you praise Me in this way, when I am the son of Devakī?” She answers: “I consider You Time, not merely Devakī’s son.” The reasons are that You are the Lord, the controller; beginningless and endless; all-pervading; and moving equally everywhere. One might object: how can You be equal when You were Pārtha’s charioteer? She answers: conflict arises among beings because of You, who are its instrumental cause; there is no partiality or inequality in You Yourself.

One might object: partiality in the form of punishment and favor toward me is well known. He answers: there is no such partiality. It is only the imitation of human behavior by one who acts through You, in whom an apparently unequal attitude of favor and punishment is seen.

Those are the births of the Unborn and the actions of the Non-agent: among animals, birth in the form of Varāha and the like; among humans, in the form of Rāma and the like; among sages, in the form of Vāmana and the like; and among aquatic beings, in the form of Matsya and the like.

The imitation of a human being is exceedingly wondrous, she says with “the cowherd woman.” When You had broken the curd pot and Yaśodā took up a rope to bind You, that condition of Yours at that very moment bewilders me. Your face was lowered because You stood fearing that she would beat You; Your eyes were agitated, mixed with tears and collyrium. Even fear itself fears You—yet this was Your condition.

Because Your birth and the rest are difficult to understand, being bewildering to the world, they describe them in many ways, she says in four verses beginning “some.” Some speak for the fame of the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira; or, the phrase may mean “for the fame of the Yadu dynasty,” just as sandalwood is spoken of through the fame of the Malaya lineage.

In Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva, You, though unborn, appeared as a son; “to become a son” is supplied. The use of the first person is an archaic form. The reading “to become a child” is clearer. Earlier, in the forms of Sutapā and Pṛśni, You had been requested by those two for the welfare of this world.
This is said with the intention of giving prominence to Brahmā’s prayer.

An alternative interpretation is this: ignorance of the Self whose nature is supreme bliss gives rise to identification with the body; from that identification comes desire, and from desire come actions. For the cessation of the suffering caused by these, he will undertake actions such as hearing.

He now establishes this interpretation as the conclusion and states the fruit of hearing and the rest. Those people rejoice in the deeds recited by others; they see Your lotus feet themselves, and see them soon—the word “only” is understood throughout. What are those feet like? They are the feet in which the cessation of the stream of becoming, the succession of births, is present.

With the intention that Your abandonment of us today would be improper, she speaks in four verses beginning “also.” O Lord, do You perhaps even now wish to abandon us, Your exceedingly affectionate friends and dependents? We have no other refuge. Why? We are those upon whom suffering has been imposed by kings. “O You whose own action was expected” is a form of address to one from whom protection was expected; the reading ending with a visarga makes “You” an adjective.

One might object: “Your relatives, the Yadus, and your sons, the Pāṇḍavas, are heroic and capable; why do you speak so helplessly?” She answers: whenever You do not see us, then, despite the names and forms by which the Yadus and Pāṇḍavas are famous and prosperous, who are we? No one—we are utterly insignificant. Just as, when the soul who rules the senses is not seen, there is no meaningful name or form, so it is with us.
Moreover, just as this earth, which we protect, now shines because it is marked by the signs of Your feet—vajra, goad, and the like—so then, when You have departed, it will not shine.
Moreover, these settlements and lands are prosperous and well furnished with abundance.

If the Pāṇḍavas depart, it is harmful; if the Yadus depart, it is also harmful. Thus, with her mind agitated in both ways, she prays that Your affection for them not cease. The addresses beginning “Lord of the universe” show Your power to cut the bonds of affection. “Firm” means firmly established.

What follows from this? She says: “May my mind, being directed to You alone, bear uninterrupted love.” “Flood” means a full stream. Just as the Gaṅgā does not heed an obstruction, so may the mind not heed obstacles.

Having made this request, she bows again. She addresses Śrī Kṛṣṇa repeatedly while remembering His favors: friend of Arjuna, the friend of Kṛṣṇa; best of the Vṛṣṇis; destroyer of the royal lineages that oppose the earth; and One whose unconquered power is never diminished. “Govinda” means the Lord possessing the wealth of wish-fulfilling cows, and the One whose incarnation removes the distress of cows, brāhmaṇas, and the gods.

He whose entire glory has risen was praised with words containing graceful, sweet phrases. The verb means “to praise”; the long syllable is used in accordance with the meter. “Gently” means slightly. His smile itself is māyā; it will later be said that a smile can bewilder people.

Accepting the request “may my mind have no other object,” He came from the place of the chariot to Gajasāhvaya, Hastināpura. He took leave of Subhadrā and the other women, headed by her, intending to go to His own city. King Yudhiṣṭhira lovingly requested Him to remain there for some time, and so He was detained.

He introduces the account of Bhīṣma’s departure. Although Vyāsa and the others had awakened him, he remained covered by grief and did not attain discernment. Why? It was the Lord’s intention: the king had to go to Kurukṣetra with him for the great festival of the departure of the Lord’s devotee Bhīṣma, and Bhīṣma himself had to awaken him. Those who did not know the Lord’s intention, which ordained these two tasks, could not understand it. Even when Śrī Kṛṣṇa awakened him, he did not awaken. The reason was the Lord’s wondrous action: just as He went to reconcile the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas yet, while speaking appropriately, firmly established their conflict, so here, while awakening him, He firmly established his bewilderment.
He elaborates upon this lack of understanding in six verses. “With a material self” means with a mind covered by ordinary lack of discrimination. O brāhmaṇas.

“For the sake of another’s body” means for the body that is food for dogs, jackals, and the like. “By me” means by me [the killing was done]. An akṣauhiṇī is the number of troops called an akṣauhiṇī. Vyāsa gives its enumeration: 21,870 chariots and the same number of elephants, 109,350 soldiers, and 65,610 horses. Those who know the true principles of counting call this the proper numerical constitution of one akṣauhiṇī.
“Friends” means relatives; “companions” means close friends; “fathers” means uncles.

One might object: the instruction based on sacred memory says that killing enemies in a righteous war is not sinful. He answers that this rule is only for the protector of subjects. The meaning is: killing is permitted when one’s own subjects are threatened by another, but Duryodhana killed them while they were under my protection, solely from greed for the kingdom; therefore this is certainly sinful.

Even if the killing of men in war is accepted as righteous, I am not capable of removing the treachery toward the women whose relatives were killed by me, although that treachery was not explicitly commanded. It is the householder’s [duty and means] that is involved here.

One might object: the revelation says that one crosses all sin, even brahma-killing, by performing the aśvamedha and by knowing it in this way; therefore sin should indeed be destroyed by the aśvamedha. He rejects this argument, which has arisen from lack of discrimination, with an example. Just as muddy water is not cleansed by thick mud, and impurity caused by a little wine is not cleansed by a great quantity of wine, so one act of killing living beings, arising through negligence, cannot be cleansed by sacrifices whose chief feature is extensive killing.

One may ask: how could Time overtake Kṛṣṇa? He answers by pointing to Him: “Nothing is to be done by Him,” meaning that He has no desired action left to perform. “Of whom there is a desire to know” means that the question concerns the One whose intention is being sought.

Having determined that pleasure, pain, and the like are governed by fate and depend upon Īśvara, he became a follower of that Lord. O Master, Lord of the lineage passed down through generations, protect the helpless people.
He says that Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone is to be followed as the Supreme Lord. This alone is Bhagavān, the Lord of all. Why? He is the Primal Person. And why is that? Because He is Nārāyaṇa directly.
He establishes that point: “power” means influence and majesty.

Through ignorance you think Him to be a maternal cousin, the son of Devakī; dear, an object of affection; a friend, one who creates affection; the best of well-wishers, one who helps without expecting help in return; and, through your trust, you made Him your minister.

One might object: if He is Īśvara, how did He engage in such low work as driving a chariot? He answers: there is not even the slightest inequality in His judgment of what is suitable or unsuitable, what is high or low, because He is free from blame and from attachment and the like. Why is that so? He is without ego; beyond duality; of equal vision; and, above all, the Self of everyone. Alternatively, this is a chain of reasons, each explaining the preceding one.
Even though He is equal toward all, He has shown compassion toward me. O King, [this is the meaning].

He now prays that Śrī Kṛṣṇa remain until the giving up of his own body, in two verses. “As long as” indicates delay; “I leave” indicates independence. “This” is understood as non-Self. His lotus face is beautiful with a gentle smile and reddish eyes. He is the object of meditation; He whom others merely conceive in meditation stands before me and waits for me—that is the meaning.
Having heard those compassionate words.

He says that he described duties according to the ordinary human disposition. “According to the class” means the duties of one’s social class; “according to the stage of life” means the duties of one’s āśrama. The characteristics of both—the path of renunciation and the path of activity—are arranged according to the two conditioning factors, detachment and attachment.

He states the special teachings there with “giving.” “Duties of liberation” means restraint, control, and the like. “Duties of Bhagavān” means practices that please Hari, in the form of observances such as the Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī vows. Condensation and expansion are themselves the two methods, the two means; [he taught] by both of them.

He described dharma and the rest according to each person’s qualification, together with the specific means suited to that person; and he described the histories in the various narratives just as they are found there.
“Whose death was according to his will” means that death came according to his own intention.

“Leader of thousands” means Bhīṣma, who leads and protects a thousand chariot warriors stationed near him in battle. In the reading “possessing thousands,” it means one whose speech has the value of thousands. He fixed his mind upon Him whose two garments were yellow and shining, and whose eyes remained unclosed.

By this very pure concentration, he had destroyed all inauspiciousness. Through the merciful glance of that Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the exertion caused by weapons had departed from him. Therefore the wandering of all the senses had ceased; abandoning the body that had arisen from them, he praised Janārdana.

Before asking for love of Śrī Kṛṣṇa as the supreme fruit, he first offers the attainment produced by his own practice. The mental concentration produced by various dharmic means has been offered to Bhagavān, the best of the Sātvatas. He is without desire; alternatively, “not satisfied” means without being satiated by any lesser object. He is the One from whom all worldly greatness has departed, meaning that there is nothing greater than Him. He has attained His own bliss, the supreme bliss that is His own nature. Sometimes He accepts prakṛti, His yoga-māyā, in order to play; this does not mean that, like the jīva, He becomes dependent through concealing His true nature. The statement that He plays is expanded by saying that from Him the stream of creation proceeds.

He now describes Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s form and prays for love. “May my love be for the body that is the one supremely beautiful thing in the three worlds.” The body is dark in color like the tamāla tree; it is clothed in a pure yellow garment shining like the morning rays of the sun; its lotus face is covered above by masses of curls; and it belongs to the friend of Vijaya, Pārtha’s charioteer. May my love there be faultless, without a motive or expectation of reward.

He prays for love while further describing His friendship with Vijaya. In battle, the dust raised by the horses made His locks gray; the curls moved in every direction; scattered drops of sweat, produced by exertion, adorned His face and revealed His affection for His devotee. May my mind delight in that Śrī Kṛṣṇa. His skin was pierced by my sharp arrows, and His armor was torn and shining as it broke apart beneath them.

“Place my chariot between the two armies,” Arjuna had said. Hearing the words of His friend, He immediately placed the chariot between the armies of His own side and the opposing side. As He stood there as Pārtha’s friend, He acted in friendship: by the glance of His vision, He took away the lives of the opposing soldiers. Under the pretext of showing Arjuna “here is Bhīṣma, here is Droṇa, here is Karṇa,” He drew out the lives of all of them merely by His glance and secured Arjuna’s victory.

He brought about victory not only by taking away the lives of Arjuna’s enemies, but also by taking away ignorance. “The face of the distant army” means Bhīṣma and the others standing at the front of the army, as Arjuna looked upon them. Arjuna had withdrawn from killing his own relatives, as the Gītā says: “Having spoken thus, Arjuna sat down on the seat of his chariot, casting aside his bow with its arrows, his mind overcome by sorrow.” “Bad understanding” means the mistaken thought, “I shall kill them,” and the like.

He says in two verses that Kṛṣṇa showed him great favor. “His own vow” means His promise, “I shall not take up a weapon; I shall only assist.” Abandoning that promise, He suddenly leapt down from the chariot and ran toward Bhīṣma in order to make my promise true—my promise that I would make Śrī Kṛṣṇa take up a weapon. He ran like a lion to kill an elephant, holding a chariot wheel. In His intensity, forgetting the play of being human, the earth that bears the weight of all beings moved at each step. The garment that had fallen on the road lay behind Him. May that Mukunda be my refuge.

When He rushed forward, Bhīṣma, a smiling archer and aggressor, was struck by my sharp arrows; his armor was shattered, and he was drenched in blood. He passed even Arjuna, who was forcibly trying to restrain Him, and advanced toward me to kill me. Thus, although He appeared to the world to favor Arjuna, in truth He showed me His own favor: He made the words spoken by His devotee, “May they not become false,” come true. May that Bhagavān be my refuge.

Even while acting in ways that appeared unjust, Kṛṣṇa was intent on protecting His devotee, and Bhīṣma longs for love of Him. “Vijaya” is Arjuna; his chariot itself was a family to be protected, even at the cost of hundreds of acts of apparent injustice. Kṛṣṇa held the goad and the reins of the horses, and the splendor of that charioteer’s service made Him beautiful. “The one wishing to die” is Bhīṣma. One might object: why ask for love of One who acted unjustly? He answers: He is Bhagavān, possessed of inconceivable majesty.
