Having crossed it, the one who has a pure subtle body alone reaches Maharloka, the station of knowers of Brahman, honored by the others, because beyond it ordinary heavenly beings have no further course. There dwell the sages, such as Bhṛgu, whose lives last for a great cosmic age.

Then, afterward, at the end of the cosmic age, seeing the three worlds being intensely burned, he proceeds to the station of Parameṣṭhī, which lasts for two parārdhas. It is filled with aerial cars enjoyed by perfected lords. “U” indicates excellence.

He explains that there is no sorrow, fear or mental pain there except for Him. What suffering arises? Through compassion, beings who do not know the meditation on Bhagavān see the endless suffering of birth. Among those who reach Brahma-loka there are three destinations: those who arrive through an abundance of merit become administrators in a later cosmic age according to the gradation of their merit; those who arrive through worship of Hiraṇyagarbha and the like are liberated with Brahmā; and those who worship Bhagavān break through the universe by their own will and ascend to the Vaikuṇṭha destination.

He now describes the method by which the devotee who is presented in this context pierces the universe. The process is as follows: from the nature presided over by the Lord arises mahat; from it ego; from ego, through the subtle element of sound, space; through touch, air; through form, fire; through taste, water; and through smell, earth. These combined elements form the Virāṭ body of fourteen worlds. Its earth covering, the cosmic shell, is fifty crore yojanas across according to one reading; other coverings, formed from the succeeding elements, are each ten times larger, and the eighth, the covering of nature, is all-pervading. Having attained each succeeding element and the identity of Earth through the subtle body, he proceeds without fear of “How shall I go?” With that self in the form of earth he enters the contiguous waters, without haste, enjoying as he wishes because he has no fear of wetness or burning. He then becomes luminous and, when enjoyment ends, reaches the great Self; alternatively, the Vedic word is its measure.

He describes crossing the subtle elements and their objects. Through the presiding sense of smell he enters smell; through the breath, touch; he enters the quality of space, sound; and through the vital air, together with each corresponding active sense, he enters intention, the respective action.

Having described crossing the gross and subtle elements, he now describes attaining mahat by reaching the ego that forms their covering. The yogī reaches the knowledge-principle after dissolving the ego. The ego is the source of diverse effects and is threefold—tāmasa, rājasa and sāttvika. From the tāmasa ego arise the inert subtle elements; from the rājasa arise the ten outward-turned senses; from the sāttvika arise the mind and the deities of the senses. These dissolve into their respective forms of ego; through that process the ego reaches the mahat-tattva, and then he reaches primordial nature, where the guṇas are restrained and dissolved.

With that self in the form of primordial nature, becoming blissful, at the end of the limiting adjuncts he reaches the peaceful, unchanging supreme Self, which is bliss. “He does not become attached” means that he does not return.

“Paths” means two routes or methods. O king, the immediate liberation described as “having broken through the crown, he releases [the body] after reaching the Supreme,” and the gradual liberation described by “if he is proceeding,” are the two paths. These paths are taught by the Veda, not invented by the author. The question asked by you concerned both routes in the matter of liberation; the southern path is also implied by the request to state the opposite. Thus these are the two paths you asked about.

There are many paths of liberation for a person wandering in saṃsāra, such as austerity and yoga, but this alone is the proper one: from the practice of devotional yoga there is no other auspicious path that is joyful and free from obstacles.

“Bhagavān” here means Brahmā. “Unchanging” means free from modification, and he was one-pointed in mind. Having examined the Veda completely three times, he determined only that in which love for Hari arises.

One might ask, “Love arises from an experienced object; how can there be love for Bhagavān, who has not been experienced?” He answers: Bhagavān is perceived through one’s own Self as the knower of the field and the indwelling controller. By what means? Through the visible objects such as the intellect. He establishes this in two ways: scriptural indications show that the perception of inert objects cannot occur without the self-luminous inner witness, and inference shows that the intellect and the other faculties, being instruments like an axe, are employed by an agent. The existence of the independent agent, Īśvara, is thereby established.
With “therefore” he concludes the answers to the questions beginning “what should be heard” and so forth.

He illustrates the fruit of hearing and the rest: the topics of the Lord, who shines as the very Self of the good, are nectar. They purify the mind, which has been polluted by sense objects, and lead one to the vicinity of His lotus feet, the feet of Śrī Viṣṇu.
There are noble and expansive topics because of the qualities of Urugāya.

With the intention, “Make the life that is being wasted fruitful through Hari’s topics,” he speaks in three verses beginning “life.” The sun rises, sets and moves onward; whatever moment is spent apart from Hari’s topics, it steals away as [wasted] lifespan.

One might ask, “Is living itself not the fruit of their lifespan?” He answers: they are like trees. One might say, “They have no breath.” Then they are bellows, leather bags. One might say, “They have no food and the like.” He answers: they do not eat. “They do not urinate or engage in sexual union—is that so?” Even animals in human form are [like this].

He describes them as comparable to dogs and the rest. Their ears have never received [the Lord’s name]. Because of their contempt for sacred things they are like dogs; because of their attachment to impure objects they are like village pigs; because of their attachment to painful objects, like thorns, they are like camels; and because they carry burdens, they are like asses.

He says in five verses that their limbs too are fruitless. Alas! The ears of a person who does not hear are merely empty holes. If his tongue does not sing [the Lord’s name], it is a false and wicked tongue, like that of a frog.

If a head adorned with a cloth turban and crown does not bow, it is merely a burden. The two hands are like the hands of a corpse. The wrists on which golden bracelets shine are [also useless]. “Also” indicates the other limbs as well.
The eyes that do not behold the forms of Viṣṇu are like peacock feathers. They take birth like trees, meaning that their eyes are comparable to tree roots.
“Does not obtain” means does not approach, touch or hold. “The foot of Śrī Viṣṇu” means that which is attached to Śrī Viṣṇu’s foot. “Does not smell” means does not inhale its fragrance and rejoice.
One whose core, strength and hardness are like stone. He now describes the bodily transformation: the hair rising on the body is the manifestation of joy.
All this is futile for one without devotion. You speak what is dear and agreeable to the mind; therefore, having been properly asked, tell us what the son of Vyāsa said to the king.
The discerning and wise, by approaching and serving his feet, cast away attachment in both this world and the next, and are freed from fatigue and effort.

Showing the failure of all practices for those devoid of devotion, he bows: the thoughtful yogīs, whose conduct is auspicious, [gain nothing] without offering austerity and the other practices to Him. The repetition of “whose fame is auspicious” indicates the primacy of hearing His glories and the like.

He shows that devotion is the cause of supreme purification. Those born in sinful groups, such as Kirātas, and others who are sinful by action become purified when they take shelter of the Bhāgavatas, the devotees who have taken refuge in Him. He removes the doubt that this is impossible with “the Powerful One,” meaning one who is able to accomplish it.

Remembering that He is worshiped by all, he prays: He is the Self of those who know the Self, and is to be worshiped as the Self. The qualifications “made of the three Vedas” and the like indicate that He is to be worshiped according to the respective paths. May that Lord be pleased—He whose form is a sign to be seen with supreme wonder by sincere, guileless devotees.
Remembering that He protects all, he says: He is the protector in every danger.

Remembering that He bestows knowledge, he says in two verses beginning “whose feet.” Meditation upon His feet itself is samādhi, by which one is purified. According to one’s inclination, this may be with distinctions such as with attributes or without attributes; alternatively, “ruc” means radiance, and “according to one’s mind” is the meaning.

Formerly, at the beginning of the cosmic age, while the Unborn was extending creation in His heart, Sarasvatī, inspired by Him, arose from His mouth. She possesses her own distinctive characteristics, those taught in grammar and the other disciplines. He is the foremost of sages, the giver of knowledge.

He now prays that He adorn his own words, which delight the listeners and possess the beauty of love, compassion and the other sentiments. Suspecting that one person’s words cannot adorn another’s, he reveals that the Lord is the inner controller of all words. Having created these bodies from the great elements, He dwells within them as the indwelling controller. Scripture establishes the designation “Puruṣa” for Him. He enjoys, illuminates or protects the sixteen elements—the eleven senses and five elements. The middle voice is archaic. The reason is that He is the Self, the conscious knower, of the sixteen; he is not being described here as a finite living being, since that would contradict the prayer.
He bows to Śrī Vyāsa. “Gentle” means the devotees; he is the one whose lotus mouth is a source of nectar.
He now introduces the dialogue of Brahmā and Nārada as the answer to the questions. The Vedas were present in His womb at the time of creation. He speaks what Hari directly said.

“Yoga” means breath control and the other practices. “Austerity” is the one-pointedness of mind produced by them. “Knowledge” is the result produced by them, and “destination” is their fruit. By this it has been stated that everything is dependent upon Him.
When asked, “What do you do?” he answers: Although He created me, I create what is to be created by Him. I create by His glance. The reasons are given by “of the seer” and the following words.

One might ask, “Why is there this distinction between the living being and the Lord, so that you are impelled and He is the impeller?” He gives the cause of that distinction in three verses. Even the Lord, who is without qualities, is said in the following verse to be bound by these three qualities. How are they characterized? They are taken up by māyā through His own independence for the purposes of maintenance and the rest.

Although in reality the Lord is always liberated, where and by what do the living being, the person who is the subject of māyā, become bound? By the effect, called adhibhūta; the cause, called adhyātma; and the doer, called adhidaiva—their essential relation. The substance is the great elements; “knowledge” means the deities; “action” means the senses. They bind by their respective identifications and by the supports that are their causes.

Therefore He is controlled by māyā through these guṇa-born signs, the limiting adjuncts that cover the living beings. His course and essential nature are very difficult to perceive; alternatively, His course is perceived only by His own devotees.
He describes the method of His creation. “Karma” means the unseen result belonging to the living being. Desiring to become manifold, He desired to manifest in various forms.

“Intermingling of the guṇas” means their agitation and abandonment of equilibrium. “By nature” means transformation into another form. “Puruṣa” means the Lord, and His presiding over the three is the common qualification. “Mahat” means the mahat-tattva.

From mahat-tattva, which is transforming, the threefold ego arises. Although it too is threefold, rajas and sattva are prominent in it because of the powers of action and knowledge; in ego, which covers, tamas predominates. Therefore among the effects of ego, the tamasic elements beginning with space are numerous, while the rajasic and sāttvika effects are fewer. The same predominance of tamas is found in living beings covered by those adjuncts.

As it transforms and takes another form, he describes its three divisions: vaikārika is sāttvika, and taijasa is rājasika. The characteristics of the three are stated in reverse order: the power in matter, the power in action, and the power in knowledge. O Lord, You are able to know.

“Bhūtādi” qualifies the tamasic [ego]. It is well known that sound first arises from the tamasic ego; sound, however, is the subtle form of space, and its distinctive quality is produced through sound, meaning that space arises through the subtle element of sound. The same is to be understood for touch and the other elements. Sound is a sign: if someone cries “Elephant!” from behind a wall, the sound gives knowledge both of the elephant that is seen and of the seer who sees it. The neuter form is used because the word qualifies the sign.

Because air is connected with space as its cause, it too possesses sound. Its distinctive mark is vital air, which sustains the body. “Vigor, strength and power” are the excellence of the senses, mind and body; they are the cause of those capacities.

“Arose” means came into being. Fire possesses form in itself and, because air and space are its causes, also possesses touch and sound. Water and earth similarly possess more qualities because of their greater connection with the preceding elements.
“Resonance” means sound.
“The particular” means Earth. Earth possesses more qualities because of its greater connection with the preceding elements.

By the word “mind” the moon, its presiding deity, is also to be understood. The other ten deities are the vaikārika, the effects of sāttvika ego. The five presiding deities of the ear, skin, eyes, tongue and nose are the directions, air, the sun, Varuṇa and the Aśvinī Kumāras. The five presiding deities of speech, hands, feet, the anus and the generative organ are Fire, Indra, Upendra, Mitra and Prajāpati.

Because intellect, the power of knowledge, and vital air, the power of action, are effects of the taijasa ego, the senses, whose special forms are knowledge and action, also arise from taijasa ego. He lists them: ear, skin, eyes, tongue and nose; speech, hands, feet, anus and generative organ. Their order is not intended here.
Having described the creation of causes, he now describes the creation of effects. When these elements were unconnected and unmixed, they were unable to construct the body, the abode.
Then, taking on the principal and subordinate states of primordial nature and its qualities, they formed both the collective and the individual body—the universe.
The living one, the Supreme Self, stood presiding over time, karma and nature, and made the inert conscious, causing it to live.
Having pierced and separated them, he remained distinct. This is the meaning of “having emerged from the root and remained.”

He describes the arrangement of the worlds through His limbs. The waist is the rear portion at the roots of the thighs; the hips are the front and lower portion. Below are the seven worlds beginning with Atala, and above are the seven beginning with Bhūḥ.

He now shows the origin of the social orders. “Brahman” means the brāhmaṇa and is called His mouth, with the intended nondifference of cause and effect; the same applies to “arms.” “Kṣatra” means the kṣatriya.

For the purpose of meditation, he now shows the different arrangements of the worlds and presents the view of seven worlds in two verses. Bhūrloka extends from Pātāla up to the waist, from the feet to the waist.

Because this is for meditation, the reversal of the upper and lower parts in the phrase “from the two breasts” is not a fault. Alternatively, “from the breasts” means from the two lips that produce sound. Brahma-loka, called Vaikuṇṭha, is eternal; it is not within the created universe. A traditional note clarifies that this is Satya-loka, the seventh world above the others.

He now presents the view of the fourteen worlds. There, the seven beginning with Bhūḥ and the others, already mentioned, are [shown] by the hips and the rest; by the waist and the rest he speaks of the seven lower worlds—“in that waist,” in two verses. They are pure because they are residences of devotees of Hari.
He speaks of the view of the three worlds. Bhū-loka is together with Pātāla and the other [lower worlds].

He gives this with an illustrative example. The śruti says: “This breath is the sun,” and “this sun is the breath.” Just as the sun, illuminating its own seat, the disk, also illuminates outside, so Virāṭ, illuminating the body, illuminates the Brahmāṇḍa both within and without.

To show that He is spoken of eternally, he explains the meaning of “of immortality”—“He,” and so on. “Of fearlessness” explains the word “immortality” occurring in the mantra. He explains the word “by food” with a reversal of case-ending. “Mortal” means subject to death; “food” means the fruit of action, because He has crossed beyond it. Therefore He is not only the self of everything, but also the Lord of immortality, of His own bliss—this is the meaning.

Having wondered, “How can the one whose nature is the phenomenal world be spoken of as eternal?” he removes that doubt by explaining “Such is His greatness.” Even the greatness of this Lord, whose nature is the phenomenal world, namely His lordship over immortality, is difficult to cross and boundless, because He is not overcome by the phenomenal world. “Such is His greatness” means “His glory”; by saying “He is greater,” the very meaning is stated.

Thus it has been said that the Lord is eternally liberated. He now shows that bondage and liberation are arranged according to the condition of the beings dependent on Him, explaining “All beings are one foot of Him.” “In His feet”: the Bhū and other worlds are called abodes because beings stand there; they are like feet, or portions, of Him who is the support of existence. In those feet, in those worlds that are His portions, they know all living beings. In the mantra “All beings are one foot of Him,” the common grammatical case is intended to express the non-difference of support and what is supported. The singular “foot” is explained as referring to the generality.

Showing the variety of results among beings, he explains “His three feet are hidden in heaven.” The three feet belonging to this Lord are immortal, everlasting happiness, in the higher worlds, not in the three-world system. Showing the threefold division expressed by the word “three-footed,” he says: Maharloka is the head of the three worlds; the worlds above it are its heads. In those worlds, immortality and the rest are placed in order.

In the three-world system there is only perishable happiness. Although Maharloka is a place of gradual liberation, its happiness is not imperishable because its residents leave their station at the end of the kalpa. In Jana-loka there is immortal, imperishable happiness because its residents do not leave their own station for as long as they live. But the residents of Maharloka, tormented at the end of the kalpa by the heat of the burning three worlds, go then to Jana-loka; therefore there is an appearance of insecurity there. In Tapoloka there is no such condition, but only security. He will indeed say: “When the three worlds are being burned by the fire of Saṅkarṣaṇa, the sages beginning with Bhṛgu, tormented by the heat, go from Maharloka to Jana-loka.” In Satya-loka there is fearlessness, liberation, because of its proximity to that [liberation].

He explains the meaning of “three feet above,” establishing this distinction according to differences in eligibility. “Those without offspring” means the āśramas of lifelong brahmacārins, vānaprasthas and yatis; they are outside the three worlds. The householder, however, is within them, because one without the great vow is without the vow of celibacy.

He shows that this difference of eligibility is due to differences in the stages of one person, not to subjects that are utterly different, by explaining “thence he moves in every direction.” “Viṣvaṅ” means one who goes variously and well. The person, the knower of the field, moves along the two paths, the southern and the northern. What are these two paths like? They are accompanied by eating and non-eating, and are the means of attaining enjoyment and liberation. Here this second qualification is given as the cause: one of them is ignorance in the form of action, and the other is knowledge in the form of worship, which is its means.

“Accompanied by eating” means conscious beings endowed with the activities of eating and the like; “without eating” means the unconscious, such as mountains and rivers, which lack these activities.

Because the egg was born from Him, and within it Virāṭ—composed of the elements, senses and qualities—was also born, that Lord transcended the universe, the Virāṭ body and the material egg. “Like the sun” is the very example mentioned earlier.

If the Puruṣa alone is everything, then worship of the Puruṣa by sacrifices, and of the means of sacrifice, would not be established, because the sacrifice and its means would be non-different from Him. Anticipating this objection and removing it, he gathers and presents the meaning of the mantra beginning “When the gods extended the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as oblation.” “Of this” means of the indwelling Lord within Virāṭ, since He is the subject under discussion. “Born in the navel” means born from that [navel]. “I did not see the implements of sacrifice.”

Then, when those implements had to be prepared, the statement “these implements were assembled through the limbs of the Puruṣa” is connected with the fourth [ṛk]. The plants are the sacrificial posts. “The place of offering” is the sacrificial ground. Since the text says “this,” it is understood that He, seated in a place suitable for sacrifice, speaks. The time beginning with spring is endowed with many qualities. “The place of offering” means that in which the gods are worshiped.

The objects are vessels and the like. The plants are rice and the like. The oils are ghee and the like. The juices are the sweet taste and the rest. The metals are gold and the rest. Earth and water [are also included]. The fourfold priestly function is the rite beginning with the Hotṛ and the other priests.

The names are Jyotiṣṭoma and the like. Since the ṛk and the rest have already been mentioned, “mantras” means the utterances beginning with svāhā and the like. The sequence of the deities is their designation in order. Kalpa is a ritual manual beginning with Baudhāyana. “With this I shall sacrifice” is the resolve. Tantra is the method of performance.
The paths are the strides of Viṣṇu and the like. The thoughts are meditations on the deities. [It is] the dedication of what has been performed to Bhagavān.
I am the one by whom the requisites were collected and prepared. By that very sacrifice. The meaning of the mantra “with that sacrifice they sacrificed the sacrifice” is indicated.

He elaborates the meaning of “then the gods sacrificed” in the two [verses] beginning “from that.” [The sacrifice is] manifest in the form of Indra and the rest, and unmanifest in itself. In this way the meaning of “from that Puruṣa born at the beginning” is shown.
In time, at their respective occasions.

He concludes the answer to the question “What is the foundation?” with “Nārāyaṇa.” “Placed” means established or presided over. The reason for His being Bhagavān is that He is inherently without qualities. At the beginning of creation He is the one in whom the powerful qualities were taken up through māyā.

He concludes the answer to “You are beyond,” which was stated earlier: “This same Bhagavān is the Lord of the minds of all.” “I create” is the meaning. He Himself performs maintenance, as he says “the universe.” “In the form of the Puruṣa” means in the form of Viṣṇu. He is called the bearer of the three powers because He bears māyā, which consists of those powers.

He concludes the general answer to all the questions of this Fifth Chapter—“What is this universe, and of what nature are You?” What was stated was: “There is no other object beyond Vāsudeva in truth,” and it was strengthened by the śruti, “the Puruṣa alone is all this.” All this, consisting of effect and cause, something to be brought into being, is stated to arise from Bhagavān and not to be separate from Him.

Having established and concluded the statement “You are that, from whom I came; not knowing Me, the Lord, you speak,” he concludes with “not [mere] speech.” Because I have eagerness, an increase of devotion, and because Hari has been held and meditated upon in a heart endowed with that devotion, O Nārada, the activities of my speech, mind and senses are meaningful and true; this is not merely due to my own power.

Here he proves the point by his own experience, through agreement and difference, in two [verses]. Although I am the highest even according to the Veda and the other [means of knowledge], and although I have resorted to yoga, I did not know the arising or birth of myself from the Self; what then could I say about another? This will be explained in the Third Canto concerning the lotus-born one.

Then I bow to that foot of the Lord, which is easy to serve, most auspicious, and cuts off worldly existence, for those who have approached Him for shelter. “Those who have come” means those who have surrendered. Then, by the maxim that if even He is of inconceivable greatness, how much more so others, he says “for He.” He Himself has not crossed the expansion of His own māyā; the word “pari” expresses negation. The meaning is: He has not known its limit. How could others know it? “I bow to His foot” is connected with what came before.

One may object: If He is omniscient, how does He not know its end? He answers with an example: just as the sky does not reach the end of itself, so [it is with Him]. The non-perception of a sky-flower does not destroy omniscience. Thus it will be said: “The lords of heaven did not reach Your end because of Your endlessness; what of You, within the hosts of universes, each with its coverings?” The śruti also says: “He who is the overseer of this in the highest heaven—He alone knows, or perhaps He does not know.”

He elaborates this in the two [verses] beginning “I do not.” Vāmadeva is Rudra. “He whose movement of truth” means He whose ultimate nature is reality. Rather, we see and know this phenomenal form, made by His māyā. Even that is only equal to the self, according to the measure of our own knowledge, and not the whole [of Him]. “Those whose minds are deluded” is the reason both for not knowing Him and for knowing the phenomenal world.
It may be seen that everyone describes Him. To this he replies: “whose.”

He shows the acts of the incarnations in brief. He is that first Bhagavān who, becoming the Puruṣa incarnation, performs creation and the rest. “The self in the self, by the self” means that the agent, the locus, the instrument and the object are all Himself. “The Puruṣa incarnation” and “creation and the rest” are a concise statement.

It was said, “They do not know Him in truth.” What is that truth? He answers: knowledge alone, true, is the reality. The qualifications exclude knowledge that takes the form of an object such as a pot. “Pure” means free from the form of an object; “inward” means within all; therefore it is right knowledge, free from doubt and the like; “established” means steady; and “without qualities” means free from the guṇas. The effect of the guṇas is unsteady because of their mixture. Although knowledge occurring as a mental modification is also knowledge of the self, and is not inherently subject to the defect of instability, it is distinguished here because it becomes so through the defects of the internal organ. These same qualifications establish its truth. Moreover, whatever has modification is seen to be unreal; therefore he says that it is without beginning and end, free from birth and destruction. Consequently it has no change consisting in existence after birth, nor growth, transformation or decline. It is full. The reason throughout is that it is eternal and nondual: eternal at all times, and ultimately nondual even when duality is perceived.

Note: Just as water in a pond exits through openings, enters fields as channels, and takes on their four-cornered form, so the luminous internal organ goes through the eye and the other gateways to the place of an object and takes on the form of that object; that transformation is called a mental modification.

Here he makes the experience of the learned the proof. O seer Nārada, they know when the self, senses and inner disposition are tranquil—when the body, senses and mind are clear. At other times he gives the cause of their not knowing: when that very self-luminous reality is covered over by the arguments of those who assert non-being, it becomes concealed.

He explains the incarnations in detail, beginning with “the first” and continuing to the end of the chapter. “Of the Supreme, the great” means the Puruṣa who sets prakṛti in motion. The līlā-body described as “having a thousand heads” is the first incarnation. He will indeed say: “When, having fashioned the city of Virāṭ from the five elements created by Himself, Nārāyaṇa, the first god, entered it with His own portion and obtained the designation Puruṣa.” As it is said: “They know Viṣṇu’s three forms called Puruṣa: the first, the creator of the Great Principle; the second, situated in the egg; the third, situated in all beings. Knowing these, one is liberated.”

Although all are generally called incarnations without distinction, the distinction should be understood: time, nature, and the existent and non-existent—the material nature consisting of cause and effect—are powers; mind and the rest are effects; Brahmā and the others are incarnations of the guṇas; Dakṣa and the others are manifestations of power. “Mind” means the Mahat-tattva. “Matter” means the great elements. No sequence is intended here. “Modification” means ego. “Quality” means sattva and the rest. “Virāṭ” means the collective body. “Svarāṭ” means the Vairāja. “Standing still” means the immovable, and “moving” means the mobile, including individual bodies.

“I” means Brahmā. “Bhava” means Rudra. “Yajña” means Viṣṇu. “Dakṣa and the others” means these lords of progeny. “And those beginning with you” means the steadfast ones [such as Nārada]. “Protectors of the worlds below” means the rulers of Pātāla.

The lords of the Gandharvas and the others; the lords of the Yakṣas and the others. The sandhi in “Rākṣoraga” is an archaic form. The foremost of the ṛṣis and the fathers; the rulers of the pretas and the others.

To say no more, whatever is headed by Bhagavān—all that is the supreme reality; this is the syntactical connection. “Bhagavat” means endowed with lordly opulence; “mahasvat” means endowed with splendor. “Ojas” and “sahas” are the powers of the senses and mind; [He is] endowed with them. “Bala” means skill. “Śrī” means beauty; “hrī” means aversion to evil action; “vibhūti” means prosperity; “ātman” means intellect; [He is] endowed with these. “Arṇa” means color. “Adbhutārṇa” means wondrous color, that is, an astonishing color. Form itself is the essential nature, and whatever is formless as well—all that is the supreme reality and its manifestation.

To speak of the incarnations in pure sattva, he says “chiefly.” They dry up the impurities in the ears—the dirt produced by listening to tales of the unreal—and therefore are so called. “Supeśas” means beautiful; the loss of the s in that word is archaic. O seer, I shall enumerate them for you; let them be drunk by you as they are enumerated. Or “let them be drunk” is a present participle: let them drink the impurities of the ears away.
Hearing that statement, he took the one seeking refuge by the hand, that is, by the trunk. What did he do? He split and tore open the mouth of the crocodile, and [took him] from that mouth.

He speaks of the Vāmana incarnation. Among Aditi’s twelve sons, the twelve Ādityas, Viṣṇu is the presiding deity of sacrifice. Although the youngest, He is greater in qualities than the eldest. He then describes those qualities. Because of this He crossed these worlds with His steps. This occurred immediately after the promise was made. The reason is that He took the earth from Bali in the form of Vāmana. One may ask: If He is the Lord, why did He act like a weak person? He answers: without a request, one who follows the path of dharma cannot be moved or deprived of his sovereignty.

One may object that moving him even by a request is improper. With the intention of giving him something greater—His own sālokya and the other forms of blessed proximity—He took it away, as is explained by “not for wealth.” The lordship of the gods, obtained by Bali through force and to be granted later, is not his true aim. Why? The words are divided as “he received the water.” The water that was the washing of Urukrama’s feet, the foot-washing water, was held everywhere by Bali at his topknot—“at the crest,” meaning on his head. Moreover, although Śukra tried to stop him and cursed him, O Nārada, Bali did not wish to do anything other than what he had promised. To complete the third step, he even accepted his own body for Hari. Therefore, for one who faithfully gave the three worlds together with his body, lordship of the gods is not the object.

He speaks of the Haṃsa incarnation. Being greatly pleased by devotion arising from an exceedingly increased devotional feeling, He spoke bhakti-yoga properly to you. “Knowledge” means the means of knowledge. What is it? It is called the Bhāgavata. What kind is it? It is reality itself, endowed with reality, and it illuminates the truth of the self. He states the result of the qualification “with increased feeling” by saying “that” and so forth.

He speaks of the incarnation in the various Manvantaras. He bears the discus of His own splendor, namely His own power, Sudarśana. The meaning is that He bears power which is unobstructed like a discus. He further explains this: being the protector of Manu’s dynasty, while standing even in Satya-loka, situated above the three worlds, He expands His beautiful own fame and imposes punishment on kings.

He speaks of the Dhanvantari incarnation. Descending into the world as Dhanvantari, He destroys the diseases of greatly diseased persons by His own name alone. “By His own fame” is an expression of exaggerated praise. He is the one from whom comes life free of death, immortality. “Av” means that which had previously fallen or been obstructed by the demons; He obtains His share in the sacrifice. The reading “he obtained what was obstructed” has the same meaning. He directs and teaches the Veda concerning the subject of lifespan.

He speaks of the Paraśurāma incarnation. By fate, [the kṣatriyas] were nourished for the destruction of the world, or they were raised only to be offered to death. They offend the brāhmaṇas; therefore the path abandoned by them is the path of the Veda. For this reason he seems to seek the torment of hell. Hari, the great-souled one, uproots this kṣatra, which has become like a thorn of the earth, with a battle-axe whose edge is long and sharp.

He speaks of the Rāma incarnation in three [verses], beginning with “to us.” He was favorably disposed toward us, Brahmā and the others, and came with the form of Bharata and the others. Being the Lord of māyā, and remaining under the command of His teacher, Daśaratha, He entered the forest together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa. Rāvaṇa attained destruction by opposing Him.

For that Rāma, the ocean gave a path. He who wished to burn Laṅkā, the city of the enemy, quickly [did so], just as Hara wished to burn Tripura. The genitive is used in the sense of the dative; alternatively, it is an ablative. Because fear came to the ocean from Rāma, who wished to burn [the city], its limbs trembled. What kind of ocean? One whose limbs trembled because of the fear it had received. The reason was that Sītā, his friend, was far away; because of her, anger was agitated, and his glance became intensely red. In that ocean was the circle of makaras, serpents and crocodiles, greatly scorched by that glance.

Moreover, in the battle, by contact with Rāvaṇa’s chest, the tusks of Airāvata, the vehicle of Mahendra, were injured and broken. By those tusks, falling in their respective directions, the quarters were made white by their own whiteness and illuminated. Those quarters he enjoys, or protects. The pride-born laughter of that Rāvaṇa who stole his wife—“Who else is equal to me?”—He will remove at once, together with his life-breath, simply by the twanging sounds of His bow. He moves with superiority between the hostile armies. In the alternative reading, “the laughter established by victory over the quarters” means that He removes the pride produced by the victory of the whitened quarters.

He speaks of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s incarnation in ten [verses], beginning with “when the earth.” The earth, afflicted by the armies of kings who were portions of the demons, was relieved when He was born together with Rāma as His portion. Who was born? The Lord Himself, whose hairs are white and black. The white and black hair indicates beauty, not an alteration caused by age, because He is free from change. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa says: “He pulled out from Himself two hairs, white and black.” The Mahābhārata says: “Hari also plucked out two hairs, one white and the other black. Those two hairs entered the two women in the Yadu dynasty, Rohiṇī and Devakī. One became Balarāma, the white hair of that Lord; the second became Kṛṣṇa, Keśava, the hair that was black in color.”

The purpose is not an incarnation of mere hairs. Rather, it indicates that these hairs of Mine alone were capable of removing the earth’s burden, and it also indicates the colors of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa. Otherwise there would be a contradiction with the preceding and with the statement “Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān Himself.” What kind of Lord is He? His path is unperceived by people because He is the Supreme Lord. If His lordship is questioned, what is the proof? Extraordinary deeds themselves cannot otherwise be accounted for. He answers: these are the deeds in which the glory of the Self is manifested.

He elaborates this with “by a child” and the rest. As a child He took the life of Pūtanā. While crawling on His knees, having reached the space between the two exceedingly tall trees that touched the sky, He brought them down. If He were not the Lord, this could not have happened.

He would revive the cowherd boys and the others who had drunk poisonous water by a shower of nectar from His merciful glance. Playing in the Yamunā, He would drive out the serpent Kāliya, for the purification of her pool, so that it became free of poison. His tongue was restless because of the force of the exceedingly strong poison.

“Divine” is a worldly expression meaning “as if otherworldly.” He will lift them up. “Pure” refers to the summer connected with the forest; it means dried up. Therefore, because of the forest fire, their end was certain, and He will save them together with Balarāma. His valor is difficult to comprehend. “Lying down at night” refers to the night of subduing Kāliya, on the bank of the Yamunā. “Having closed the eyes” should be understood in connection with the Muñja forest, as explained in the Nineteenth Chapter of the Tenth Canto.

The means by which one is tied is an upabandha: the cord, the rope. His mother Yaśodā took that means of binding Him. It did not reach around His belly as a measure of the binding; it did not become sufficient, that is, the rope remained short. The cowherd woman Yaśodā, seeing Him, was awakened and made aware of His own lordship. That deed too is “as if divine,” and this is connected with the preceding phrase throughout.

He will free them from the fear that came from Varuṇa’s noose. The son of Maya is Vyoma, by name. The description “active by day and lying down at night” shows the absence of a separate practice for attaining Vaikuṇṭha. He will take the people dwelling in Gokula to Vaikuṇṭha. The word “indeed” expresses wonder.

When the god Indra [became hostile], desiring to protect the animals, He will hold Govardhana Mountain playfully in one hand, without effort, in whatever way one might hold it. He will hold it like a raised mushroom or umbrella. He was seven years old.

At night, when the moon’s rays made everything white, He played in the forest with graceful, lovely steps. His extended and intensified gait, endowed with a special form of singing, awakened the desire of the gopīs. He will take the head of Śaṅkhacūḍa, the abductor of the gopīs.

All those beginning with Pralamba, through Hari as the cause, will attain His abode, Vaikuṇṭha, which is not fit to be seen by ordinary sight. Khara is Dhenuka; Dardura, “frog-like,” is Baka; Ibha is Kuvalayāpīḍa; Kuja is Naraka; and Kapi is Dvivida.

Those who took up bows in battle and prided themselves in the assembly are called “those who shine in battle.” One may object: Pralamba, Khara, Kapi, Balvala, Rukmi and the others were killed by Balarāma; Kamboja and the others by Bhīma and Arjuna; Śambara by Pradyumna; and the Yavana by Mucukunda—not by Hari. He answers: “Bala,” “Bhīma,” “Pārtha” and the others are the deceptive names of the one who killed them. The seven bulls were subdued by Him at a later time. All these deeds too are “as if divine,” and they should not be understood otherwise.

He speaks of the Vyāsa incarnation. In each successive age, seeing that the understanding of people had contracted and that their lives were short, and recognizing that the Veda-collection made by Himself was difficult to comprehend and its far shore was distant, He Himself appeared in Satyavatī as Hari. “Branches” means divisions into branches.

He speaks of the Buddha incarnation. The enemies of the gods were firmly established in the path of the Veda, and by the strength of that path they had cities. The cities are those made of iron, silver and copper by Tripurāsura. By means of an appearance whose speed could not be perceived, He would cause their understanding to be deluded and their minds to be enticed into accepting what was unsuitable. Assuming the dress of a heresy, He would speak much non-dharma. “Delusion of understanding” means abandoning what is fitting; “enticement of understanding” means accepting what is unsuitable.

He speaks of the Kalki incarnation. When even in the homes of good people there is no longer any discussion of Hari, when the three twice-born social orders have become heretics and śūdras have become kings, then He will become the chastiser of Kali in the form of Kalki. Here it should be understood that, before the dialogue of Brahmā and Nārada, incarnations such as Varāha are future; the Manvantara incarnations include both those that have occurred and those yet to come; Dhanvantari and Paraśurāma are then present; and Śrī Rāma and the others are future. In some places references to past and future are poetic.

He speaks of the manifestations of māyā, the guṇas and power according to the differences of creation and the other functions. “Creation” is creation; “maintenance” is abiding; “sacrifice” is Viṣṇu; dharma, sacrifice, the Manus, the gods and the kings are included. At the end, there is dissolution; Hara is Rudra. The serpents are under the control of anger. These are the manifestations of the māyā of Bhagavān, who bears many powers.

I have spoken this briefly; no one is capable of speaking of it in detail. Even one who has measured and counted the atoms of the earth—who could count the might of Viṣṇu? What kind of Viṣṇu? He who supported the three worlds and Satya-loka. Why did He support them? With His own unobstructed foot-speed in the Trivikrama deed, He made the abode characterized by the equilibrium of the three guṇas tremble, beginning with primordial nature and extending beyond it. Or, “whose movement is by shaking” is intended. For this reason He supported it. Alternatively, “up to the threefold summit” means that, pervading Satya-loka, He supported everything. Thus the Viṣṇu hymn is explained: “Let me proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu—He who measured even the earthly regions; who, striding three times, established the highest world, the seat in which the gods dwell together.”

He elaborates this with “I do not know the end.” I do not know the end of the Puruṣa’s power of māyā, that is, the greatness of His māyā. Even Śeṣa, who has ten thousand mouths and sings His qualities, does not reach or determine the limit.

If no one knows Him, how can they be liberated? He answers: by His grace alone. Those to whom He gives mercy, if they become followers of His feet without deceit, cross the difficult divine māyā. By the conjunction “and,” they also know the splendor of māyā. Their crossing of māyā is directly evident: they no longer remain attached to bodies that are food for dogs and jackals.

Even in the absence of direct knowledge, the knowledge “This is māyā” exists in many by His grace; he says this with the three verses beginning “I know.” “You” includes Sanaka and the others, hence the plural. Prahlāda is the foremost of the Daityas. Manu is Svāyambhuva; his wife is Śatarūpā; his children are the two sons Priyavrata and Uttānapāda and the daughters. Prācīnabarhiṣa has the elision of the final syllable according to Vedic usage. Aṅga is Vena’s father. Ākūti, Devahūti and Prasūti are the three [daughters]. Śatadhanvan and Anu [are intended]; the sandhi is archaic. “Rantideva” is the easy reading. In the single verse, Devavrata is intended together with these, that is, in the form “Rantideva-Devavrata.” Śuka is [the son of] Upendra Datta. “Foremost are those of whom Vibhīṣaṇa and the others are the chief.”

What more need be said? By holy association, everyone comes to know; he says this with “they indeed.” Those whose devotion is directed to Hari, whose steps are wondrous, and whose conduct is instructed by the character of those devotees—if they become such, then they too know; this is the meaning. What need is there to say that brāhmaṇas who retain what they have heard know the Lord’s māyā? With the reading śubha, those who hold the auspicious form of Bhagavān in their minds know—what need is there to say more? With the reading śubha-dhāraṇā, there is an archaic metrical irregularity.

What is that nature of Bhagavān by fixing the mind upon which they cross māyā? In response to this expectation he speaks in the two verses beginning “eternally.” “That which the sages know as Brahman” is Bhagavān’s status and nature. What is that Brahman? He says: it is unceasing, eternal happiness and free from sorrow. The reason for unceasing happiness is that it is eternally tranquil; hence it is of the nature of eternal happiness. The reason for being free from sorrow is that it is fearless. Why is it fearless? Because it is equal, without difference. Hence it is fearless, for “from the second, fear arises” (Bṛhad-āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.2). Why is it so? Because it is mere awareness, a single taste of knowledge.

Objection: even knowledge is seen to differ by taking the forms of blue, yellow and so on, and by the differences of instruments such as the eye. No; it is pure, stainless. Objection: has not the impurity in the form of coloring from object and instrument been shown? He answers: it is beyond the real and unreal, devoid of association with object and instrument. The coloring belongs only to the mental modification, not to knowledge; this is the meaning. Objection: even so, would there not be difference from the knower? No; the essence of the self is itself the nature of the knower Self; it is not different from it.

Objection: “I ask about that Person who is known through the Upaniṣads” indicates cognition through words; how then is it of the nature of awareness? He answers: “where the word is not.” The function of words is only in removing superimposition, not in producing awareness; this is the meaning.

Objection: let freedom from sorrow be due to the absence of differentiated knowledge, but since happiness is the result of an action accomplished by many factors, how can it be unceasing happiness? He answers: there is no action-result of the four kinds—produced, obtained, transformed, or refined—which is brought about by an action accomplished through many factors. As through actions the awareness-aspect is merely manifested by the senses, so through actions the bliss-aspect is merely manifested; it is not produced and so forth; this is the meaning. Objection: even in the absence of production and so on, might it be something to be transformed through removal of māyā’s impurity, like rice when husks are removed? He answers: māyā, as though ashamed to remain facing Him, retreats and moves far away.

Therefore, for those whose minds are controlled in Bhagavān of this kind, who have accomplished their purpose, he says that nothing whatever remains to be done. “Sadhryaṅ” means moving together or being a companion; the disciplined ascetics direct and steady the mind toward Him, in whom they establish it. The distinction of the agent is removed and there is no agent; therefore they abandon the means, that is, they give it up. Since it is no longer useful, they do not value it. The example of disregard for a means when it is no longer useful is this: a well is a place from which one drinks, and a digging tool is the instrument for digging it; just as Indra, himself manifest as rain, does not take up that tool, so they do not. Alternatively, “svarāṭ” means one who shines by himself: just as a poor man, having become prosperous like Indra, abandons the well-digging tool taken up during his laborer’s condition, so they do; this is the meaning.

Thus it has been stated that Brahman—unceasing happiness and free from sorrow—is Bhagavān’s very nature, and that for those who attain Him there is nothing to attain or do. Now he says that before that [attainment] He alone is the giver of every result and the impeller of every action. He alone is the sovereign giver of the fruits of auspicious aims. The reason is this: the auspicious action prescribed for beings such as brāhmaṇas, qualified by natural qualities such as tranquility and sense-control, is known to proceed from Him. Or, the effect prescribed for beings beginning with mahat is known to arise through their own nature, their transformation. Thus He alone is the giver of heaven and the rest.

Objection: how can the result of heaven and so on arise for the performer of action who has died? He answers: when the gross elements that began the body—earth and the rest—separate and the body disintegrates, the space located there does not disintegrate with it. Since the unborn [Self] was not born together with that body, He is the Lord of that person’s auspicious results.

He concludes the meaning of the three chapters: “This has been stated in summary.” He repeats it: the effect and cause, the real and unreal, are not other than Hari. Objection: if they are non-different from Hari, the transformations belonging to them would accrue to Him. No; Hari, who is their causal source, is distinct from the effect, being other than it.
This collection of the vibhūtis has also been spoken.

Having resolved and thought, “By what has been described devotion will arise in people,” describe the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata in this way, with Hari’s pastimes predominant. Do not describe it merely as doctrine in a way that obstructs the taste of devotion; this is the meaning.
One might object: the pastime depends on māyā, so what is the use of describing it? He answers with “māyā.”
Determination of the varṇas and āśramas means determining them by their respective natures.
“Yuge yuge” means in each age; [the subjects are] the dharma for each age and the conduct accompanying Hari’s incarnations.

“With distinctions” means [dharma] connected with varṇa and āśrama. The dharma of guilds or classes of people who live by their respective occupations is characterized by rules of conduct. [This also concerns] royal sages, who have authority to protect subjects, and all people living in distress and emergencies.

The enumeration of all principles, beginning with prakṛti, is saṅkhyā; their characteristic means their essential nature, and their characteristic by cause means their definition in terms of being the cause of their respective effects; this is the meaning. The procedure for worshiping the Puruṣa means the method of deity worship, and [the procedure] of aṣṭāṅga-yoga.

Through the powers of yogeśvaras, the path beginning with arcis, by means of powers such as aṇimā. The breaking of the subtle body is pralaya. The Vedas are the Ṛg Veda and the rest; the Upavedas are Āyurveda and the rest; dharmas are the Dharmaśāstras; [the text asks about] their nature. The nature or course of Itihāsa and Purāṇa also [is asked].

“Samplava” is an intermediate dissolution. Or, it means complete floating or emergence; “vikrama” is maintenance; “pratisaṃkrama” is the great dissolution. “Iṣṭa” is Vedic action; “pūrta” is Smārta action, as [the text says]: “Wells, reservoirs, ponds and the abodes of deities; the giving of food and gardens—this is called pūrta.” In this connection is the procedure for desire-motivated acts such as Agnihotra. The procedure for the three aims—dharma, artha and kāma—is the method that avoids contradiction.
“Anuśāyin” means living beings whose adjuncts have become merged. “Ātman” means the living being. “Vyavasthānam” means abiding in a nature other than bondage and liberation.
“Udāste” means [He] remains apart during dissolution.
By the word “ca,” even what was not asked is included.

“Pramāṇa” means a right knower. Since you have a disciplic succession through Brahmā, Nārada and Vyāsa, he says, by general reasoning, “others.” Or, he says “others” because those other than you are mostly merely followers of what has been followed, not knowers of truth.

Objection: while you are agitated by fasting and the anger of a brāhmaṇa, how can there be listening? He answers with “not.” They do not go away; that is, they do not become agitated. [This is] the nectar of Acyuta’s glory.
“Upāmantrita” means invited and questioned. “Satpati” means the Lord of the good.
“Brahma-kalpa” means the Kalpa at the beginning of creation. He began to give answers to the questions precisely through the narration called the Bhāgavata; this is the meaning.
“Ṛṣabha” of the Pāṇḍus means the best. By “in order,” the order of the introduction is intended here, not the order of the questions.

An exalted seat worthy of worship. It is surrounded by four [powers] having the forms of prakṛti, puruṣa, mahat and ahaṅkāra; sixteen [powers] called the eleven senses and five great elements; and five in the form of the tanmātras. It is surrounded by His own natural opulences, such as sovereignty, unlike elsewhere in yogins, where [such opulences are] unstable and adventitious; “common” is the meaning. Even while being thus, He enjoys in His own abode, in His own nature; therefore [He is] the Lord.

His inner organ was flooded with the delight that arose from seeing Him. His body thrilled with horripilation, and his eyes held tears from the abundance of love. “Viśva-sṛk” means Brahmā. “By the path of the paramahaṃsas” means by the path of knowledge.

Bhagavān addressed that Brahmā, who was worthy of receiving His own command and appointment in the work of creating beings, or who had become engaged in the creation of beings. [He spoke] with words whose radiance and beauty were a slight smile.
With the desire to create as the reason, I was thoroughly pleased by the long-accumulated austerity. “Dustoṣa” means difficult to please.
“Mā” means me. The exertion for the fruits of the highest good, whose limit is seeing Me, is the effort of the means. Therefore there is no result beyond it; that is the meaning.

This too was obtained by you solely through My grace, he says. “The wish” is My wish, “This should be given to you”; this is its manifestation. What is it? He says: the seeing of My world. Do not think that this was obtained by me through the power of austerity and that I am independent, since even the undertaking of that [austerity] was caused by Me; he says this. Having heard the words, “Perform austerity in secret,” you performed the highest austerity.

That too was instructed by Me alone for you. When? Then, at the beginning of creation, when you were bewildered about the work to be done. Moreover, austerity is My own power: austerity is My heart, My inner power; [austerity is] the Self, My nature, as the śruti says, “whose austerity is knowledge-made.”
“I swallow” means I destroy. “I bear” means I protect. “Vīrya” means power.
“Adhyakṣa” means presiding ruler. Though He knows, being situated in the cave—in the cave of the intellect—the syntactic connection is with the following [words].

“Nāthamānasya” means of one entreating, begging or suffering. “O Lord, be my lord, give hope, grant.” “Nāthitam” means requested. The roots nāth and nādh [are used] in asking, distress, lordship and blessing. He explains “nāthitam” itself: “May I know your higher subtle form and lower gross form as they are.”

Just as you play, so place in Me the mind directed toward that [subject]; this is syntactically connected with the following “place.” You play by destroying the universe expanded by many powers, by creating it in various ways, by sustaining it, and by taking up, through yourself, your own self in the form of Brahmā and the rest. [Just as a spider] covers itself with threads, so [you do].

Do you ask for knowledge of reality while anxious only about creation? No, he says: having been instructed by You, Bhagavān, I shall perform it, being alert and not lazy. Then what need is there for this knowledge? So that, through Your grace of this kind, while endeavoring to create beings, I may not become bound by ego and the rest.

Arrogance will certainly arise in me; he prays that it not arise for some time, with “as long as.” O Lord, having been made by You like the friend of a worldly friend, honored as Your own by the touch of Your hand and so on, I remain in Your service, the creation of beings. As long as I divide and create people with distinctions such as superior and middle, let there not arise in me, made proud by Your honor, the intense arrogance that I too am unborn and independent. Or, “let my arrogance not be puffed up”; that is, let it not become excessive.

Knowledge is [knowledge] arising from scripture. Vijñāna is experience. Rahasya is devotion, as indicated by “I shall speak even what is very secret” and similar passages. Its aṅga means its means or practice.

Objection: even incapable of seeing You, how could I be eligible for knowledge? He answers with “whatever.” “Yāvān” means according to nature; “yathābhāva” means possessing such a kind of existence; [and] whatever forms, qualities and activities belong to Him.

This explains clearly the meaning of “whatever.” “I alone existed before creation; nothing else”—the gross, the subtle and the supreme, the primordial cause of both, which at that time, being turned inward, was merged in Me. At that time I alone existed, and I did not do anything else. Even afterwards, after creation, I alone am. Whatever this universe is, that too am I. At dissolution, whatever remains is also I alone. Thus it is said that I am complete, because I am beginningless, endless and non-dual.

“Through union with My own māyā”—since māyā too was asked about and its use will be stated below, he defines māyā. Whatever, without the real object, appears as a real object, or whatever, through some cause, appears in the Self, the substratum, though it is not stated or defined, and whatever real thing does not appear—that know to be My māyā. A reflection such as a double moon is the example for something perceived without the object. Darkness is the example for something existent that is not perceived: just as Rāhu, though situated in the planetary orb, is not seen.

“Yathābhāva” clarifies this. Just as the great elements, after creation, enter the material products because they are perceived in them, and before entering, exist in them as causes, so I am in these elements and material products, and I am not in them. This is the nature of My existence.

He states the means. One desiring to inquire into the Self should inquire only into this extent. He explains it: anvaya is continuation in the effects as their cause; vyatireka is distinction from them in the causal state. Likewise, in waking and the other states, there is continuation as the witness of each respective state; and there is distinction in samādhi and the other states. Thus, by anvaya and vyatireka, whatever is present everywhere and always—that alone is the Self.

He graciously fulfills what was requested, “while endeavoring to create beings”: practice this teaching of Mine properly. “Samādhi” means one-pointedness of mind. In the kalpas, the various creations, [you should think], “I shall not fall into delusion, identification with agency.”
Having instructed [him] in this way, He concealed His own form from Brahmā, the supreme being established in the highest sovereignty.
To Hari, for whom the sense-objects had disappeared and whose form is direct perception, he stood with joined hands.

Thus, after the previously mentioned dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada had begun, he says this with five [verses] beginning “the lord of creatures.” Seeking the welfare of beings and considering [it], he undertook yama and niyama with that desire which is itself an object of desire for its own purpose. Or, with the desire for his own purpose [thinking], “Let My progeny practice yama and niyama.”

Among the sons who receive inheritance—sons who take ancestral wealth as their share—he, being the dearest, pleased that father whom he served by good conduct and the like; this is syntactically connected with the following.
Desiring what? Seeking to know Viṣṇu’s māyā.
“Niśāmya” means having seen or known; that is the meaning. “Mā” means me.
Bhagavān spoke briefly in the four verses; he spoke [it] in detail. [The Bhāgavata] is that in which the objects characterized by the ten characteristics are present.
With the intention “I learned the Bhāgavata through disciplic succession,” he says “Nārada.”

“I shall answer your questions through the explanation of the Bhāgavata alone,” he says with “what was said.” As in “The worlds with their protectors were formerly formed from the limbs of the Puruṣa” (Bhāg. 2.8.11) and similar passages: [you asked] how this universe came to be from the cosmic Puruṣa; I shall narrate that to you properly; listen.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.

He shows [the senses’] importance. The prāṇas are the senses: just as servants act after a king who acts, they act after him who breathes and moves; they cease activity after him who ceases activity, like servants after a king.

“Kṣipata,” one who moves or acts, is the cause of hunger, thirst and so on. “Of the Lord” is stated for meditation through the non-difference of the Virāṭ and the living being. [The mouth] arose. From that came “jaksataḥ,” meaning one desiring to eat. First, it became divided.

The palate is the seat, the tongue is the sense organ, various tastes are the object, and Varuṇa is the presiding deity. Everywhere the fourfold set—seat, sense organ, deity and object—although not stated, should be inferred.

For one wishing to speak, [the organ] arose from the mouth itself. Fire is the deity, speech is the sense organ, and utterance is speaking. By “of the two” he shows that the action depends upon the sense organ and deity.

When the life-wind in the sky is violently moving, the deity in the nose is air, which carries smell; hence [it is said so]. This shows that smell is the object. The nose is the sense organ, for one desiring to grasp smell.

“Without light,” devoid of illumination, is to be supplied. This is an avyayībhāva compound, as in “without flies.” At that time, for one wishing to see the self, the body and other things, the eyes are the seat, the sun is the deity, and the eye is the sense organ; from that comes grasping the quality, form. This shows that form is the object.
“By the ṛṣis” means by the Vedas, by which [the Self] is made known. [This concerns] one wishing to grasp the awakening of the Self. From that, “grasping the quality” means grasping sound.

Softness, hardness, lightness, heaviness, slight warmth and cold are intended. Although extreme heat is also an object of the senses, because no one desires to grasp it, “warmth” is stated. In the reading guru-uṣṇa, the substitution of ṣaṇ is Vedic. Desiring to grasp these properties of an object, the skin was split; that is, the skin, the seat of the skin-sense, was produced. In it the hairs and the plants as deities were produced. According to the Purāṇas, when an object is lifted by hand, knowledge of lightness and heaviness shows that these too are objects of the skin-sense. Within and without the skin, wind is enclosed. What is meant is this: the skin-sense itself, grasping touch outside together with itching, is called “hair”; there the plants are the deities. That which grasps touch within and without is called “skin”; there wind is the deity. In the Bahvṛca śruti, however, one portion alone is specified: “The skin was split; from the skin came the hairs, and from the hairs the plants.”
“Ruruhatu” means the two were split. Strength is the sense organ, Indra is the deity, and the action of taking, which rests on both, is the action.

“Abhikāmikā” means desired, sought and beneficial. Together with the feet, sacrifice itself—Viṣṇu—stands as their presiding form. By “actions,” the power of action called movement is stated as the sense organ. “Havya” means the substance to be offered for sacrifice, the object attained by movement. “By men” shows that the same arrangement exists even in individual living beings, and shows their eligibility for sacrifice and the rest.

“Progeny” means offspring; bliss, love, immortality, heaven and the rest are [desired] by those who seek them. The penis is the seat, the organ is the upastha, and Prajāpati is the deity; this should be known. The pleasant happiness connected with desire rests on both.

“Dhātu-mala” means the impure residue of eaten food and the like, for one desiring to expel the insubstantial part. The anus is the seat, the organ is the pāyu, Mitra is the deity, and excretion is the object.

“By the city” means by the body; from the body, desiring to move into other bodies and wishing to go everywhere. The connection is “the navel door was split open.” [He is] one who goes away through apāna. Separation means death. The navel and the rest are the seat and the other [members of the fourfold set]. For it is commonly known that death occurs at the navel when the connection between prāṇa and apāna is severed.

For one wishing to take and store food and drink, the abdomen, intestines and channels arose. The abdomen is the seat; the intestines are the instrument, in the place of a sense organ, for storing food; the channels are for receiving drink. Of those two groups, the rivers and oceans are respectively the deities. Satisfaction is filling the abdomen; nourishment is bulk produced by the transformation of the essence. They are supported by those [groups] and caused by both. For the desire to store food, the four are abdomen, intestines, ocean and satisfaction; for the desire to store drink, the distinction is abdomen, channels, river and nourishment.
For one wishing to meditate very intensely. Desire is longing. The heart and mind, the moon and resolve are the seat and the other [members of the fourfold set].

Having divided and explained the distinction of adhidaiva and the other categories, he states the nature of their constituent dhātus and the rest, with “skin” in two verses. Skin is gross; the flesh situated above it is subtle. The seven dhātus, from skin through bone, stated as a dual compound used in the singular sense, are made of earth, water and fire. Although they are composed of all five elements, they are described thus because air and ether do not nourish them in the form of food and the like.

They are of the nature of qualities, their selves being in qualities such as sound; that is, their nature faces the objects. The qualities are sound and the rest. “Bhūtādi” is ahaṅkāra, so called because the elements arise prominently from it. They have an auspicious nature imagined by ahaṅkāra, but are not so in reality; that is the meaning. The reason is that the mind alone is the nature of all modifications, such as desire, anger, greed, delusion and grief. It merely makes saṅkalpa and vikalpa regarding tamasic objects, not the discrimination of what should be rejected and accepted. Buddhi is the form of knowledge of things as they are, but does not grasp ultimate reality; this is stated for the sake of dispassion. By this the nature of buddhi and mind is also stated.
He concludes: “this.” [The total is] eight together with prakṛti.

Having stated the gross, he states the subtle, the aggregate liṅga body. It is therefore subtle, the cause of what is beyond it, and beyond the senses. It is unmanifest because it is not made manifest by the eyes and the other senses. Why is it so? Because it is without distinguishing marks, beginningless, middleless and endless, devoid of origination, maintenance and dissolution. It is eternal, always of one form, free from decay and the rest; that is the meaning. Therefore speech and mind [cannot reach it]; the dual compound is used in the singular sense. Hence it is beyond.
For the sake of worship, he rejects the two forms superimposed on Bhagavān: “these two” means they do not truly grasp or accept them, because they are created by māyā.

To elaborate what Bhagavān said to Brahmā—“He whose form, qualities and actions [are such]” (Bhāg. 2.9.30)—he states the forms beginning with Brahmā and their actions, beginning with “He.” That Bhagavān, assuming the form of Brahmā, bears names, forms and actions as words and their objects; that is, He creates. Being endowed with actions and activity through māyā, He is in reality without action.

He elaborates this with three and a half verses beginning “the Prajāpatis.” The words ending in the accusative, beginning with “He bears,” are syntactically connected. There, the names such as Prajāpati, the forms denoted by each name and the actions belonging to each are to be understood separately, according to their respective intermediate distinctions.

After “mountains” comes the address “O king.” They are twofold in the form of stationary and moving beings, and fourfold in the form of those born from wombs, eggs, sweat and sprouts. He also bears those whose abodes are water, land and sky; this is connected with the preceding “He bears.”

The king’s question, “How many are the courses of action, and of what kinds, O best of brāhmaṇas?” is also answered by this, because it is relevant here. “Kuśala” means excellent, “akuśala” inferior, and “miśra” middle; “miśra” is an alternative reading. The courses of mixed meritorious and sinful actions are their fruits.

He elaborates the variety of the courses of action according to the distinctions beginning with sattva with one and a half verses. Sattva and the rest are three courses. “Deva” and the other words indicate ṛṣis and the rest. One’s own nature, the guṇa, is injured or colored by the other two guṇas.

Having stated creation in the form of Brahmā, he speaks of preservation in the form of Viṣṇu. That same Bhagavān, establishing and protecting this universe through incarnations beginning with the animal forms, nourishes it in the form of dharma and increases it through enjoyments.
He speaks of destruction in the form of Rudra: “then.” He restrains and destroys what was created from Himself.

By negating agency and the rest, he explains the purification of the tenth [characteristic]. In this manner, in the form of creating and so on, He is taught by śruti: “From this Self arose ether” and “He desired, ‘May I be many; may I be born.’” But even sages cannot see Him only in this form.

What is that previously mentioned, and why is it so? In the work of the birth and the rest of this universe, the Supreme Lord has no such nature of agency. Śruti too does not teach this as its purport; rather, it repeats or mentions it. For what purpose? To deny agency. For agency is something superimposed and manifested by māyā. Thus śruti says, “Without parts, actionless, peaceful, stainless and without blemish” (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19), and “Indra moves in many forms through māyās” and similar passages.

He summarizes the stated meaning: “this.” A kalpa connected with Brahmā is a mahā-kalpa; a vikalpa is an intermediate [kalpa], included here as an example and stated briefly. Of what kind? In a mahā-kalpa are the natural creations beginning with mahat, and in an intermediate kalpa the secondary creations. “Stationary creations” is a type common to the other mahā-kalpas and so on.

He promises the detail that will be described. The measure, gross and subtle, is the characteristic of a kalpa: “It is of this extent and this form.” Its division—the intermediate kalpa in the form of a Manvantara and so on—I will explain properly and in detail later, in the Third Canto. There, listen as the Pādma kalpa and the rest are explained in full.

For the purpose for which the description of creation and so on was given, desiring to hear that very thing directly, he asks another question: “what he said.” Kṣattā is Vidura. “Tīrthas belonging to the earth”; or “the fields of the earth.” [This is] the dialogue of Kauṣārava, Maitreya, and that Kṣattā, based on spiritual knowledge. Tell [me] again the cause by which he came there.

“Asked by the king” means this: what you ask is exactly what the king also asked Śuka. Śuka, placing the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya first, spoke the entire meaning of the Purāṇa according to the questions formerly asked by the king. I shall tell you that very thing; listen in the same way.

By whom the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata was transmitted from his own mouth and from Brahmā’s mouth, spoken to Brahmā and Nārada, I bow to that guru, the Lord.

Let the good ask only about what is controlled by the thread-like device by which the universe makes the three worlds dance; let them ask about whatever has slipped in my account here. May this Bhāvārtha-dīpikā on the words connected with the Second Canto be illuminated by the good, so that it may become a lamp of truth. May the good look upon it with goodwill and forgive my boldness; I made this for my own understanding, not wholly [for others].
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.

Even struck in the vital places by harsh words entering the ears like arrows, he was free from distress. The reason is that he greatly honored māyā, thinking, “Ah, the greatness of māyā,” and considered it the cause there; before its removal he himself departed. Having done what? He placed a bow at his door, thinking, “Surely these will die; what use is a bow?” Or, he placed the bow [thinking], “Do not think that I will fight together with Bhīma and the others.”

Then he explains the manner of pilgrimage of one who had departed, with eight verses beginning “he.” Having departed from Hastināpura, he went, wishing to make holy, to the steps or places of Hari, whose feet are tīrthas. It is indicated that what was obtained by the merit of the Kauravas—indeed their fortune—went away in that form. Having a thousand forms on earth, many forms beginning with Brahmā and Rudra, He went to those tīrtha-steps, the holy places over which He stands as presiding Lord; that is the meaning.

Among the meritorious places, the gardens and the rest, there are bowers, places hidden by creepers and the like. [He went] to rivers, lakes and tīrthas whose waters are free from mud, and to abodes and sacred fields. Of what kind? Properly adorned with the forms of Ananta. “Ananya” means alone.

Also, wandering over the earth, he practiced vows. His livelihood was pure, sacred, secluded and not crowded. Always bathed, bathing at every tīrtha. He whose bed was the ground. “Avadhūta” means an unadorned body; his avadhūta dress was one wearing bark and the like. Therefore he was freely unnoticed.
[The earth] in which there was only one army-wheel, whose only royal emblem was the white umbrella, with Ajita Śrī Kṛṣṇa as helper.

There at Prabhāsa he heard the destruction of his friends, the Kauravas, caused by mutual rivalry. The example for mutual destruction is this: just as a forest that shelters a fire born from bamboo is burned, so. [The phrase] is directed toward inward arising.
He served eleven tīrthas, beginning with Trita, famous by their respective names.

“By the twice-born and gods” means made by ṛṣis and gods. The weapons belonging to each limb are called praty-aṅgas because they apply to each limb; the principal discus marks the temples, whose golden finials bear the sign. He served the various abodes of Viṣṇu—sacred fields and tīrthas—in which these [marks] were present. By seeing temples marked with the discus, remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa arises.
“Having crossed beyond” means having gone past. As far as Uddhava had arrived, at that time he himself too approached the Yamunā.

“He” is Vidura. In an alternate reading, “former son” means a former disciple in political science; in another reading, “one by whom political science was obtained.” “Pratīta” means famous. “His own” means his relatives; he asked about their welfare. The reason for asking is that they are Bhagavān’s people, who are to be protected.

First he asks about the welfare of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa. “Kaccit” is a question. “Born from His own navel” means Padma Brahmā; by following him [and his prayer] they have descended—are they well? “Kṛta-kṣaṇau” means they have given opportunity to all and made a festival for all. Although they are eternally well, the question is whether, endowed with the stated qualities, they reside in the house of Śūrasena.

With nine [verses] he asks about the Yadus. “Bhāma” means worshipful. “Śauri” means Vasudeva. Or, “bhāma” means a sister’s husband. Kuntī is Vasudeva’s sister; hence in common usage Devakī is Pāṇḍu’s sister. “Varān” means objects or boons. “Vadānya” means exceedingly generous. “Together with the satisfaction of the lords of the boons” means together with the contentment of their husbands or lords.
