“Lord of the army” means commander. In the first creation, in a former birth, she obtained as a son Smara, Kāma, who existed [then].
Ugrasena is lord of the Sātvatas and the rest. Śrī Kṛṣṇa is lotus-eyed. [He asks about] one who, abandoning desire for a king’s seat or kingdom, remained far away through fear of life.
O gentle one. Hari’s son, resembling Him, lives happily. Guha is Lord Kārttikeya. [He asks about] him whom Bhavānī formerly held in her womb.
Yuyudhāna is Sātyaki. “Kṣema” means welfare. He by whom the secret of the bow, obtained from Arjuna, was learned. [He asks about] his path, related to Adhokṣaja.

The son of Śvaphalka is Akrūra. “Wise” means learned. Therefore he has surrendered to and followed Bhagavān. Hence “anāmīva” means sinless, a mark of devotion. “He acted” means he rolled about. He is one whose composure was split and shattered by love. “Svasti” means welfare; he lives.

[He asks about] Devakī, the daughter of Devaka, the Bhoja. Viṣṇu is her son, as He is the son of Aditi, the mother of the gods. “Is all well?” As the three Vedas reveal the meaning in the form of the sacrificial spread, so she bore Him.

He who fulfills the desires of the Sātvatas, the worshipers, is a kāma-dugh. The reason for His being Bhagavān is that the Vedas proclaim Him the source, the cause, of word and scripture. Why? He is manomaya, the impeller of the mind. Why is that? He is the fourth principle, the presiding deity, of the fourfold inner organ of sattva. Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha are the presiding deities, respectively, of citta, ahaṅkāra, buddhi and mind. The mind’s being the source of word is well known: mind is the prior form and speech the later form. Thus the śruti first presents another inner self, manomaya, and says that its head is Yajur, its right wing Ṛg and its left wing Sāma. The teaching of Śikṣā likewise says: “The Self, together with buddhi, joins meanings to the mind for expression; the mind strikes the body-fire, and it impels the wind; the wind moving in the chest produces a deep sound.”

“Api svit” means “what indeed?” The others too proceed in welfare. Those who properly follow their own deity, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, with the state of exclusive devotion, excluding the self distinct from their body and the rest [as an object of devotion], [are meant]. This includes Hṛdīka and the sons of Satyabhāmā, beginning with Cārudeṣṇa and Gada.

Now he asks about the Kurus with six [verses]. “Api” means whether. With Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa, Vijay and Acyuta, acting like his own arms, Yudhiṣṭhira protects the bridge of dharma, the boundary of dharma, by the path of dharma. In whose assembly there is a succession of victories through Arjuna’s service—or, [he asks about] one whose opulence is of this kind.

Among the Kurus who committed offenses, has Bhīma, very wrathful like a serpent, released or not the great sin committed by him and contemplated for a long time? [This is] while he moves through the various paths of the mace.

Among the leaders of chariots, [he is] the bearer of fame. Or, he gives fame to his own people, and their enemies have been destroyed by him. He is one whose [enemies] were hidden and covered by a mass of arrows.

“Uta svit” means “what indeed?” The twins are Nakula and Sahadeva; they sport. The sons of Mādrī, also sons of Pṛthā, surrounded by Pṛthā’s sons, sport like two Suparṇas. Having done what? Having taken and seized their own inheritance, their kingdom, from Duryodhana. Like Garuḍa taking his own inheritance, nectar, from the mouth of Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt. Or, [the reading is] “like two Suparṇas”: if two Garuḍas were to bring nectar, then [it is] like that. “Akṣiṇīva” has sandhi according to the class of words such as maṇi.

What welfare should I ask about Pṛthā, since her maintaining life without Pāṇḍu is itself astonishing? “Dhriyate” means she lives. It is not entirely astonishing, because she lives for the sake of her children, not for enjoyment. Yet it is astonishing, he says, to live without one who was so constituted. He explains it: [he is] one whose bow is a second helper.

It is reasonable that Pṛthā lives for the sake of her children, he says. O gentle one, I grieve for the living Dhṛtarāṣṭra. What is that? [He is] falling down. The reason is that he betrayed and wronged his dead brother Pāṇḍu through hostility toward his sons. Moreover, he wronged his brother while he was alive: by him I, his friend and brother, was driven out and exiled from my city.

Ah, it is astonishing that, even knowing his bad conduct, you have been made to suffer though virtuous. He says: by Hari’s grace, seeing His greatness and path, free from astonishment, I wander happily on this earth, hidden and not noticed by others. Of what sort is He? By His power of imitating mortality, which covers His opulence, He imitates human behavior and moves and confounds people’s sight and mental activities.

One might object: what need has Hari for such a pastime, by which His devotees suffer exile and the like, and He Himself suffers defeat through becoming an envoy, being bound and attempting the rest? It would be better to kill them immediately after their offenses, not overlook their offenses. He answers: certainly, although the Lord was capable of killing the Kurus at the very time of their offense, because of the three prides of those who had gone astray and become arrogant, and out of the desire to remove the distress of the surrendered, He overlooked the Kurus’ offense. The intention was that, if they were killed then, all wicked kings would not be killed. The three prides are pride of learning, pride of wealth and pride of birth; these very things are restraints in good people.

Therefore, that Bhagavān’s birth and actions are for the destruction of all ill-behaved people and the like, and not otherwise, he says by the reasoning from a stronger case: the birth of the unborn and the actions of the inactive are for attracting people and inducing them to engage in action. If it were otherwise, then let alone the story of Bhagavān’s birth and the rest; who else, being beyond the guṇas, could accept connection with a body or an expansion of action?

Therefore, he says, narrate the story of this inconceivable play of māyā. He was born among the Yadus for the sake of the surrendered world-protectors and the others who stand under His command. His fame is a tīrtha that carries one across saṃsāra.

Objection: why is He the Lord of the higher and lower when dependence is perceived? He answers with two [verses]. This also troubles me, being difficult to reason about and hard to accomplish; he explains it: His imitation of birth in the prison-house in Vasudeva’s house, not a sudden manifestation as Nṛsiṃha; His residence in Vraja as if hiding from fear of Kaṃsa; and His residing in and fleeing from Mathurā as if from fear of enemies such as Kālayavana.

This conduct of Hari pains my mind when I remember it. He shows this by saying: O father, O mother, be pleased. [He speaks of] those for whom no atonement or service was performed. The plural “of us” indicates the intention of Rāma and the others.

Objection: then why should He not be simply non-lordly? This is only your faith. He answers with three [verses]: who could be capable of forgetting Him, even while smelling and serving the dust of His lotus feet? His flashing eyebrow-branch is Death itself.
There is no need to establish His lordship, since even you have seen it; he says this with “seen.” [They are] those whom people desire to attain by proper yoga.
In battle, purified and made sinless by Arjuna’s weapons.

Even though such supreme opulence exists, His following Ugrasena troubles us greatly; this is the connection with what follows. He has no equal or superior—meaning, there is no one whose equality or superiority exists in relation to Him. The reasons are these: He is the lord of three, whether the three persons, worlds or guṇas; through the wealth of His own sovereignty, He has attained every enjoyment by the nature of supreme bliss; and His footstool is praised by the long-standing guardians of the worlds, who offer tribute or worship and whose crowns touch its tip. The sound of the collision of the crowns of those bowing is imagined as praise.
O Vidura. “Bhṛtān” means servants. He himself, while standing, informed the servants’ lord Ugrasena, seated on the royal seat, the throne of Brahmā: “O Lord, determine; consider.”

Thus, indicating that His favor continues by grace alone and showing His compassion even to offenders, he says: Ah, what a wonder of compassion! Although she intended to kill Him, He made the wicked Bakī Pūtanā drink the deadly poison Kālakūṭa gathered in her breasts. Even she obtained the proper destination of Yaśodā’s nurse. He gave a good destination merely for assuming the guise of a devotee. Whom else should we worship?

It is well known that Bhagavān favors the devotees. True, I consider even the demons devotees, because, like devotees, they see Bhagavān directly, their minds being absorbed through anger. Thus in battle they saw Him, with Garuḍa, the son of Kaśyapa, on His shoulder, and with the discus-weapon Sunābha as His enemy. Therefore favor toward them too is fitting. He will say: “Therefore, by any means, one should place the mind in Kṛṣṇa” (Bhāg. 7.1.30).

Now, to state the manner of His disappearance, he tells that conduct from the beginning in summary. He was born in the wife of Vasudeva. Kaṃsa, the lord of the Bhojas, was in the prison-house. Having been asked by unborn Brahmā, He Himself desired to bring happiness to this earth.
He went from here to Nanda’s Vraja, with the father as the cause. He remained for years with hidden splendor and concealed radiance.
He played. [The place] was crowded and filled with trees and birds making their calls.
The word “as if” is connected appropriately everywhere. He had the gaze of a lion who was both innocent and a child.

Having reached greater age, He herded the cows. What were the cows? An abode of Lakṣmī’s beauty and other wealth. In the multicolored herd were white cows and bulls. His flute made sound, and He delighted them.
He drove away and killed, as playthings made of grass and the like, lions and the rest.
Raising the dead cowherds and cows, He gave them that very water, naturally situated and free from poison.

By breaking Indra’s worship, the worship of the cows was made; that was the cow-sacrifice. [He honored] Nanda, the king of the cowherds. By the word “wealth” and the rest, the breaking of the pride of Indra, who possessed immense abundance, is also indicated.
He rains out of anger. The mountain itself, Govardhana, became a playful parasol, by means of which [He protected them]. O fortunate one.
“Mṛṣṭa” means polished and bright. He adorns the circle of women; therefore [it is called] so.
Thus, having successively contemplated what was stated in the two verses, he placed [them] in his own kingdom.
“Dhṛta” means protected.
Together with the younger brothers.
“Sāṅkhya” means discrimination between prakṛti and puruṣa.

“Snigdha” means that His glance was accompanied by a smile; “pīyūṣa-kalpayā” means like nectar, or, in another reading, in the form of a stream of nectar; “ātmā” means the body. “Kṣaṇadayā” means night; “given a moment” means given an opportunity or a festival, and He is one whose affection toward those women lasted for a moment.
In householder duties. “Yogas” means the means of sensual enjoyment. Dispassion arose, that is, indifference.
When Bhagavān is dispassionate even toward things under His control, who would put trust or affection in things under destiny? If by yoga one has followed Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of yoga.
“Śepuḥ” means they gave a curse. In Bhagavān’s intention, they were knowers.

Those cows endowed with many qualities such as age and good conduct.
And daughters. “Vṛtti-karī” means sufficient for livelihood.
So that it may be an offering to Bhagavān. Those whose lives are for cows and brāhmaṇas.

He shows extraordinary conduct: the actions of one without desire, inactive; the birth of one unborn; and, as Time Himself, taking shelter in a fortress because of fear of enemies. The householder state of one who delights in His own Self with many women—on this subject even the intellect of the learned is distressed by doubt.

Also, when the mantras were being presented and recited, you called me and asked—indeed. “Akuṇṭhita” means unobstructed by time and the rest; “akhaṇḍa” means continuous; “sadātma” means knowledge free from doubt and the like, whose essence is the power of knowledge. [You asked] like one who is bewildered, though you were alert.

[You asked about] the secret and reality of Your own Self, its revealer. For whom? For Brahmā. The universal pronoun is an archaic usage. If it is possible and suitable for even us to grasp it, then speak. O Lord, [tell us] that by which we shall cross the suffering of saṃsāra without effort.
To Him by whom the intention in the heart was made known, who is situated in the heart.

The Lord whose feet were worshiped is Himself the tīrtha and the guru; therefore, through Him, I studied and attained the path of awakening to the essential Self, the knowledge of the ultimate Self. I circumambulated the Lord.
By seeing Him there is joy, and by separation there is distress; endowed with both, I shall go to Badarikāśrama.

“Mṛdu” means free from harm to others; “tīvra” means difficult to practice; “dīrgha” means lasting to the end of the kalpa. “They practiced austerity” is the meaning. They are promoters of the world, causes of the welfare of the world.
By knowledge, by discrimination.
Through trust, through confidence.
Because the servants of Viṣṇu move about, accomplishing the purposes of their own servants. For those who have accomplished their purpose, no other duty exists; that is the meaning.

“Having worshiped for the sake of truth” means this: by Bhagavān alone, through mere remembrance, your essential nature has almost been instructed. Now, only for the removal of doubt and the like, some knower should be worshiped. That knower to be worshiped by you is Maitreya, not I, because he was appointed to instruct you in my very presence.

When they had met death through Brahmā’s curse, [it is said] that Hari too, the Lord of the three beginning with Brahmā, abandoned His human form.
By the time that has Brahmā’s curse as its pretext, in the form of His own power. His desired aim is unfailing. The curse is not powerful here; Bhagavān’s will alone is [the cause].
When I had ceased, he became eligible for knowledge.
He is not even slightly inferior to Me, provided he is not agitated by qualities, the sense objects. He teaches the world knowledge concerning Me.
With this intention, he worshiped the Veda-maker, the source of word.
Others are like animals, with unsettled selves and unsteady minds. [They are] what was seen or thought by the mind.
From the vicinity of Kālinḍī, Vidura, already accomplished, after a few days reached the divine river, the Gaṅgā.

With the intention that especially the narrations of Śrī Kṛṣṇa should be spoken, he says, “He.” He who first assumed potency for the purpose of the universe’s creation and the rest, and then accepted incarnation among the Puruṣas, performed activities surpassing human beings; speak those in detail.
He was asked for that reason: the highest good alone is the purpose of human beings.

He expresses great respect with five [verses], beginning with “sādhu.” [Maitreya is] one whose mind is fixed on Adhokṣaja alone, and who, in the course of the reply, expands the glory of that Self, his own [Lord].

If Hari has been grasped [by you], this is not extraordinary. Why? Dhṛtarāṣṭra too was born from Bādarāyaṇa’s seed—this is true—but in you there is a distinction from him; therefore [the verse] says “grasped.”

Then how is there śūdra-hood, and how are you a benefactor of the world? He answers, “because of Māṇḍavya’s curse.” In the field of your brother Vichitravīrya, in the maidservant accepted as that field, you were born as Yama himself.

Also [he says] “bhavān” (“you”). Why? [Because you are the one] for whose instruction in knowledge he appointed me. By the particle ca, it is understood that he himself also instructed [you], merely through remembrance.
They are [the narrations] whose subjects are the matters beginning with the maintenance of the universe.

Here, to describe the creation-līlā, he states the prior condition: before creation, this universe was the Supreme Self, Bhagavān, alone. “Ātmanām” means “of the living beings”; “ātma” means their own nature; “vibhu” means their master. Nothing else consisting of seer and seen existed.

He says “not characterized by various conceptions” because, although it existed in causal form, there was no apprehension of it as separate. Alternatively, without joining the negative prefix a, the meaning is: that which in creation is apprehended through various conceptions was then one alone. Why? Māyā, the will of the Self, had followed [the Self] into dissolution. Or the meaning is that the desire of the Self to remain alone had continued.

Here he explains the manner of Māyā’s arising in two [verses]. This very Seer, though a seer, did not see the seen, because at that time the sole sovereign alone shone. He thought himself, as it were, nonexistent, because without the seen there is no status as seer. He explains: [He is] one whose powers beginning with Māyā were asleep. Yet he did not think himself actually nonexistent, because the seeing, conscious power belonging to him was not asleep.

That [Māyā] indeed has the form of tracing the relation between seer and seen. “Sat” means the seen; “asat,” the unseen. “Ātma” means nature. Her nature is the sat and asat, because she takes the form of tracing both.

By the movement of Time—that is, by the power of Time—in the guṇa-filled Māyā, whose guṇas had become agitated, Adhokṣaja, the Supreme Self, through the Puruṣa who is a portion of Himself and is in the form of the overseer of Prakṛti, placed potency, the reflection of consciousness. “The possessor of potency” means one endowed with conscious power.

From the unmanifest Māyā impelled by Time. Leaving aside the word tattva, he states the characteristic of mahat; hence the masculine designation vijñānātmā. Because sattva predominates, [mahat] manifests the universe situated in its own body, like a tree in a swollen seed, making it visible. Since it dispels darkness, it is called “the dispeller of darkness.” The Sātvata Tantra says:

“Of Viṣṇu they know three forms bearing the name Puruṣa: first, the creator of mahat; second, situated in the cosmic egg; third, situated in all beings. Knowing them, one is liberated.”

With one and a half [verses], he explains the arising of ahaṅkāra, beginning with “that too.” The portion in the form of the reflection of consciousness is the efficient cause; the guṇas are the material cause; Time is the agitator. Bhagavān, whose self is that and who is dependent on that, the overseer of all, having come within the range of its sight, Himself transformed Himself into another form.

He states the characteristics of ahaṅkāra: the effect is adhibhūta, the cause is adhyātma, and the agent is adhidaiva; their self is the support. The reason is that it is made of the elements, senses, and mind, and possesses their modifications. By “mind,” the deities too are indicated.

He elaborates this by its divisions, beginning with “vaikārika.” Vaikārika is sāttvika; taijasa is rājasa. The deities too are vaikārika, meaning that they are products of sāttvika ahaṅkāra. From the deities presiding over the senses, the manifestation of objects, beginning with sound, takes place.

The intended connection is “they are taijasa alone.” The particle eva is used so that there may be no doubt that the knowledge-made [senses] are sāttvika. The tāmasa [ahaṅkāra] is the cause of the subtle elements, sound being the first; from sound space arises. [Space] is the liṅga of the Self, manifesting through its own quality in the form of sound, or as the space in the heart. Alternatively, liṅga means body, in accordance with the śruti, “Brahman has space as its body.”

Air is [produced] by transforming the touch that has arisen from space itself and followed from it, carrying [that element] into another form. Thus, everywhere, the production of the gross elements through the subtle elements is to be understood.
Then [it produces] light/fire, accompanied by space and [air] itself and endowed with great power; it is the illuminator, the eye [of the world].

O fortunate Vidura. In another reading, bhāvya means “effect.” Whatever is each lower effect, of those effects, through association with the higher causes, they know progressively and in due order successively more qualities. Thus space has sound alone as its quality, because there is no association with the others. Air has touch and, because it is associated with space, sound as well. Similarly, fire has those two and form; water has those three and taste; earth has them all.

Having come together with one another, the mutually competing gods, powerless in the work of the universe and dejected, praised Hari, beginning with “We bow.” [His lotus feet are] a parasol for pacifying the distress of those who have taken shelter. “Ātapatra” means an umbrella. The reason is that those whose shelter is the sole of His lotus feet cast the suffering of saṃsāra far outside and abandon it, like travelers who, upon reaching their own home, abandon the fatigue of the road.

Expressing their fatigue, they speak. “O Dhātṛ” means “O Father”; “yat” means “because”; “bhava” means saṃsāra; “ātman” means “in the Self,” or it is a vocative. “Śarma” means happiness. In the reading “ṛte yat,” the meaning is that they do not obtain happiness without worship of Your feet. One might object: the suffering caused by ignorance is removed by knowledge, so what is the use of taking shelter of the shade of My feet? They answer: taking shelter of Him together with knowledge is itself what bestows knowledge.

Because one cannot take shelter of what is unknown, they state the means of attaining knowledge of Him. “Mārganti” means “they seek.” We have taken refuge in Your feet, which are the holy place, and which [the sages] seek. With what do they seek? With the birds of the Veda, the chandas, whose nest is Your lotus mouth. Just as birds emerge from their nest, wander here and there, and enter that same nest again, so the Vedas arise from You and culminate in You. Therefore they seek Your feet by relying on the Vedas. [They seek them] in a secluded, unattached mind. Moreover, [Your feet] are the source of the excellent Gaṅgā, among the rivers whose water removes sin and gives the joy that destroys sin. Therefore, even while serving Gaṅgā, they reach Your feet, its source.

One might ask: how can those whose minds are drawn to sense objects search for Him? They answer: having placed [Him] in the heart and meditated, they become steady through knowledge whose strength is dispassion. But how can meditation occur in a mind with attachment? They answer: when it is cleansed and purified by faith preceded by hearing and by devotion.
Remembering His favor to devotees, they say [the verse beginning] “of the universe.”

Fearing the objection that, since He is always present as the inner controller, going [to His feet] is purposeless, they say “yat.” “Sānubandha” means “with its accessories”; “asat” means “insignificant”; “puryām” means “in the city,” that is, in one’s own body. Even while dwelling there, [He] is very far away and difficult to attain.

One might object: if the lotus of His feet is very far from some, even though He is situated in the heart, it should be so for others too without distinction. They answer, “those.” Their minds are carried far away from within by eyes and senses turned outward through evil activities; therefore they surely do not see those [devotees]. This is well known. How could association with those [devotees] arise for them? Which [devotees]? Those connected with the splendor of Your stepping and walking—Your devotees adorned by the stories of Your līlās and the like.

In the reading “patha” and “lakṣyā,” [the meaning is:] those in whom the splendor of Your footstep and play is the object; they do not see the paths that are Your ways, or the good paths such as hearing. Alternatively, the sense is that devotees such as these surely do not see those mad [offenders]. Because of the absence of saintly association and the absence of hearing Hari’s topics, [the Lord] is far away for them even though He is situated in the heart.
With two [verses] beginning with “by drinking,” they make this explicit. Having obtained knowledge whose strength has dispassion as its essence, they attain the unobstructed abode, Vaikuṇṭha.

Samādhi in the Self means steadiness of mind; that alone is the means called yoga, through its strength. Through jñāna-yoga, liberation comes with exertion, whereas through saintly association, beginning with hearing Your topics, it comes effortlessly. But for those filled with “I” and “mine,” it does not [come] in any way; this is the meaning.

Having thus praised [Him], they pray in four [verses]. “Therefore,” O Primal One, we are Yours, since, with the desire to create the worlds, You created us, producing us successively. Being separated by the three selves, whose natures begin with sattva, and therefore being divided because their natures are mutually opposed, we were created for that universe, the instrument of Your sport and an implement of Your play; we cannot return it and offer it to You. Therefore, give us Your own eye—this is the connection of the fourth [verse] with the preceding three.

To elaborate their inability, they state the great variety of the work. “O Unborn, at each appropriate time we offer You the tribute, the enjoyment, in full. In whatever way we eat food”—by this, only the food is ours; in lordship, the enjoyment is Yours alone. The living beings belonging to both You and us, while situated there, are free from obstruction and without impediment. Alternatively, anūhā means without conjecture, without doubt. The śruti likewise says: “They said to him, ‘Declare for us the abode in which, being established, we may eat food.’”

They say that, because You are the creator, You must necessarily arrange the sustenance of us and of these living beings who have functional designations. “Sānvayānām” means “together with the effects”; alternatively, anvaya means “that which follows,” and You alone are the primal cause of those together with their effects. The reasons are that You are kūṭastha, unchanging; puruṣa, the overseer; and purāṇa, ancient. They establish this with “You”: O Deva, being unborn, You first placed the seed in the power, Māyā, which is the causal womb of the guṇas beginning with sattva and of actions beginning with birth. That is, You deposited it there. What kind? The omniscient one, in the form of the mahat-tattva.

“By prāṇa” means by the skin-sense that pervades the body like prāṇa.
“The accomplishment of sound” means knowledge.

“Tvac” means skin. “Oṣadhī” means plants. For the skin-sense alone, owing to a difference of location, there are two objects: itching and touch. The difference of name and the difference of deity there have been explained in the Second Canto itself.
“Ka” means Prajāpati.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.
“Lord of heaven” means lord of heaven. “Vārtā” means the power of buying, selling, and so on. “Vṛtti” means livelihood.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.
“Vikriyā” means a modification in the form of resolve and so on.
“Ātman” means ahaṅkāra. Abhimāna, through which one thinks, “I,” is Rudra. “By karma” means by the “I”-modification. “What is to be done” means action.
“Sattva” is a designation of buddhi and citta without distinction. “Great” means Brahmā. “With citta” means with consciousness.
He explains the production of the three worlds with “from the head.” “Vṛttis” means transformations.

He elaborates this with two [verses]. “With extreme power” is the meaning. “Paṇ” is used in the sense of dealing. Those who engage in dealings, through sacrifice and so on, are called paṇas, human beings; following them, the cows and others who are instruments for this also entered the earth.

The third is darkness, through its tāmasa [aspect]. The middle between heaven and earth is the sky, the intermediate space; that itself is Bhagavān’s navel. In it are situated the groups of Rudra’s attendants, the beings beginning with the bhūtas.

“Avartata” means “arose” or “became active.” Brahman means the Veda. Because of being foremost, arising from the mouth, and being chief among the varṇas—like the mouth—and also being the first teacher, it too is said to arise from the mouth; this is the implied connection. The Veda is the livelihood of the brāhmaṇa through teaching and the like. The meaning is that the brāhmaṇa was born from the mouth together with that livelihood. The same should be understood below for the other three varṇas, born from their respective limbs together with their respective livelihoods.

“Kṣatra” means the occupation of protection; the kṣatriya who follows that kṣatra also arose from the arms—that is the meaning. He explains this following with “who.” “Pauruṣa” means a portion of Puruṣa, Viṣṇu. It protects from injury and disturbance caused by thorns, thieves, and the like.

“Viśaḥ” are occupations beginning with agriculture. Those that produce livelihood for the world are causes of sustenance. Arising from the thighs of that all-pervading one, the Vaiśya born from them procured livelihood for human beings through his own occupation.
That [occupation] being the means, by whose occupation Hari Himself is satisfied.

Here he speaks with the special status of all these first-born [classes] in mind: by their respective duties they worshiped Hari alone, in the form of sacrifice. Here “yat” means “because.” The Virāṭ is produced from Hari’s power alone, from that power; therefore the intended point of the statement of their non-difference is precisely their worship of Hari.

O Vidura, who would have faith or desire to undertake and describe fully this Virāṭ form, expanded by the strength of Bhagavān’s Yoga-māyā, He who is of the form of deity, action, and self, endowed with the powers of Time, karma, and nature? Even the desire is impossible; a complete description is far beyond reach—that is the meaning.

O dear Vidura, nevertheless I will speak the glories of Hari, as heard from the mouth of the guru. Even that [I will do] not in its entirety, but according to my understanding, following my own mind. [I will do so] to honor and purify my own speech, which is impure because it expresses things other than Hari.

Even without knowing [the full meaning], he says that in chanting or hearing according to one’s capacity, the exclusive result is certain: “the attainment of exclusivity indeed.” “Śruti” means the ear; “upākṛtā” means explained; “upasaṁprayoga” means placing [it] in the presence.

There should be no insistence on excessive knowledge, because even Brahmā is difficult to know. He asks rhetorically: was the glory of Hari, the Self, ascertained even by the original poet Brahmā, with a mind matured by yoga, after a thousand years? With the rhetorical expression “this much,” it is said that it was not known at all.
Because Hari Himself, the Self, does not know the course of His own Māyā as “it is this much,” owing to its being infinite.

Therefore, because He is difficult to know, he merely offers obeisance, beginning with “from whom.” Speech, which had set out to know Him, even together with the mind, turns back without reaching Him because He is difficult to know. Not only speech and mind: I, Rudra, the overseer of ahaṅkāra, and these other gods who preside over the senses [also turn back].

Because you have spoken well. What is this? This [world], the abode of Hari’s power called ātmamāyā—the māyā relating to the living beings—appears as misfortune and the like. It is meaningless, unreal, and rootless, like the cutting off of one’s own head and so on. Its root, the root of the universe, is one’s own ignorance; apart from that there is no [other root].

Because of limited knowledge I had earlier become doubtful—he says, “one who...” The person who is extremely deluded and attached to the body and so on, and the person who has reached the Lord beyond buddhi and Prakṛti, both flourish and live happily, each in his own way, because they are free from the affliction of doubt. But one who wishes to abandon the world through reflecting on its misery cannot remain steady because he lacks experience of his own bliss; he suffers—this is the meaning.

Now I am fulfilled, since you have cut away my doubt; only the continued appearance of what has been sublated remains, and that too will cease through your grace. “Not of the Self” means “of the non-Self”: although perceived, the world has no reality; here there is no entity, only perception. Having ascertained this through service to your feet, I will also drive away that perception.
The rati-rāsa of the feet of Madhu’s enemy is a festival of love, intense, irresistible, and natural. It crushes and destroys the affliction of saṁsāra; hence it is called a vyasana-destroyer.

“Durāpā” means difficult to obtain. [The service is] on the paths to Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Viṣṇu, which are the great [devotees]. In those [great souls], through service to the great, one hears Hari’s topics; from that comes love for Hari, and through that even identification with the body and so on ceases—this is the purport.

To ask about another matter, he repeats what was stated in three [verses], beginning with “having created.” [The principles are] together with modifications, the senses and so on. Having drawn forth and created the Virāṭ with their portions...
He describes the form of the one who entered with “whom”; he distinguishes the Virāṭ with “where.” “These” means all these worlds. “With expansion” means without contraction.

The five beginning with prāṇa and the five beginning with Nāga make ten. “The senses” also [are included]. The repeated expression “objects and senses” is intended to indicate their presiding deities; [the Virāṭ is] together with them. Because prāṇa nourishes everything, it is accompanied by them. Thus, when you said “threefold,” prāṇa was stated as threefold. Its manifestations, beginning with Brahmā, are denoted by the word “creation.”
“Where” means “in which”; in them this universe is spread, pervaded.

Thus, the Vidura–Maitreya dialogue was introduced as the answer to Parīkṣit’s question: “Maitreya was indeed formerly asked this...” Therefore he now states Vidura’s questions themselves through the end. It is to be connected with what follows: “describe the lord of the Prajāpatis, Brahmā,” and so on. “Caklṛpe” means “arranged” or “created”; “sargas” are the nine kinds of primary creation, and “anusargas” their divisions.
O son of Mitrā, “saṁsthā” means arrangement or placement.

“Saṁvyūha” means the arrangement or division of the creations. [They are] the gārbha, sveda, dvija, and udbhijja. Gārbha are the jarāyuja, womb-born; those born from sweat and from two [shells] are the sweat-born and egg-born; and the udbhidas are the sprouting beings.
[Describe] the creations beginning with sarga, and the support of the one who creates them.
“Rūpa” means characteristic mark; “śīla” means conduct; “svabhāva” means nature, beginning with tranquility; “vikarṣaṇa” means division.
“Vitānas” means expansions. “The paths” means the paths of naiṣkarmya, of knowledge and its means, and of Sāṅkhya; “tantra” means [their] system or method.
“Pāṣaṇḍas’ paths” means their modes of practice; that itself is the disparity or deviation.
“Nimittas” means means, without mutual contradiction.
[Describe] the position of the planets and so on in the wheel of Time.

“By which” means by which path [Hari] becomes satisfied. “Of whom” means of what sort.
The meaning is: even what has not been asked, even what has not been requested, but is appropriate for me, should be spoken.
“Pratisaṅkrama” means dissolution. In that dissolution, when this Supreme Lord is lying [asleep], who lie after Him? Who sleep after the sleeping [Lord], as fly-whisk bearers follow a sleeping king?

“Saṁsthāna” of the Puruṣa means the reality of the jīva; “svarūpa” means the nature of the Supreme Lord; [explain] the portion by which the two are one, and that knowledge as well. “Naigama” means Upaniṣadic.
Tell also the means of that knowledge spoken by the sages. Without a guru this does not occur; hence he says “spontaneously.”
“Me” [in “my questions” and “speak to me”] is due to friendship, to affection; because the syntactic connections differ, there is no repetition of the word “me.”
[The giving] of fearlessness to living beings through instruction in truth.

And he became four-faced in that kalpa—this is expressed by “in that.” While circling, remaining there, and moving his neck, his eyes turned for the purpose of observing the worlds.

To show that his agency in creating the worlds arose only through the worship of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, through which knowledge and action powers manifested, and not independently, he first describes his bewilderment. Even after taking shelter of the lotus that had arisen from those waters, he did not directly know that lotus in its entirety, the reality of the world, or himself. “U” expresses wonder. What kind of waters? In them the entire circle of waves was shaken here and there by the dissolution wind, the breath at the end of the age.

He states the thought of that ignorant [Brahmā]: “Who am I on the back of the lotus? This lotus alone is here, with nothing else; from what was it born? That on which it is supported, existing below it, must surely be present.” The connection is with the following: “having looked in this way.” The śruti likewise says: “He saw, standing on a lotus leaf; he thought, ‘There is that on which this rests.’”

Because his activity was directed outward, he states in two [verses] beginning with “he” that he did not reach it even after a long time. The lotus stalk has channels with inner holes. Searching for the navel, the support of that lotus stalk, he went downward but did not find it then.

O Vidura, “self-creation” means its own cause. “Three-rimmed” means Time. The weapon of the Unborn Viṣṇu is the weapon in the form of Sudarśana. Producing fear in embodied human beings, it is said to be a hundred years.

By turning inward, however, he saw Bhagavān—this is stated in two [verses]. Then he stopped searching. His desire, his mental wish, had not been attained. “His own seat” means the lotus. His breath was controlled, his mind restrained; therefore, having mounted and taken shelter of samādhi-yoga, he sat down.

After a hundred years of the life of Puruṣa, the yoga became fully accomplished; through it knowledge arose in him. What he had not seen even while searching earlier, he saw shining by itself within the heart.

He describes what he saw with nine [verses] beginning with “like a lotus stalk”; the connection is that he saw it in all nine. Śeṣa was white and long like a lotus stalk; his coils, his body, were themselves the couch, and [the Lord was] upon it. Where was that couch situated? In the water of dissolution, whose darkness was destroyed by the radiance of the jewels serving as crowns on the many heads, joined on every side with hoods as parasols.

What sort of Person? He eclipsed by the excess of His own beauty the splendor of a mountain made of emerald stone. With His yellow garment He eclipsed the beauty of the twilight cloud that was His lower covering. With His own crowns He eclipsed the beauty of the mountain with its many golden peaks. Jewels, waterfalls, plants, flowers, and masses of blossoms were like a forest garland upon Him; the bamboos were His arms and the trees were His feet—He was that [mountain], and it was He. The meaning is this: if jewels and the like are situated upon Him like a garland, bamboos like arms, and trees like feet, then He eclipsed the mountain’s beauty with His own garlands of jewels, pearls, tulasī, and flowers, and with His arms and feet.

Moreover, He was marked by a body called “measure,” because it is measured in length and breadth by its own measure; that body was beautiful and incomparable. Alternatively, “measureless” means unbounded. Or, by length and breadth in their proper proportion, it was such that the three worlds were contained in it. He was endowed with a body whose beauty on every side was produced by many kinds of divine and unprecedented ornaments and garments. Though naturally supremely beautiful, His body had an assumed appearance and accepted ornaments [for the devotees]. Alternatively, in answer to the question “with what did He eclipse [the beauty]?”, the connection is “with such a body.”

He displayed and slightly raised the wish-fulfilling lotus of His feet to persons who worship for their desired fruit through secluded, pure, Vedic paths. The nails alone were moons; their rays were beams; the fingers were beautiful petals opened by them.

With a smile that removes the distress of the world, adorned with flashing earrings, with the radiance of bimba-like lips, a well-formed nose, and a beautiful eyebrow, He honored and respected the worshippers.

His garment was tawny like kadamba pollen, and with it, together with a belt, His hips were beautifully adorned. O dear one, His chest marked with Śrīvatsa was beautifully adorned with the priceless necklace beloved of His chest.

He characterizes Him through the metaphor of a great sandalwood tree. The excellent armlets, ornaments, and foremost jewels spread over His arms like thousands of endless branches. A sandalwood tree too has branches covered with fruits, flowers, and the like. The unmanifest Pradhāna is the root below. Alternatively, the unmanifest Brahman is His root, because He is the manifestation of Brahman; the root of a tree is also not visible. He is the great tree in the form of the worlds. His branches and trunks were wrapped and touched by the coils, hoods, and bodily limbs of Ananta, the king of serpents, just as the śruti says, “O tree, grow with a hundred branches.” A tree too is surrounded by snakes.

Although He was already described through the mountain metaphor with “eclipsing the splendor,” he describes Him again with other characteristics. Bhagavān Himself is the mountain; it is the abode of the moving and nonmoving beings, and so is a mountain. He is the friend of the king of serpents, and a mountain too is the friend of the king of serpents. He is covered by water, as are mountains such as Maināka. His thousand crowns are his golden peaks, as Meru and other mountains have golden peaks. Just as a jewel appears in the interior of a mountain, the Kaustubha jewel appeared clearly in the interior, the middle of His form.

Moreover, He was covered by a forest garland hanging down from His neck. The Vedas are the bees of the Veda-tradition; with Śrī, whose [companions] they are, [Brahmā] saw Hari in the mountain and the other forms—he understood, “This is Hari.” He is inaccessible to the sun and the other [luminaries], impossible to comprehend by their own activities. Moreover, He is difficult to approach because of the principal weapons such as Sudarśana, whose radiance extends through all three worlds and which run around for protection.
When he thus saw Hari, then and there he saw in His navel-lake the lotus from which the worlds are created, His breathing, the wind of dissolution, and the sky.

[The lotus is] the seed of karma, the cause of the creation of the worlds. [Brahmā] was tinged with rajas, endowed with the rajo-guṇa. Therefore, desiring to create the beings, he saw only this fivefold sequence beginning with the navel-lotus. Even toward creation his mind became intent and elevated, fixed on Bhagavān, whose path is the unmanifest.

Here, showing the activities of the incarnations associated with the modes, he offers obeisance: “who indeed is one, three-footed.” Brahmā and the others are the three feet, or trunks, of whom; each of the broad sprouts is a branch and sub-branch in the forms of Marīci and the Manus and so on. Having become such, He grew; obeisance to that tree in the form of the worlds. Having done what did He grow? His own self alone is the root, the support; having split Pradhāna and divided it into the form of the three modes. “Three-footed” means You alone. “I, Brahmā, Girīśa, and the all-powerful Viṣṇu Himself”—we are the causes of maintenance, creation, and dissolution. He grew after becoming three-footed; that is the meaning.

After stating the imitation of the activities of the mode incarnations, he bows while showing that very form called Time and its activity, with the two verses beginning “loka.” [He bows to] one intent on forbidden action, fixed in contrary action, in the auspicious, beneficial, personal activity taught directly by You, the activity in the form of worship of You. It is said in the Gītā: “Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever austerity you perform, O son of Kuntī, do that as an offering to Me.” As long as he remains heedless in that, with his mind not offered, so long [he remains] of this world. Obeisance to Time, who does not blink.

Let the matter of the world be set aside for now. Because of You in the form of Time, even though I have ascended that station lasting two parārdhas, I fear it; being afraid, I performed austerity, desiring to reach You alone and to restrain Time. What was I like? “One of many sacrifices” means one whose sacrifices are many, or whose years are many. I performed many sacrifices, or practiced austerity for many years; that is the meaning. Obeisance to You, Adhiyajña, the presiding Lord of sacrifice.

Now he describes the activities of the playful incarnations that will occur at the respective times: in animal and other births, having accepted forms by His own will, He sported, desiring to preserve the limits of dharma made by Himself. In reality, although He has rejected the happiness of sense objects through the experience of His own bliss, He is still the Supreme Person, because He is untouched by the properties of the respective limiting adjuncts. This is stated in the Gītā: “Because I am beyond the perishable and also higher than the imperishable, therefore in the world and in the Veda I am renowned as Puruṣottama.”

Now he offers obeisance to the one visible form, with the two verses beginning “yo ’vidyayā.” Although not overcome by avidyā, whose five functions are the cause of sleep, He performed yogic sleep. “Obeisance to You” is connected with the next verse. He made the course of the worlds into His belly, dissolving it there. The serpent alone is His bed, whose touch is comfortable to Him. In the inner waters, which bear a garland of terrible waves, He displays—almost mockingly—the sleep-pleasure of the undiscriminating person sleeping there: “This is what such a person’s sleep is like.” Hence the qualifiers beginning with “in the waters.” Or, He expands the resting pleasure of a person exhausted in the previous kalpa. In that case, the qualifiers indicate that, for the benefit of others, even suffering difficult for Himself must be endured.

Moreover, His navel-lotus itself is His abode; the three worlds are His instrument. Or, He serves the three worlds through creation and the rest; by whose grace I became such. In whose belly is Bhava, the manifestation of saṃsāra; whose eye, at the end of yogic sleep, is like a slightly blossoming lotus.

Having thus praised, he prays: “so ’yam” with four verses. “May He gladden the universe with sattva, knowledge, and bhaga, lordly opulence. May He join my sight with understanding, so that I may become able to create.” He is dear to those who bow, and I am one who bows; there is no other to be prayed to. Because He is Bhagavān. He alone is the friend of all the worlds, because He alone is one, pervading as the inner controller.

Whatever action He will perform together with Ramā, His own potency—whatever contains the power of Viṣṇu Himself—may that [power] engage my mind, even as I create this universe by His command. May I thereby abandon attachment to action and the impurity created by it, sin such as partiality.

Since I arose here from the navel-lake of Him who exists in the waters, whose power in knowledge presides over the mind formed from the mahat-tattva, may the utterance of the words that are the limbs of the Veda not be harmed as I expand this form. “May it not perish” is the meaning, according to the maxim concerning brahma-varchas being consonant-ending.
Expanding with a smile born of greatly increased love, [He does so] for the world’s victory, its manifestation. The word ca also indicates “and for my grace,” and [He does so] having risen.

To Him from whom his own birth came, [Brahmā], having seen Him through bodily austerity, worship, and samādhi—respectively, one-pointedness—praised Him according to his ability and stopped, as if tired.
O Veda-womb! Do not enter lassitude produced by sorrow. What you requested—“May He touch my sight” and so on—has already been accomplished earlier by that very [grace].
Then how do I not know? Thus he says with “bhūyaḥ,” “again.”
With devotion and concentration, you will see Me pervading and situated in yourself and in the world; [you will see] also the living portions of your self.
He says that delusion ceases upon seeing Me everywhere: “yada tv.” Praticakṣīta means “should see.”

Then, when false knowledge has ceased, he is liberated, he says with “yadā.” Seeing the self—the jīva—devoid of the elements and so on, the entity whose nature is purity, united with Me, his own self, he attains self-sovereignty, liberation.
Because He is the more venerable, older one; the meaning is that He is exceedingly so.
He states grace itself, with the four verses beginning “ṛṣim”: because your mind is bound to Me.
Because you consider this form of Mine to be unconnected with the elements, the senses, the qualities beginning with sattva, and the self in the form of ahaṅkāra.

While you were searching in the waters for the root, the support, of the lotus by its stalk as a path, there should have arisen doubt concerning Me: “It has this as its support, yet it is not seen.” Then, when there was doubt whether it exists or not, My self, My own form, was shown by Me within the heart, not outside.

O Brahman, what you did—the praise of Me marked by the rising of narratives about Me—[is this]. This—freedom from bondage, fixing the mind on Me, knowledge of Me, seeing My form in the heart, praise of Me, and steadfastness in austerity—all of it is My grace.
Although perceived as possessing qualities, you described Me as indeed without qualities.
Regarding My being pleased, what need is there to say? Thus he says with “ya.”

He says that there is nothing greater even than My pleasure: the result of highest good accomplished through public works and the like—pūrta and the rest—is My pleasure alone; this is the opinion of those who know the truth.

Here he states the reason, with “aham”: I am the self of selves, of living beings conditioned by ahaṅkāra. Therefore, among even those most dear, I am the dearest, being without defect. “For whose sake” means “for whose purpose.”

Therefore you are already fulfilled; nevertheless, create for My pleasure, he says with “sarva.” You are the self of this threefold world; create the progeny that remain in Me. With what? With your own self alone, independent of another. In regard to the need for a means of knowing, he says “consisting of all the Vedas.” “I am the self, the source and cause” indicates an abundance of the powers of knowledge and action. “As before” states that your previous practice also exists. “Those who remain in Me” says that they are already situated, so only their manifestation needs to be done—thus their effortless character is stated.
Having manifested this creation, Padmanābha, in the form of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, disappeared; He became hidden.
The fourth [creation] consists of the organs of knowledge and action. The fifth is the vaikārika [creation]: the deities presiding over the senses and the mind.

The sixth is the creation of darkness, of the fivefold avidyā. A-buddhi is the covering of the living beings, and the projection that produces it; therefore it is called abuddhi-kṛta. Hear it from Me.

He says it should be heard without agitation. “Whose subject is intelligence” means: the intelligence whose object is Hari removes saṃsāra; this is Hari’s play. Or, “this” means [the creation] in the form of the creation beginning with darkness. “Those who partake of rajas” means the Brahmā-form. In this interpretation, abuddhi-kṛta is nominative; its meaning is “made by inattention.”

The main [creation], as it were first made, is the main creation. “Those who stand” means stationary beings. He states its sixfold nature: those that bear fruit without flowers are vanaspatis; herbs are those that end in the ripening of their fruit; creepers require support for climbing; those with bark as their essence are bamboos and the like; creepers which, through their hardness, do not require support for climbing are vīrudhs; those that bear fruit from flowers are drumas, trees.

He states their common characteristic: those whose current is upward have upward circulation of food. They are predominantly darkness, with consciousness unmanifest. “Inner-touch” means that they know touch alone and nothing else; even that is only inward, not outward. They have many distinctions, such as irregular transformation and the like.

He describes the creation of the tiryak-srotas with “of the animals.” It has twenty-eight divisions. The characteristics of the animals are these: “without knowledge” means without knowledge of tomorrow and the like; “abounding in darkness” means fixed only in knowledge of food and the like; they know the desired object through the nose alone; “not knowing in the heart” means without prolonged reflection. Thus the śruti says: “Then, for the other animals, eating and thirst are their only recognition; they do not speak what is known, they do not see what is known, and they do not know tomorrow or this world and the other world.”

He states the twenty-eight divisions themselves: those beginning with the cow and ending with the camel are two-hoofed, nine [types]. Those beginning with the dog and ending with the lizard are five-nailed, twelve [types]. Thus these land animals are twenty-seven. The makara and the like are aquatic. The kanka and the other birds are taken together as sky-goers, as non-land animals. Thus there are twenty-eight divisions. Among them, the kṛṣṇa, ruru, and gaura are special kinds of deer. Other animals likewise are included in these categories as appropriate.

That whose movement of food is downward is arväk-srotas. The shortening [of the word] is an archaic form. The creation of human beings is the characteristic of human beings. Those in whom rajas predominates [are humans].

These three are indeed vaikṛta, not like the Kaumāra [creation], which is of both kinds. “And the deva-creation” is to be supplied. The vaikārika deva-creation was already described among the prākṛta [creations]. But this one is vaikṛta because it is lesser than that, and it is included within [the category] because it is a deva-creation. The creation of Sanat-kumāra and the others is prākṛta and vaikṛta, because they are created as gods and as human beings; that is the meaning.

Moreover, [a Manu] holds a period of somewhat more than seventy-one yugas. The descendants of Manu become protectors of the earth successively. The Saptarṣis and the rest are present simultaneously, at the same time. The lords of the gods are Indras. Those who follow them, beginning with the Gandharvas, also [are present].

For the sake of dispassion he says: in day-and-nights of this kind, a hundred years is the maximum lifespan of all living beings; even that lifespan of Brahmā is as though diminished, as though exhausted—this is a common saying. “Almost gone” is the meaning.

Complete [the verse] with “falling from the abode of Hari because of the difficult-to-cross curse of Brahmā.” Or, “from the abode of Hari itself they became deprived of their glory.” “Devoid of pride” means that their arrogance was destroyed.
“From the residence” means from the place of Vaikuṇṭha. “O sons” means “O gods.”
They attained the splendor, the power, of Kaśyapa.
The twins entered the womb together. By their splendor your splendor was overwhelmed and obscured. No countermeasure is possible here, because now Bhagavān Himself desires to arrange it in this way.

Even so, if you say that some means should be considered, he says with “of the universe”: He alone is the lord of the three modes; at the time of the predominance of sattva, He will provide our welfare. “By deliberation” means through consideration.
