“Pratīccha” means “accept; receive.”
“Udyatasya” means of an object that has arisen and come of itself; “prativāda” means rejection.
“Kīnāśa” means a miser. “Avajñayā” means through insult, through dishonor.
He whose brahmacarya has a limit is an upakurvāṇa. “Given by me” means given by me.
“Unbestowed” means that, because the decision has been made only in me, she has not been promised to anyone. “Ādya” means first, because before this there was no marriage; or it means principal.

“Bhūyān” means “may it be.” [The marriage rite] is well known from the mantra beginning, “I take your hand for good fortune, with me as husband” (Ṛg Veda 10.85.36). “By her own bodily beauty alone” [means] by splendor, the beauty produced by ornaments and so forth.
“Seeing whom, he fell” [means] he fell on seeing her. [He was one] whose mind was bewildered and agitated by delusion, and whose beauty was [displayed] by her two tinkling feet.

[She is] the crest-jewel of women, an ornament; unseen by those who have not served the feet of Śrī, unfit even to be seen [by them]. “Uccapada” means Uttānapāda’s. “Abhiyātām” means one who has herself come [to him].

“Bhajiṣye” means “I will accept.” “Time” is the phrase, “As long as offspring is produced there is household life; thereafter, renunciation.” He states that very [time]: “as long as the brilliance of my self bears the embryo.” Or, “as long as the brilliance—semen—departed from my body bears [the embryo].” Thereafter I regard the Pāramahaṃsya knowledge, the principal teachings directly and emphatically spoken by Śukla, Viṣṇu, and the nonviolent disciplines beginning with tranquility, as to be practiced abundantly.

[It may be objected:] Your father, the Prajāpati, commanded [you] only regarding creation, not renunciation. In that regard he says “from whom”: “Saṁsthāsyate” means “will go to dissolution.” “Vāva” means “only.” The meaning is that, after discharging the three debts, renunciation alone is enjoined by Bhagavān for persons like me.
“O Ugra-dhanvan, Vidura!” means “O Vidura!” “Lulubhe” means that [Devahūti’s heart] was enticed by the sage’s face, and he too was enticed. Or, he enticed [her] by his face.
“Sa” means Manu. “Anu” means afterward. [He did so] having known the queen’s clear resolve [concerning her daughter].
“Pāribarhān” means gifts to be given at the time of marriage. “Bhūṣāḥ” means ornaments; “vāsāṁsi,” garments; “paricchadān,” household equipment and so forth.
“Prattām” means given. “Sadṛkṣāya” means to an equal, a suitable match. “Gata-vyathaḥ” means one whose anxiety has gone. [He was] one whose mind was agitated by eagerness.
[He spoke] “O mother! O child!” in order to endure separation from her. This is an ṛṣi-style sandhi. “Śikhāḥ” means the hair; he sprinkled the locks with [the water from] his eyes.
“Abhipretya” means knowing. From the country of Brahmāvarta, the subjects went out to meet their lord.

“Yajña-puruṣa” means Viṣṇu. “Yataḥ” means “where,” the place in which he worshipped [Him]. “Bhuvam” means “place.” “Labdhā” ends in the tṛn suffix; its meaning is “having obtained.” Or, [the construction is] “he worshipped that Yajña-puruṣa from whom he obtained [the earthly] place.” By this it is said that earth is superior even to heaven, and that among [the places on earth] that place too is superior.
“He states what was introduced”: [the city] named Barhiṣmatī in which he dwelt. Having previously lived there, he entered that dwelling and enjoyed pleasures—this is the syntactic connection.
Without opposition to the other [aims] beginning with dharma. [He was one] whose good fame was sung at every dawn; nevertheless, he himself, listening to Hari’s own narrations, enjoyed pleasures.
“Yoga-māyā” means arrangements of desired pleasures. “Yat”/“yataḥ” means “from which”; “ābhraṁśayitum” means to make [him] fall even slightly, to overcome.

“Yāma” is [from] “gone”: that whose [essence] has gone is called yāta-yāma, like cooked food whose essence has gone; hence anything whose essence has gone is called yāta-yāma. They were ayāta-yāmas, their essence not gone. Those yāmas, divisions of time, caused his own interval—his Manvantara—to pass, while he listened to and meditated on Viṣṇu and performed and spoke [His] narratives.
“The three states of experience” means those beginning with waking, or [the three modes] beginning with sattva, which were overcome by him.
“Divyas” [means] atmospheric [afflictions]. “Mānuṣās” [means] arising from enemies. “Bhautikās” [means] arising from cold, heat, and so forth. “Vaiyāse” means “O son of Vyāsa! O Vidura!”
He states his superior knowledge with “yaḥ”: [he knew] the common duties of human beings.
His offspring is Devahūti; [hear] her rise and power.
In the Twenty-third [chapter], then, enjoyment is described in the desire-moving airplane created by yoga and endowed with every prosperity. “Prasthite” means when the departure has been undertaken.
“Dambha” means deceit. “Agha” means prohibited conduct. “Tejīyāṁsam” means exceedingly powerful.

“Suhṛt” means dear. “Not considered for my sake” means not counted [as something to be expended]. “Samucita” means praiseworthy; although worthy, it was disregarded because of attachment to my service—that is the meaning.

“Tapas,” “samādhi,” and “vidyā” are forms of worship; among them, ātma-yoga is one-pointedness of mind. By that, the Bhagavān’s favors—divine enjoyments—were obtained; behold those very [favors], now brought under your control too. I give you divine sight, by which you will see them. “What of the other enjoyments?” Nothing at all; they are exceedingly insignificant. The reason is that the arrangements of desires in them were broken by the raised brow of Bhagavān Urukrama. They are called “milked by one’s own dharma” because they are obtained through chastity. They are difficult to attain, [being obtained] through the transformations of us who are kings, the modifications for those respective enjoyments.

“All the yoga-māyās and vidyās” means worships of their respective objects; seeing her husband, expert in them, speaking thus, she became free of anxiety. “Saṁpraśraya” means humility and “praṇaya” means love; by these two she was overwhelmed. With a voice faltering, accompanied by a glance of slight bashfulness, she spoke, her face bearing a blossoming, smiling laugh.

“Bata” expresses joy. “Dvija-vṛṣa” means O best of the twice-born; “bhartaḥ” means O husband. “All this has been accomplished in you” means I know that it is already fulfilled in you. But may the condition you stated be fulfilled for the time being. “Sakṛt” means up to the mere occurrence of pregnancy. Since, when the husband is superior and is the cause [of offspring], childbirth is a great gain for women, and, with the compound reading, when the husband is superior, the birth and expansion of qualities occurs for chaste women, therefore, after the birth of a son has brought about the expansion of my qualities, let everything you said take place—this is the meaning.

“Aṅga-saṅga” means sexual union; he says that first the necessary preparation should be made: “O Lord, in that union, learn and arrange the procedure and means according to instruction, according to the science of love.” By that means—oil massage, food, drink, and so on—may this body of mine, emaciated and distressed by the intense desire to enjoy, become fit for sexual pleasure. [She is] one afflicted by the mind-born [god of love] whom you yourself have produced and agitated. “That” means then; consider an appropriate dwelling, that is, deliberate and think about it.
Then, at that very moment, he manifested [it].

He specifies that very [airplane] with the nine [verses] beginning “bestower of all desires.” It was furnished with all jewels and so forth. “Sarva-ṛddhīnām” means of all prosperities; “upacaya” is their accumulation, and “udarka” is the subsequent increase, that in which this occurs. “Upaskṛta” means beautified.
“Upary-upari” means in houses constructed one above another. “Kaśipu” means beds; [the airplane was] lovely with them, and lovely with couches and so forth.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.

“Dvās” means at the doors; the threshold made of coral is udumbara, and [the building] shone with it. It was furnished with doors set with diamonds. [This was] in the pinnacles—the upper parts of the palaces—made of sapphire.

“Cakṣuṣmat” means as though possessing eyes, [namely] those [walls] with the finest rubies; or, as though possessing eyes—by what? By the finest rubies. [It was] furnished with variegated canopies, groups of canopies.
“Kṛtrimān” means artificial [swans and pigeons] too; considering them their own kindred, [the residents] climbed them again and again, and [the airplane] resounded.

“Vihāra-sthāna” means a place for play; “viśrāma,” a sleeping chamber; “saṁveśa,” a place for enjoyment; “prāṅgaṇa,” outside the house; “ajira,” outside the enclosure. “Yathopajoṣam” means according to one’s own comfort; [the arrangement was] as though causing wonder even to himself.
“Nātiprītena” means not very pleased, because her body was dirty and because there were no attendants.
“In this lake” means in Bindu-saras. “Āruha” means climb. It was made by Śukla, Viṣṇu, by the falling of a drop of bliss. “Yāpaka” means one that conveys and brings [one to the desired result].
“Samādāya” means having brought [them]. “Sa-rajam” means soiled. “Veṇī-bhūtān” means matted [hair].

“Śabala” means variegated or discolored; “stanau” means the two breasts, [hence] that whose breasts were discolored. [It is a lake] in which the auspicious waters of Sarasvatī abide; or, one in which auspicious water-abodes and aquatic creatures abide.
“Sā” means she, having submerged there, saw a wonder. He speaks of it in ten [verses] beginning “in the lake’s interior.” “Utpala-gandhayaḥ” means fragrant like lotuses.
“Tubhyam” means to you. “Karma-karīḥ” means attendants. “Vayam” means we. The women said, “Command us,” that is, “Give us orders.”

Then, with bathing—with oil suitable for bathing and so forth. “Parārdhyāni” means excellent. “Varīyāṁsi” means very dear [to her]; “dyumanti” means shining. “Pāna” means a drink; “amṛta” means tasty; “āsava” means intoxicating.

“Ādarśe svam ātmānam”—the rest is [“she saw herself”]. The self is described by four [qualifications]. “Kṛta-svastyayana” means one for whom an auspicious rite has been performed. The masculine [form] is due to agreement with the word “ātman.”

“Virajam” [is explained as follows]. “Snātam” means washed after rubbing [with unguents]. “Kṛta-śiraḥ-snāna” means one by whom an oil bath has been performed. [The phrase] means simply adorned. “Niṣka” means a pendant; one who has it on the neck.

[The golden girdle] is one on which there are many jewels. “Rucaka” means an auspicious substance, such as kuṅkuma. This is stated in the Viśvaprakāśa: “Rucaka [is used] for an auspicious substance, a neck ornament, and teeth.”

“Sudatā,” “subhruvā,” and “cakṣuṣā” are singular forms. By these, [her] face was shining. What kind of eye? One whose side-glance was smooth, charming, and moist. “Padma-kośa-spṛt” means one that competes with a lotus bud, from “it competes with a lotus bud.”
“Having seen” [is understood], and when she remembered her husband, the ṛṣabha, beloved of sages, then wherever he was, there she herself also remained.
“Seeing herself,” [means] seeing herself; and seeing his yoga-power, she [was filled with] the wonder, “What is this?”

In that airplane the sage shone. “His majesty was not diminished” means that his independence was not diminished. “Upacīrṇa” means served; [he was] one whose body had been served. [He was] exceedingly beautiful, like [a sky] filled with blossoming water-lilies. The sage is to be understood as like the full moon, the airplane like the sky, those women like stars, and their eyes like water-lilies.

By that airplane [he traveled] through the valleys and caves of Meru, the chief of mountains in which the eight Lokapālas sport. [He sported] among places whose beauty came from a cool, fragrant, gentle wind, the friend of Kāma, and which were praised by Siddhas; they had an auspicious sound from the descent of the celestial river Gaṅgā. He sported with a troop of women, a collection of jewels among women.
In the divine gardens beginning with Vaiśrambhaka, and in Mānasa Lake, he was delighted.
“Atyaśeta” means having passed beyond; he remained [there].
“Uddāma-cetasām” means of the steadfast, whose minds are exalted. “Vyasana” means saṁsāra; “atyaya” means its destruction, from which [it occurs].

“Prekṣayitvā” means having shown. “Gola” means a sphere. “As extensive as it is through its own arrangement” means as extensive as the arrangement of islands, varṣas, and so forth. [It is] that in which there are many wonders.
“Navadhā” means dividing into nine, making the self into nine forms.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.
“Śaradaḥ” means years. “Vyatīyuḥ” means they passed as if in a little while.

Regarding [Devahūti] with great affection as his own self, in the form of half his body. When that was so, good offspring would arise. “Nava-dhā” means ninefold. “Knower of every resolve” means knowing her wish for many children. “Vibhu” means capable of doing so. “Knower of the self” [indicates] that, being unattached to her, he produced daughters; this is the meaning. According to the Smṛti, a male results when the male’s semen is predominant, and a female when the female’s is predominant.
Immediately thereafter; on the very same day. [They were] ones whose every limb was beautiful.
Observing that he was about to renounce, she smiled outwardly, but inwardly, with a distressed, agitated, tormented heart, she spoke—this is the syntactic connection with what follows.
The nails themselves were jewels; by their splendor her foot was beautiful, and she wrote on the earth with that foot, indicating boundless anxiety.
“Upovāha” means fulfilled or accomplished. “Fearlessness” means: may he remove the fear arising from future misery and from saṁsāra.

Here she expresses her distress. [She is distressed thinking that] suitable husbands equal to herself must be sought by your daughters themselves. Accepting the fear of saṁsāra, she says “someone.” “For freedom from sorrow” means for instruction in knowledge. Since debts are discharged through [having] children, might there be, through your remaining here for some time, a son who knows Brahman? That is the meaning.

If [someone says], “Enjoy sense objects; what need is there of knowledge of Brahman?”—there she says, “Let there be enough of this; let it be fulfilled.” “By which the higher Self was abandoned”—such am I.
While lamenting what she herself had done, she speaks [the next] four verses, beginning “in sense objects.” “Me” means by me. “The supreme state” means: you are a knower of Brahman.
How may this association be for fearlessness? In that regard she says “association”: through knowledge of Adhiyajña.

The action that proceeds by its own nature, if it is not for dharma, does not become directed toward dharma; even if it is [directed toward dharma], if it does not become a means to detachment through desireless dharma, then through that [detachment] it would not culminate in service of Hari, whose feet are a holy place. That is the meaning.
“Na mumukṣeya” means “I have not desired to be released; I have not made a desire for liberation.”

In the Twenty-fourth [chapter], then, he tells of Kapila’s birth and of his father’s renunciation after giving him permission, upon release from the three debts. “Śālinī” means praiseworthy. “Spoken by Śukla” refers to “Together with me, with my own portion and partial manifestation” [3.21.32], and so forth.
“Do not grieve thus” means do not feel, regarding yourself, “I am unfortunate.” “Adūrāt” means quickly.
By “dama,” sense restraint; by “niyama,” one’s own dharma; and by austerities and gifts of wealth [worship Him].

“Heart-knot” means the bondage marked by ego and consisting of conscious and inert [elements]. “Cutter” means he will cut it. “Audarya” [means] as a son. [He is called] one who causes Brahman to be contemplated because he teaches [Brahman].
“With faith” means believing.
“Bahu-tithe” means after much [time]; “kāle” means when time had passed; “kārdamam” means relating to Kardama.
“Ghanāghanā” is one word. [They were] rain-bearing clouds. “Gāyanti” means they sang; “nṛtyanti,” they danced.
“Apavarjitā” means released.
“Pariśritam” means surrounded.

Having come, what did he do? He says this in the two verses beginning “Bhagavantam.” For the purpose of distinctly teaching the Sāṅkhya in which the elements are enumerated, Brahmā—unborn, self-ruling, and possessing knowledge established by itself—worshipped the Bhagavān who had taken birth and, with his senses gladdened, addressed Kardama thus; this is the syntactic connection of the two [verses]. By the conjunction “ca,” Devahūti too [is included].

Here, with five verses beginning “by you,” he addresses Kardama: “Apaciti” means worship has been performed. “Yat” means because. “Nirvyalīkataḥ” means without deceit; “samyag gṛhītavān,” he accepted properly.
“Anumanyeta” means “he should consent”; “yad etāvaty eva” [means] only in this much.
“Anekadhā” means in many ways. “Prabhāvaiḥ” means by powers; “vaṁśaiḥ,” by lineages; “bṛṁhayiṣyanti” means they will increase.
“To the foremost sages” means to Marīci and the others.
But the son is directly the Lord—that is why he says “I know.” “Śevadhi” means treasure, the bestower of all desired things.

He addresses Devahūti in three [verses]. “Jñāna” is stated in scripture; “vijñāna” is direct perception; those two are the means called yoga. By them he will uproot the tangle of karma, whose roots are latent impressions. [He is] one whose lotus feet are marked with a lotus. “O daughter of Manu!” “Avidyā” means ignorance of one’s own nature; “saṁśaya” means false cognitions; your heart-knot is made of these.
“Susaṁmata” means being greatly honored. “Gantā” means he will attain [the name and fame].

“With the Kumāras” is understood. “Saha-Nārada” means together with Nārada. Having arranged Marīci and the others for marriage, Brahmā, Haṁsa, went together with these five naiṣṭhika [sons]. “Tri-dhāma” means the third abode, heaven, and its highest limit, Satyaloka.
“Śatadhṛti” means Brahmā.
“Vitan-yate” means expanded or made prosperous. [The phrase refers to] the presiding deity of peace. “Samalālayat” means he satisfied [them].
“Nimantrya” means having invited or asked. “Nandi” means happiness; [they] attained joy.
“Sa ca muniḥ” means he, the sage. “Tri-yugam” means Viṣṇu. “Vivikte” means in a secluded place.
“Pāpac्यमānānām” means of those being intensely burned. “Niraya” means saṁsāra. “Svīyair amaṅgalaiḥ” means by their own sins.

Why [is this rare]? It is known that all the deities are pleased; he says this is the gain of what is otherwise unattainable in the two [verses]. “Ripened through many births” means fully perfected [devotion]. “Perfect yoga” means bhakti-yoga; in it samādhi is one-pointedness; by that [they attain]. “Śūnyāgāra” means secluded places. [They strive to see] your position. “Helana” means disregard, treating lightly; “not counting” means not considering. He says, “This is indeed proper for you”: you nourish the side of your own devotees, therefore [you are] so [situated].
He expands this in two verses. You have personally descended to fulfill your own word, “I will become your son.” He desires to produce knowledge and Sāṅkhya, that is, to teach them.

“Yāni” means your non-worldly forms beginning with four arms; those very forms are suitable to you. And whatever forms please your own people, human-like forms, those too please you, although you are without a material form.
One whose footstool is worthy of salutation. “Pūrta” means full, filled with opulence and so forth.

Explaining the opulence and so forth, he says “supreme,” the Supreme Lord. The reason is that his powers are independent. He explains them: “Pradhāna” is the form of primordial nature; “puruṣa,” its presiding one; “mahān,” the form of the mahat-tattva; “kāla,” the agitator of these; “tri-vṛt,” the form of ego, both consisting of the world and of its protector. Having stated his form as pradhāna and the rest through māyā, he states his being beyond the world through the conscious power: [he is] one in whom the universe, followed by the conscious power, is dissolved into himself. “Kavi” means omniscient; [he is] the witness of the manifestation and dissolution of pradhāna and the rest.

He prays for permission to renounce. “Ā sma abhipṛcche” means I ask something. Since the debts have been relieved by your descent in the form of a son, I am fulfilled; adopting the path of the wandering renouncers, I will wander while meditating on you and remembering you.

At any rate I have descended into your home precisely to teach knowledge; therefore liberation is easy even while I remain in your home. If you insist that I must go, then go while remembering me—this is the intention with which he speaks in the six verses beginning “by me.” “Satya-laukika” means in a Vedic and worldly act. He shows the authority of his own statement: since I said to you, “I will become your son,” therefore I was born in such a way that that became true.

“Know [this]” is to be connected with the second [verse]: [my birth is] for the enumeration of the elements approved for self-realization by sages seeking liberation from defective subtle bodies. [Objection:] Is this path of knowledge of the self not already established, so that it need not now be promulgated as something new? He answers, “This”: it has become unmanifest, subtle.

“Kāmam” means as you wish. “Āpṛṣṭa” means permitted. Or, just as you asked me to go, I too ask you to remain here. With action surrendered to me, cross death through ignorance and attain immortality through knowledge, as the śruti says.
Thereafter, seeing me—the supreme Paramātmā—in your own self by your self, you will attain fearlessness, liberation.
[He will give it] to the mother, Devahūti. “Pacifying” means uprooting. “He will cross fear” means he will cross it completely; the conjunction “ca” also indicates that he will attain supreme bliss.
“Samudita” means properly spoken. “Having made him the object of circumambulation.”
This is the vow of sages: silence characterized by nonviolence.
[He is] in Brahman, that which is beyond the real and unreal. “Guṇāvabhāsaka” means the one who illumines the modes, [yet is] without modes. By unwavering devotion he is made directly perceived.

Therefore he is free from ego and the rest concerning the body and so forth. Thus “free from duality” means unaffected by cold, heat, and so forth. “Seeing equally” means not apprehending distinctions, but “seeing oneself” means seeing only the self. He is turned inward; his intellect is calm and free from distraction.

Having spoken of the removal of imagined limiting adjuncts of this kind, he speaks of attaining the position of the Supreme Lord in the three verses beginning “Vāsudeva.” “Pratīcaḥ” means of the individual soul; “ātmani” means in the Self; “labdhātmā” means one whose mind has attained the Self; “mukta-bandhanam” means one whose bondage, ignorance, is removed.
He states that attainment of the self with “ātmanam.”
Thus, by him, the Bhagavatī path has been attained. In another reading: “He alone attained that path.”

In the Twenty-fifth [chapter], asked by the mother about release from bondage, Kapila, her son, first speaks of supreme devotion. The jewel-box of yoga, entrusted by Kapila to his mother and controlled by a hidden meaning, is now clearly opened. He asks about Kapila’s yoga, after the preceding translation, in three verses beginning “Kapila.” “Tattvānāṁ saṅkhyātā” means the enumerator of the principles, the initiator of Sāṅkhya. Hence “born by himself.” “Ātma-prajñaptaye” means for teaching the truth of the self.

“Varṣmanah” means [the greatness] among men, of the mature and highest [person]; among all yogis, “varimṇaḥ” means of the most excellent. Or, [it means] because of superiority. “Viśrutau” means in fame. “Asavaḥ” means the senses; they are not satisfied by much [hearing]. In “Śruta-deva,” “śrutena” means by hearing, and “dīvyati” means shines; or, [he is] one by whom the god is heard repeatedly; this is also connected with “me asavaḥ.”
“Svānām” means of men; “chandena,” by will; [he is] one whose body is according to [their] will. Whatever action he performs, repeat those actions worthy of glorification.
Being prompted as you prompt me, [I shall reply] according to those questions, in ānvīkṣikī, knowledge of the self.
“Bindu-sara” means Bindu-saras, the lake.

“Tattva-mārgasyāgram” means the end of the path of truth; [he is] one who shows it. [She remembers] the Creator’s words, “O daughter of Manu, this slayer of Kaitabha has entered your womb,” and so forth.
From the thirsting of the unreal senses, I am greatly wearied; “nirviṇṇā” means I am weary from desires for sense objects. “Yena sambhāvyamānena” means by which, when it is being fulfilled.
“Pāra-ga” means one who takes [me] to the far shore; you alone are the excellent eye acquired by me. “At the end of births” means when [that] is to be attained, through your grace.
“Sa Bhagavān” and “bhavān” [are] the same; [you are] the eye-form risen Sun.

“Apākraṣṭum” means to remove. What is that delusion? The insistence, “I and mine,” applied by you alone to this body and so forth. The second word “iti” signifies grasping its effects, beginning with attachment.
With the desire to know nature and the person, having taken shelter of you, I bow—this is the syntactic connection. “Kuṭhāra” means cutter.
“Apavarga-vardhanam” means increasing liberation, producing delight in liberation. [She is one] whose face is beautified by a slight smile.
“Adhyātmika” means fixed in the self. “Yatra” means in which.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.

Showing that mastery of all the limbs depends on control of the mind, he says “mind.” “Asya ātmanaḥ” means of this individual; “guṇeṣu,” in the sense objects; “pumsi,” in the Supreme Person; the word “vā” has the force of “but.”

How attainment of the human goal occurs through control of the mind, he shows in three verses beginning “I.” “Vīta” means separated from impurities; when the mind is pure, he indicates that purification with “free from suffering.”
“Nirantara” means without difference. “Aṇimāna” means subtle. “Akhaṇḍita” means undivided, unlimited.
“Hatāujasa” means with its power diminished.
With purity of mind, devotion itself is the inner means; he says this with “not.”
The association of saintly persons is the root of all this; he says this with “association.” “Apāvṛta” means unobstructed, uncovered.

He states the characteristics of saintly persons in four verses beginning “forbearing.” “Sādhavaḥ” means those who follow scripture. “Sādhu” means good conduct; that itself is the ornament of those who possess it. “Etān” means these devotees with the stated characteristics. “Tāpa” means afflictions beginning with the adhyātmika; they do not torment them. Why? Their minds are fixed in me. Those who are not overcome by afflictions are called saintly persons; that is the meaning.

He establishes that association with saintly persons is a limb of devotion. “Vīrya-saṁvidaḥ” means those [narrations] in which there is full knowledge of [the Lord’s] power. [They are] nectar for the heart and ears, bringing happiness. By serving them, [one follows] Hari, in whom liberation—the removal of ignorance—is the path. First comes faith, then taste, then devotion, in sequence; that is the meaning.

Then what? He says: through devotion characterized by contemplation of my creation and the rest of my pastimes, one becomes dispassionate from sensory happiness, from what is seen and heard in this world and the next. Then, being intent, he strives to hold the mind. “Straightforward” means easy, because devotion is predominant.
Thus, by not serving the modes of nature and by knowledge and the rest, this living being obtains me here itself, in the body.

“Kācit” means “some” or “which indeed.” “Ucita” means suitable. For a woman, what kind of devotion is it? “Gocara” means suitable, within reach. “Nirvāṇa” means liberation; “your position” means your own nature; “anvāśnavai” means I shall attain it immediately and with my whole self. In the reading “añjasā,” the connection is “I, however.”
“Bhagavad-bāṇa” means that which makes Bhagavān the target. “Yataḥ” means because of which yoga.
“Vijānīhi” means explain distinctly. “Sukham” means without difficulty.

Knowing thus the purpose of his mother, he [spoke]. The reason for his becoming affectionate [is explained]: “Yatra” means in which, “tanvā,” by the body, he manifested. In which the principles are taught in sequence. What is that? The Sāṅkhya they proclaim; he taught devotion in its expansion and yoga.

He defines the supreme devotion asked about in “Some devotion suitable for you.” “Guṇāḥ” means the objects known through which; “devānām” means the luminous senses or their presiding deities; “sattve” means in Hari, whose nature is pure goodness; the activity there alone is devotion, and it is greater even than liberation. What is it like? “Animittā” means without desire for fruit. “Svābhāvikī” means established without effort. He states the cause of such activity: the Veda is that which is heard after the teacher’s recitation; what is prescribed by it is “ānuśravika,” and that alone is the action of those [devotees]. Therefore their mind is one, unchanged, being of pure goodness. He says that liberation too becomes incidental: devotion destroys the sheath, the subtle body, just as the gastric fire digests swallowed food, without one’s own effort.

He establishes the supreme position of devotion in five verses beginning “not oneness.” “Ekatmatā” means sāyujya liberation. “Activity for my sake” means actions whose purpose is me. “Prasajya” means having made attachment. “Pauruṣāṇi” means powers.
[They have] cheerful eyes, and [are] together with forms of me. The meaning is that the happiness of constant experience of the Supreme Lord is greater in devotion.

He says that self-bliss will certainly arise: “by them.” “Darśanīya” means charming; “limbs” means faces, eyes, and so forth. “Hṛtātmā” means those whose minds are captured; “hṛtāḥ prāṇāḥ,” those whose senses are captured. To those who worship [me], he grants, even without desire, the subtle path, liberation. By what means? By generous pastimes and so forth. Here “vilāsa” means play; “vāma,” charming; “sūkta,” sweet speech.

He says that the opulence and so forth there are greater. After the removal of ignorance, “vibhūti” means the wealth of enjoyment in Satyaloka and so forth; the eightfold powers beginning with aṇimā, although naturally attained as devotion follows; and the Bhagavatī prosperity situated in Vaikuṇṭha. They do not long for these—although they do not long for them, they nevertheless attain them in the world, Vaikuṇṭha.

[Objection:] If this is so, then because it is a world, as with heaven and so forth, might there sometimes be destruction of the enjoyers and enjoyed objects? [He answers:] O one whose form is peace! Or, “peace” means pure goodness; in Vaikuṇṭha of that form, those devoted to me never perish and do not become without objects of enjoyment. “My unfailing weapon” means my wheel of time; it does not consume them. The reason is that they worship me in every relation—as a son, as a friend, as a teacher, as a well-wisher, and as a cherished deity. Those who worship me with every attitude are not consumed by my wheel of time; that is the meaning.

He says that there is no liberation for nondevotees, even somehow, with “not.” “Apart from me, Bhagavān” means apart from Bhagavān, apart from me. “The Self of all beings” means the Self. By the three adjectives beginning with Bhagavān, his power, independence, and beneficence are stated.
He makes the opulence explicit with “from fear of me.” The śruti also says: “From fear of him the wind blows; from fear the sun rises; from fear fire, the moon, and Death, fifth, run.”
Here, where liberation comes only from worship of me, he establishes good conduct as authority with “by knowledge.”
He concludes with “so much.” “Offered to me” means that the mind becomes steady; “this alone is so much” means this alone is all.

In the twenty-sixth [chapter], discrimination between the person and nature is described through Sāṅkhya, by the differences of origin and characteristics of all things. What was spoken by the creator to his son, and what was spoken by Kṣattṛ to Mitrā’s son—this Sāṅkhya concerning the self the knower of truth chiefly speaks to his mother. In the statement that they call the tradition of principles “Sāṅkhya,” three things—Sāṅkhya, devotion, and yoga—are introduced. Having spoken of devotion, he now speaks of Sāṅkhya with “then.”

“Knowledge” means knowledge in the form of seeing the self; therefore it is the cutting of the heart-knot and the removal of ego. I shall describe to you what they say is for the highest good. The meaning is that distinct knowledge of the self arises only from knowledge of the characteristics of the principles.

Here he defines the person with “beginningless.” The self alone is the person. What is that self? It is one whose radiance is inward-directed. “Beginningless” excludes the view that consciousness is momentary. “Beyond nature” excludes the view that it is subject to saṁsāra. It is another, unattached. “Without qualities” excludes the view that knowledge and the rest are its qualities. “Self-luminous” excludes the view held by Mīmāṁsakas and others that it is an object of knowledge; by this, the Prābhākara view that it shines as the substrate of knowledge is also rejected. The reason for being self-luminous is “by whom the universe is pervaded”: [the universe] shines, this is understood. By these very reasons, the person’s being beyond nature is also established.

Here nature is twofold through the distinction of the covering and projecting powers. Through the covering power it is the ignorance that is the limiting adjunct of the living being; through the projecting power it is the supreme Lord’s māyā. The person is also twofold as the living being and the Lord. One who transmigrates through non-discrimination from nature is the living being; one who controls nature and performs the creation of the universe and so forth is the Lord. He describes the process of the living being’s saṁsāra through non-discrimination from nature in the five [verses] beginning “this very.” “Subtle, unmanifest, divine” means the power of Lord Viṣṇu, which he approached in play and accepted by chance alone—this is the syntactic connection.

He describes her play with “through the qualities.” Through that power, which conceals knowledge, she is called the concealer of knowledge. Thus the Śvetāśvatara śruti speaks of the unborn one, red, white, and black, who produces many offspring through the qualities, and of the unborn one who enjoys her and the other who leaves her after enjoying her. “He became bewildered” means that he forgot the self.
“Meditation on the other” means superimposition of nature; through that, when actions are being performed by nature’s qualities, he thinks agency exists in the self.

“That” means the very thinking of agency. For this person, although he is truly inactive because he is only a witness, bondage through actions arises. Although the Lord is independent, dependence in enjoyment produced by bondage to action, and transmigration—the stream of birth and death—of the self whose nature is happiness, all this arises from non-discrimination from nature; that is the meaning.

It may be objected that because agency and the rest are perceived in a common locus with consciousness, they should be accepted as belonging to the self. He says no. “Effect” means the body; “cause,” the senses; “agent,” the class of deities. When these states are reached, they know nature to be the cause of the person. Since the immutable has no change by itself, agency and the rest are produced by ego in the body and the rest, which are transformations of nature. But in enjoyment they know the person to be the cause. The meaning is this: although agency and enjoyment are located in ego, because the transformation ends in inert matter the limiting adjunct is predominant, while because enjoyment ends in consciousness the associated self is predominant.

Having thus known the transmigrating person and nature, its cause, he now asks about the Lord, the cause of the world, and his nature, with “of nature.” “Of this universe” means of the gross and subtle effect, both real and unreal, whose essence is the two—nature and person.

Here he defines nature. Whatever is the pradhāna, that they call nature. What is that pradhāna? It is intrinsically undifferentiated, yet the support of differentiated things. Then is it Brahman? No, it has three qualities. Is it the mahat-tattva and so forth? No, it is unmanifest and not an effect. Is it time and so forth? No, it has the form of effect and cause, consisting of the real and unreal. Is the living being nature? No, [the living being is] eternal.

He counts those [principles] in order to state the characteristics of the other principles, beginning with “five.” Through difference of number, this is the twenty-fourfold collection; they know that collection in which these twenty-four are present as the prādhānika, consisting of the pradhāna and its effects, as Brahman.
He explains this in three [verses] beginning “the great elements.” There are exactly that many, five.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.
“Internal self” means the inner instrument. “By the form of characteristics” means by the distinguishing form.

As much as was stated by me, just that much is counted by the knowers of truth. Regarding time, he states two opinions: “that time is the twenty-fifth.” The k-a affix has the sense of smallness. The meaning is that it is a particular state of nature itself.

Some, however, call the power of the person, the Lord’s force, splendor, and might, “time.” He defines that same time in two ways: it is that from which fear arises. From whom? From one who has reached nature; therefore from the agent, the living being, bewildered by ego in the body. By this it is characterized as the destroyer.
He defines it through being the cause of creation, with “of nature.”

Who is this Lord? He says with “within.” Within all living beings, this Lord is fully present, free from transformation, in the form of the person as the inner controller; and outside he is this Lord in the form of time. Or, the well-known “person” is the twenty-fifth, time. Some call the power of the person time. “From which” is the definition of power. The reason the person itself is time is “of nature.” The reason when both interpretations are intended is “within”; the rest is the same. Thus nature has twenty-four divisions. When unity of the living being and the Lord is intended, there are twenty-five principles; when their difference is intended, there are twenty-six.

Now he states the characteristics along with the origin of the principles, beginning with “by destiny,” using the preceding text beginning “without combining them.” Here he states the characteristics before the arising of mind in four [verses]. “By destiny” means by the living being’s unseen result; [nature is] whose qualities are agitated in the place of manifestation, the womb, nature. “Semen” means conscious power. That nature produced the mahat-tattva. He states the form of mahat: “golden,” abundant in light.

“Universe” means the manifestation beginning with ego. “Situated in the self” means revealing it, which was situated in him in subtle form. The great one drank the intense darkness of the time of dissolution. “Immutable” means free from dissolution and projection. What kind of darkness? That which puts the self to sleep, conceals it. The meaning is that previously, at the time of dissolution, he caused the great principle to merge into nature.

Incidentally he speaks of worship of the fourfold manifestation with “that which.” He states its fame in all scriptures with “clear”: clear, distinct; “peaceful”: free from attachment and the rest; “the position of Bhagavān”: the place of attainment. Therefore they call it by the name Vāsudeva. The meaning is: in the adhibhūta form it is called mahat; in the adhyātma form, citta; in the worshipable form, Vāsudeva; its presiding knower is the field-knower. Similarly, in ego Saṅkarṣaṇa is worshipable and Rudra presides; in mind Aniruddha is worshipable and the moon presides; in intellect Pradyumna is worshipable and Brahmā presides.

“Clarity” means the capacity to receive the image of Bhagavān. “Immutability” means freedom from dissolution and projection. “Nature of water” means its state free of foam, waves, and so forth. “Supreme” means prior to contact with earth; just as it is sweet, clear, and peaceful, so [is the mind].

Indicating that his continuation [of grace] is by mercy alone, and showing his compassion even toward those who harm him, he says: “Ah, what a wonder of compassion!” Although she wished to kill him, he drank the kāla-kūṭa poison collected in her breasts. The wicked Pūtanā, though evil, attained the proper destination of Yaśodā through the nurse’s guise; that is the meaning: merely by the appearance of a devotee he granted the good destination. Whom else, then, should we worship?

It is famous that Bhagavān favors the devotees alone. True—but I consider even the demons devotees, because, like devotees, through intense absorption of mind in meditation on Bhagavān they too see Bhagavān directly. “Those whose minds were fixed on that path through anger” means those whose minds were absorbed through anger. Therefore, in battle, they saw him with Garuḍa, the son of Kaśyapa, as his carrier on the shoulder, and with the discus Sudarśana as his weapon. Therefore favor toward them too is proper. He will say later: “By any means one should fix the mind on Kṛṣṇa.”

Now, to explain the manner of his disappearance, he tells briefly, beginning at the outset, that story: he was born from a wife of Vasudeva; Bhojarāja Kaṃsa was in his prison; wishing himself to bring happiness to this earth, he was entreated by the unborn Brahmā.

He states the characteristic with “agency” and so forth: agency is in the form of the deities and the rest; instrumentality is in the form of the senses; effect-ness is in the form of the elements; and peacefulness and the rest are in the form of the three qualities of the respective causes.

He states the characteristic of the mind along with its origin in the two [verses] beginning “from the vaikārika.” Saṅkalpa is thought; vikalpa is particularized thought. Since desire arises in the mind through saṅkalpa and vikalpa, a modification in the form of desire is stated as its characteristic—not the arising of the Pradyumna manifestation, because that is not an effect of saṅkalpa and so forth, and the worshipable manifestation Aniruddha has already been stated.
“Śārada” means belonging to autumn; [it is] dark like the indīvara, the blue lotus. It is capable of being gradually worshipped and brought under control because it is difficult to grasp.

He states the characteristic of the intellect along with its origin in the two [verses] beginning “from the taijasa.” O chaste one, “knowledge” in the form of the shining forth of an object is stated in order to distinguish it from citta. “The favor of the senses” means determinate knowledge. “The supreme lord of the senses” refers to indeterminate knowledge.

The manifestation of the shining forth of an object is doubt and the rest. Inversion is false knowledge; certainty is knowledge from a valid means; sleep is slumber. This follows the Pātañjala statement: “The modifications are valid knowledge, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory.”

He states the origin of the senses: they are taijasa, born from the taijasa ego. The emphatic “alone” removes the doubt that the knowledge-senses are vaikārika; both kinds of senses are taijasa. The reason is that the activity-power belongs to prāṇa and the knowledge-power to intellect. Therefore, because prāṇa is taijasa, the senses endowed with its activity-power are taijasa; and because intellect is taijasa, the senses endowed with its knowledge-power are taijasa—that is the meaning.

He states the origin of the gross elements after the origin of the subtle elements, and their characteristics, in the fifteen [verses] beginning “from the tāmasa.” In statements such as “the ear goes to sound,” after the origin of the objects has been stated, only their relation is being described, not their origin, because they have already arisen. “It goes to sound” means it reaches or obtains sound.

He states the characteristic of sound. “Being the support of an object” means being the support of meaning; “being the speaker of an object” means denoting an object. “Being a sign of the seer” means being an indicator to a speaker hidden behind a wall. Thus it is said: a sign is that which relates the seer and the seen. The syntactic connection is that the subtle-element nature of space means subtlety, while the characteristic of sound is as stated.

He states the characteristic of space with “of the elements.” Giving openings means giving room. Being the basis of external and internal dealings means being their locus. “Self” means mind. Being the seat of prāṇa and the rest means being their support in the form of openings such as channels. Activity itself is the characteristic, the characteristic called activity. Hereafter too, it should be understood that one verse states the origin of the subtle element and gross element, the second its subtle-element characteristic, and the third the gross-element characteristic.

What is skin? It is that by which touch is rightly gathered or apprehended. Its being masculine is because its gender is fixed. Or, the meaning is that the gathering of touch proceeds from it. The statement beginning “from the sound subtle element” is made to convey the successive connection of the subtle elements.
He states the characteristic of touch with “softness.” “Being touch” means its essential characteristic; that is, the subtle-element nature of wind is also [stated].

Movement is the movement of a tree branch and the like. Arrangement is the joining of grass and the like. Attainment is the contact of a substance possessing smell with the nose, and likewise of a substance possessing coldness and the rest with the sense of touch. Sound’s leading to the ear is its relation to the ear. Being the self of all the senses means being their energizing principle. It is characterized by action, by the effect; the suffix [in the word] has the sense of an instrument. Alternatively, when analyzed as “action itself is the characteristic,” it has the sense of an instrument.

“Having the form of a substance” means giving a substance its form. Being a quality means being perceived as subsidiary to a substance. Sound, however, is perceived independently; even touch and the rest of an imperceptible substance are perceived independently, but color is not, and this special statement is therefore made. “Having the form of an individual” means that the arrangement belonging to an individual substance is itself the arrangement, perceived as a transformation. The fieriness of fire is its distinctive nature.
Illumination means making manifest; cooking means cooking rice and the like. Hunger, thirst, eating, and drinking occur through it.
The tongue is the sense of taste. “Taste is apprehended by it” means that taste is grasped by the tongue; or, the meaning is that the apprehension of taste proceeds from it.

Salt too should be understood among the bitter, astringent, and other tastes. [Taste belongs to] physical substances that are conjoined. Although one [taste] is sweet alone, it is divided in many ways; that is the meaning of taste.

Wetting means making moist. Making a lump means making earth and the like into a lump. Satisfaction means the giving of satisfaction. Giving life means living, according to the smṛti “life is made of water”; quenching means removing the distress of thirst. Softening means making soft. Even with the reading “ondana,” the meaning is the same. Increase means arising again and again from a well and the like even after what was drawn out has been removed.
The nose reaches smell.

Among mixed and other odors, salt-like [or saline] odor too should be considered. A mixed odor is a combination of smells, as in seasonings prepared with asafoetida and the like; foulness is a bad smell; fragrance is that of camphor and the like; mildness is that of the hundred-petaled lotus; pungency is that of garlic; sourness is that of tamarind and the like. Because the parts of conjoined substances differ and so forth, odors are differentiated in this way; that is the meaning.

Making Brahman manifest means giving it form through an image and the like. “Place” means standing as an independent support, unlike water and the rest. “Holding” means being the support of water and the rest. Being a qualifier of existent things such as space means being delimitiveness. The manifestation of all beings, living creatures, and their qualities such as masculinity is the making visible, through transformations without distinction.

The capacity of the ear and the other senses to grasp sound and the rest has already been stated; he says that their characteristic is the same in five half-verses. Sound is the special quality of space whose object is meaning.

He shows what is excluded by “special quality” and “sound” with “of the higher.” The property of the higher, the cause—sound and the rest—is seen in the lower, the effect, such as wind, because the cause inheres in the effect. Therefore every special quality of entities such as space, sound and the rest, is found only in earth, because four [elements] inhere there. In water and the other elements, [the qualities are present] only according to their connection, not all of them; in space, because there is no connection with the others, there is only one.

Having stated the origin of the causes, he now states the origin of the effects in three and a half verses. When these [elements] stood uncombined, not joined, the Lord, the origin of the world, entered. “Seven” is stated with the principal-elements intended; entry into all [the elements] is nevertheless intended.
From the agitated or combined [elements], this cosmic Person arose from the egg.
“The form of Bhagavān” is stated with the intention that [the cosmic Person] is non-different from the Person.
